content.content:
1	---
2	subject: Unintended AI Experiments 150 Agents 2 Useful Insights
3	date: 2026-07-21
4	---
5	
6	The past couple of weeks have been full, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course (CAN-BIKE 4). I’ve been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. I had much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won’t try to find a clever Agile analogy from this. GenAI gives me plenty to noodle on, so let’s go there instead.
7	
8	If your current feelings on GenAI are, it’s a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I’m going to touch on a few AI-related topics in this issue, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).
9	
10	## Canadian Government AI Strategy
11	Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.
12	
13	The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar “Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity”. When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they’re measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I’m sure we’ve all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.
14	
15	The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada’s AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).
16	
17	Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.
18	
19	I’m also thinking that we will see a lot of “AI Washing” in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.
20	
21	## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
22	In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week’s model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).
23	
24	I’ve had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.
25	
26	### Fable Security Audit
27	Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I’m building an application and I’m not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait for it to reset that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 
28	
29	The frontier labs don’t generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the [same league as Claude Opus 4.8](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/comparisons/kimi-k3-vs-claude-opus-4-8). The [Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters](https://www.kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3). Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.
30	
31	### Opus Research Task
32	I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for “deep research” - don’t do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. ---
subject: Unintended AI Experiments 150 Agents 2 Useful Insights
date: 2026-07-21
---

The past couple of weeks have been full, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course (CAN-BIKE 4). I’ve been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. I had much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won’t try to find a clever Agile analogy from this. GenAI gives me plenty to noodle on, so let’s go there instead.

If your current feelings on GenAI are, it’s a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I’m going to touch on a few AI-related topics in this issue, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).

## Canadian Government AI Strategy
Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.

The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar “Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity”. When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they’re measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I’m sure we’ve all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.

The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada’s AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).

Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.

I’m also thinking that we will see a lot of “AI Washing” in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.

## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week’s model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).

I’ve had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.

### Fable Security Audit
Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I’m building an application and I’m not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait for it to reset that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 

The frontier labs don’t generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the [same league as Claude Opus 4.8](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/comparisons/kimi-k3-vs-claude-opus-4-8). The [Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters](https://www.kimi.com/blog/kimi-k3). Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.

### Opus Research Task
I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for “deep research” - don’t do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my usage limit and I had to wait for it to reset that evening to finish the task.

For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with real depth. Instead, I got a 3-page report with two good insights.

Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can’t mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.

## Big Ask
One of the two insights from Opus’s Research Task? Ask your newsletter readers for referrals. To quote Opus: “single most effective newsletter growth strategy is **direct recommendations from existing subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral)**”. I’m supposed to offer you a discount or a free trial in return. In practice, I can’t see what I would offer at the moment.

If you get value from this newsletter, please share it with a friend. If someone shared it with you, [click here to subscribe](https://agilepainrelief.com/newsletter-subscribe/).

## Reading Rabbit Hole
- [The Echo Chamber in Your Pocket](https://c3.unu.edu/blog/the-echo-chamber-in-your-pocket) - Ng Chong - research on how sycophantic chatbots that always agree can deepen belief in false ideas and make users more self-centred.
- [Canada’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all) - Government of Canada - the official draft strategy full of nice words and little substance.
- [Draft federal AI strategy aims to scale up adoption, offer literacy training by 2031](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/federal-artificial-intelligence-strategy-9.7216576) - Kate McKenna, CBC - the broadcaster’s coverage of the draft, which cuts through some of the bafflegab.

Cheers
Mark

1	---
2	title: "GenAI Won't Speed Up Your Scrum Events (and Shouldn't)"
3	date: "2026-06-10"
4	lastUpdated: '2026-06-10'
5	draft: false
6	categories:
7	  - "artificial-intelligence"
8	  - "scrum-events-and-artifacts"
9	excerpt: 'A faster Scrum event doesn’t build shared understanding; it skips it. An event-by-event guide to using GenAI as a thinking partner rather than a shortcut, with the guardrails that keep collaboration intact.'
10	coverImage: '@/content/blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/images/AI-Generated-User-Stories.png'
11	---
12	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
13	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
14	import AiNewsletterSignup from '@/components/global/ai-newsletter-signup';
15	import AiUserStories from '@/content/blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/images/AI-Generated-User-Stories.png';
16	
17	Shortly after the release of ChatGPT 4o, I saw people talking about doing Backlog Refinement in minutes with GenAI. Most people have realized that's just not a good idea. Speeding through the events doesn't help. It does leave us with a question: where is GenAI useful?
18	
19	To answer that first, we need to take a step back and ask why we hold these events in the first place. At surface level it appears we hold Sprint Planning to plan the outcome for the Sprint. Of course that's true. However the real story is much deeper. Sprint Planning is really about the team having a deep conversation to understand:
20	- The Sprint Goal
21	- Their capacity for the Sprint, especially after they recheck the Definition of Done.
22	- What process or team improvement they will make in the next Sprint
23	- Which Product Backlog Items they can complete towards the Sprint Goal
24	- How they will achieve those items
25	
26	The benefit of Sprint Planning isn't a Sprint Backlog that looks like a Tetris board. It's a team that has a good understanding of what they're working toward.
27	
28	The pull with GenAI is always toward speed. But a faster event doesn't build that understanding; it skips it. For our Scrum events and activities instead of speed, ask the question: How can the GenAI tool help the team members spot details that might get missed; look at deeper issues and in general improve collaboration.
29	
30	## Where GenAI Helps, and the Guardrails
31	We already have a set of guidelines on GenAI usage for Scrum Teams (from [Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster](/blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/)):
32	
33	**Key considerations:**
34	1. Collaboration - Much of Scrum's success is getting team members to collaborate
35	2. Bottlenecks - The theory of constraints shows that improvements that aren't at a system's bottleneck are waste (usually making the bottleneck worse).
36	
37	Before using GenAI in your Scrum team, evaluate:
38	- **Collaboration**: Does this enhance team collaboration?
39	- **Bottlenecks/Value**: Is it addressing the team's bottleneck or significantly speeding up a time-consuming task? (Hint: shaving 5 minutes off a 10-minute task is not a win.)
40	- **Risk Tolerance**: Can we afford the errors the tool will make? Do we know the subject area well enough to sufficiently review and identify errors in the generated work?
41	- **Complexity & Sustainability**: Can we manage the added complexity from adopting the tool? Does the time savings account for error detection, correction, and long-term maintenance?
42	- **Enabling**: Does it make it possible to do something new and novel?
43	
44	In general, it's good for administrative work, stress-testing plans, and assembling materials. With all of these we need to keep in mind these tools mimic existing human biases (e.g. sexism, ageism, racism and more); they appear confident when they shouldn't and more. There are a myriad of mistakes that are built into the training and reinforcement learning process (take our [test](/quiz/ai-failure-modes/) to see how many you know).
45	
46	Here's how this plays out, event by event:
47	
48	## Sprint Planning
49	### Purpose
50	Sprint Planning is the team building a shared understanding of the Sprint Goal, their capacity, and how they'll get there, not a tidy Sprint Backlog.
51	### Consider
52	GenAI to help with understanding the team's capacity for the next Sprint. How many people have vacation days? In the past few Sprints roughly how much time has been lost to Production Support or other surprises?
53	
54	GenAI to review the Sprint Plan. Ask clarifying questions; Do the Product Backlog Items selected support the Sprint Goal? Have they been checked against the Definition of Done? When compared to historical capacity, does the plan allow enough time to make the committed process/team improvement? And is there enough slack to account for unforeseen events mid Sprint (e.g. Production Support or other issue)?
55	
56	GenAI to check for hidden technical, cross team or other dependencies; hidden capacity issues, such as work that is heavy on testing when only one person can help there. Recurrent patterns of problems that have appeared over several Sprints.
57	
58	### Avoid
59	Using GenAI to create Sprint Goals or select which PBIs belong in the Sprint. When we use GenAI to do these tasks, we shut down the critical thinking required for good judgement.
60	
61	Using GenAI to break PBIs down into Business Analyst; Developer; QA tasks. To the extent tasks are valuable they need to be created through collaboration; otherwise the people don't understand what is expected of each other. Better than focusing on task breakdown, consider: Pair Programming or Ensemble Programming.
62	
63	## Daily Scrum
64	### Purpose
65	Daily Scrum is about:
66	- ensuring the Sprint Goal is still achievable
67	- updating the Sprint Backlog based on what we have learned/done in the last day
68	- sharing problems (aka impediments) so we can help each other
69	- preparing to collaborate for the day
70	
71	### Consider
72	*With anything where a recording is made or an AI is listening - do a Safety Check. If the tool reduces Safety, then it's not worth using.*
73	GenAI as a notetaker and using those notes to update the team's electronic tools. (Be aware the updates need careful human review.)
74	
75	At the end of Daily Scrum, use GenAI to review the notes/transcript: ask clarifying questions; stress test the updated Sprint plan again; recheck definition of done; ... many of the other items from Sprint Planning (after all, Daily Scrum is a form of mini replanning)
76	
77	Also check for potential missed impediments; PBIs whose work is missing Definition of Done elements.
78	
79	Using a Systems Thinking lens, GenAI can help dig deeper on impediments.
80	
81	### Avoid
82	GenAI assigning tasks to people. I can't believe this needs to be said and yet some tool vendors do it. If you want to watch motivation plummet, just do this.
83	
84	Reporting your status to a GenAI tool that summarizes and shares with the team over Slack. Daily Scrum is about collaboration and helps build a team. Reporting information that gets shared on Slack increases isolation. GenAI is already increasing isolation.[^1]
85	
86	## Sprint Review
87	### Purpose
88	Most people focus on the Sprint Review as a demo of the Product work done in the Sprint. That does happen but again it's not the only, or even most important piece.
89	- Review the Product Increment (aka the infamous demo)
90	- Check the Increment against the Definition of Done
91	- Feedback from the Stakeholders on the increment
92	- Update the Forecasts based on the work accepted in the Sprint Review
93	- Update the Product Backlog based on the Feedback
94	
95	### Boring Sprint Review
96	Too many Sprint Reviews are boring, mostly because there is a long demo and a lot of show and tell. Turn the tables after a high-level demo - I get the stakeholders (strong preference for real users) to use the Product Increment to complete a specific task. (This is a trick borrowed from the world of usability testing.) A series of focused tasks will get more focused feedback than a demo alone. It is also more engaging for the users because "show and play" beats "show and tell". The team members also benefit because there is nothing like seeing your application used by someone else to see where they're confused.
97	
98	### Consider
99	**With permission** recording the show and play portion of the Sprint Review, then use GenAI to create a list of the places people struggled.
100	
101	Using GenAI to check each Product Backlog Item against the Definition of Done.
102	
103	Using GenAI to brainstorm a narrative thread that connects the work done during the Sprint. (But not a script.)
104	
105	### Avoid
106	GenAI scripting your demo. If your demo needs a script, then we're doing "Show and Tell"
107	
108	Simulating user behaviour using GenAI. Another one in the category of I can't believe this needs to be said. People have attempted to do usability testing using a series of Agents acting in the role of humans.
109	
110	## Sprint Retrospective
111	### Purpose
112	The Retrospective is the chance for the team to step back and reflect on how they work together. It is intended as a chance to improve. In too many cases it boils down to "What went well?", "What went poorly?" and "What can be improved?" Retrospectives that follow that format rapidly become a boring waste of time.
113	
114	A good retrospective gives the team an opportunity to be open and honest. To raise problems and then work on solutions. This requires varying the exercises, questions and anything else so that each retrospective is designed for the problems the team faced during the Sprint.
115	
116	### Consider
117	You don't need GenAI to make your retrospectives better. Sources like the [RetroMat](https://retromat.org/) (a website with over 100 different retrospective activities) provide a great starting point for finding new exercises for your team. Experience facilitating a good retrospective makes it easier to judge the suggestions that GenAI will make.
118	
119	Using GenAI to make suggestions for different retrospective activities that will fit the challenges you have seen in the Sprint. Caveat emptor, the tool doesn't know you or your team. Ensure the activities don't just sound good on paper, but will achieve the outcomes you expect.
120	
121	Using GenAI to help assemble a set of notes to remind people of what happened in the Sprint. *For my personal weekly reviews, I get the LLM to review all of my business context and assemble a detailed list of things that happened in the week. All the interpretation is left to me.*
122	
123	When dealing with deeper challenges, consider using Systems Thinking to uncover the problem(s) behind the surface level problem.
124	
125	### Avoid
126	Any sort of recording and transcription in the Retrospective.
127	
128	## Backlog Refinement
129	### Purpose
130	Backlog refinement is the activity where the team and the product owner work to build a common understanding of the work that will be coming up in the next Sprints. It involves: writing new user stories; splitting large items down into smaller parts; reprioritizing; deleting items that are no longer important; estimation (hint: Story points not required).
131	
132	All of these activities involve the team and product owner having a discussion about what a User Story/PBI represents. The team should be asking questions about who it is for? What problem will it solve? Why is it valuable? ... All of these lead towards the team members understanding what is going to be built. GenAI doesn't replace human understanding.
133	
134	Remember GenAI doesn't understand your context: end users; code base; security posture; ... . No matter how much information it is fed, these tools are still just generating the next most plausible token in response to your prompt.
135	
136	(If you need more depth on Refinement see: [Product Backlog Refinement Hell: 3 Problems and Solutions](/blog/product-backlog-refinement-hell-solutions/)). *Strange Scrum detail? Backlog Refinement isn't an event, it's an activity. A ridiculous amount of ink has been spilled on the difference.*
137	
138	### Consider
139	Using the LLM to help ask questions about a User Story: Does it meet INVEST? Who is the story for? Is the why statement clear? Is there ambiguity?
140	
141	Struggling to split a user story ask the model to help. Use the well known splitting patterns, ...
142	
143	Get the tool to question prioritization decisions.
144	
145	### Avoid
146	Using GenAI to generate: Epics, User Stories, Acceptance Criteria or anything else. All of these items exist as artifacts to help people (hint humans) to achieve a common understanding. When you present a team with a list of finished-looking user stories, they read, they nod, they say "I understand". However lacking a real conversation they each understand something different. The irony, the problem of Product Owners bashing out a list of "polished" user stories and getting false agreement was a problem before GenAI appeared. GenAI has simply made the existing problem worse.
147	
148	<Figure
149	  src={AiUserStories}
150	  alt="Three team members looking at a whiteboard labeled AI Generated User Story, each with a thought bubble showing different shapes, illustrating false consensus"
151	  caption="False consensus: a polished AI-generated user story gets nods of agreement while each person pictures something different."
152	/>
153	
154	## Cross-Cutting Cautions
155	**Recording and Transcripts** - This is the most popular suggestion I’ve seen. Be careful. Depending on the psychological safety level in the team, use of any recording or transcription tool may cause team members to avoid saying things that need to be said, because they don't want to go on the record voicing their true feelings. If there is a choice between honesty and using an AI transcription tool, always choose for openness. *I know this sounds repetitive, but it comes up so often that it needs to be said again.* If transcription is used, consider a rule that all transcripts are deleted after they've been used to get the GenAI assistant to do its thing. Whatever you do, don't use the transcript to generate a summary of the meeting.
156	
157	<CalloutBox>
158	If you can significantly speed up any of these events or activities with GenAI, then you’re probably not getting the value out of it in the first place.
159	</CalloutBox>
160	
161	When seeking to make anything better with GenAI, work from first principles. Take the time to understand the purpose of the event, activity, process, etc., before attempting to improve it.
162	
163	Be careful when we use GenAI, it's always eager to help. It's confident. It will propose many ideas. However it has no sense of priorities, it doesn't know your context. It can go deep on an impediment that only happens once every few months. In the moment it feels productive, however when you look back you can see it was chasing down a small detail. I know this from my own experience.
164	
165	## The Bottom Line
166	Before introducing GenAI in any of these events, make sure you're already facilitating events that people want to participate in. In my experience GenAI amplifies what you're already doing. Both good and bad.
167	
168	It can be useful, but beware the tools becoming a crutch or, worse, replacing conversation. The Scrum events and activities are about increasing collaboration. Don't replace your collaboration with GenAI. This is exactly why "GenAI can magically speed up refinement" is the [monster backlog refinement anti-pattern](/blog/how-many-of-these-backlog-refinement-anti-patterns-does-your-team-have/) of the year.
169	
170	If you want a deeper, evidence-based walk through making GenAI work for your team instead of your team working for the AI, that's exactly what my [Surviving the AI Tsunami](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/) course covers.
171	
172	[^1]: [*Research: Gen AI Makes People More Productive and Less Motivated*](https://hbr.org/2025/05/research-gen-ai-makes-people-more-productive-and-less-motivated), Harvard Business Review (May 2025). Discussed in [The Human Cost of GenAI](/blog/the-human-cost-of-genai/).
173	
174	*Image attribution: © Agile Pain Relief Consulting (June 2026). Drawn with Linea Sketch.*

Using a Systems Thinking lens, GenAI can help dig deeper on impediments.

### Avoid
GenAI assigning tasks to people. I can't believe this needs to be said and yet some tool vendors do it. If you want to watch motivation plummet, just do this.

Reporting your status to a GenAI tool that summarizes and shares with the team over Slack. Daily Scrum is about collaboration and helps build a team. Reporting information that gets shared on Slack increases isolation. GenAI is already increasing isolation.[^1]

## Sprint Review
### Purpose
Most people focus on the Sprint Review as a demo of the Product work done in the Sprint. That does happen but again it's not the only, or even most important piece.
- Review the Product Increment (aka the infamous demo)
- Check the Increment against the Definition of Done
- Feedback from the Stakeholders on the increment
- Update the Forecasts based on the work accepted in the Sprint Review
- Update the Product Backlog based on the Feedback

### Boring Sprint Review
Too many Sprint Reviews are boring, mostly because there is a long demo and a lot of show and tell. Turn the tables after a high-level demo - I get the stakeholders (strong preference for real users) to use the Product Increment to complete a specific task. (This is a trick borrowed from the world of usability testing.) A series of focused tasks will get more focused feedback than a demo alone. It is also more engaging for the users because "show and play" beats "show and tell". The team members also benefit because there is nothing like seeing your application used by someone else to see where they're confused.

### Consider
**With permission** recording the show and play portion of the Sprint Review, then use GenAI to create a list of the places people struggled.

Using GenAI to check each Product Backlog Item against the Definition of Done.

Using GenAI to brainstorm a narrative thread that connects the work done during the Sprint. (But not a script.)

### Avoid
GenAI scripting your demo. If your demo needs a script, then we're doing "Show and Tell"

Simulating user behaviour using GenAI. Another one in the category of I can't believe this needs to be said. People have attempted to do usability testing using a series of Agents acting in the role of humans.

## Sprint Retrospective
### Purpose
The Retrospective is the chance for the team to step back and reflect on how they work together. It is intended as a chance to improve. In too many cases it boils down to "What went well?", "What went poorly?" and "What can be improved?" Retrospectives that follow that format rapidly become a boring waste of time.

A good retrospective gives the team an opportunity to be open and honest. To raise problems and then work on solutions. This requires varying the exercises, questions and anything else so that each retrospective is designed for the problems the team faced during the Sprint.

### Consider
You don't need GenAI to make your retrospectives better. Sources like the [RetroMat](https://retromat.org/) (a website with over 100 different retrospective activities) provide a great starting point for finding new exercises for your team. Experience facilitating a good retrospective makes it easier to judge the suggestions that GenAI will make.

Using GenAI to make suggestions for different retrospective activities that will fit the challenges you have seen in the Sprint. Caveat emptor, the tool doesn't know you or your team. Ensure the activities don't just sound good on paper, but will achieve the outcomes you expect.

Using GenAI to help assemble a set of notes to remind people of what happened in the Sprint. *For my personal weekly reviews, I get the LLM to review all of my business context and assemble a detailed list of things that happened in the week. All the interpretation is left to me.*

When dealing with deeper challenges, consider using Systems Thinking to uncover the problem(s) behind the surface level problem.

### Avoid
Any sort of recording and transcription in the Retrospective.

## Backlog Refinement
### Purpose
Backlog refinement is the activity where the team and the product owner work to build a common understanding of the work that will be coming up in the next Sprints. It involves: writing new user stories; splitting large items down into smaller parts; reprioritizing; deleting items that are no longer important; estimation (hint: Story points not required).

All of these activities involve the team and product owner having a discussion about what a User Story/PBI represents. The team should be asking questions about who it is for? What problem will it solve? Why is it valuable? ... All of these lead towards the team members understanding what is going to be built. GenAI doesn't replace human understanding.

Remember GenAI doesn't understand your context: end users; code base; security posture; ... . No matter how much information it is fed, these tools are still just generating the next most plausible token in response to your prompt.

(If you need more depth on Refinement see: [Product Backlog Refinement Hell: 3 Problems and Solutions](/blog/product-backlog-refinement-hell-solutions/)). *Strange Scrum detail? Backlog Refinement isn't an event, it's an activity. A ridiculous amount of ink has been spilled on the difference.*

### Consider
Using the LLM to help ask questions about a User Story: Does it meet INVEST? Who is the story for? Is the why statement clear? Is there ambiguity?

Struggling to split a user story ask the model to help. Use the well known splitting patterns, ...

Get the tool to question prioritization decisions.

### Avoid
Using GenAI to generate: Epics, User Stories, Acceptance Criteria or anything else. All of these items exist as artifacts to help people (hint humans) to achieve a common understanding. When you present a team with a list of finished-looking user stories, they read, they nod, they say "I understand". However lacking a real conversation they each understand something different. The irony, the problem of Product Owners bashing out a list of "polished" user stories and getting false agreement was a problem before GenAI appeared. GenAI has simply made the existing problem worse.

<Figure
  src={AiUserStories}
  alt="Three team members looking at a whiteboard labeled AI Generated User Story, each with a thought bubble showing different shapes, illustrating false consensus"
  caption="False consensus: a polished AI-generated user story gets nods of agreement while each person pictures something different."
/>

## Cross-Cutting Cautions
**Recording and Transcripts** - This is the most popular suggestion I’ve seen. Be careful. Depending on the psychological safety level in the team, use of any recording or transcription tool may cause team members to avoid saying things that need to be said, because they don't want to go on the record voicing their true feelings. If there is a choice between honesty and using an AI transcription tool, always choose for openness. *I know this sounds repetitive, but it comes up so often that it needs to be said again.* If transcription is used, consider a rule that all transcripts are deleted after they've been used to get the GenAI assistant to do its thing. Whatever you do, don't use the transcript to generate a summary of the meeting.

<CalloutBox>
If you can significantly speed up any of these events or activities with GenAI, then you’re probably not getting the value out of it in the first place.
</CalloutBox>

When seeking to make anything better with GenAI, work from first principles. Take the time to understand the purpose of the event, activity, process, etc., before attempting to improve it.

Be careful when we use GenAI, it's always eager to help. It's confident. It will propose many ideas. However it has no sense of priorities, it doesn't know your context. It can go deep on an impediment that only happens once every few months. In the moment it feels productive, however when you look back you can see it was chasing down a small detail. I know this from my own experience.

## The Bottom Line
Before introducing GenAI in any of these events, make sure you're already facilitating events that people want to participate in. In my experience GenAI amplifies what you're already doing. Both good and bad.

It can be useful, but beware the tools becoming a crutch or, worse, replacing conversation. The Scrum events and activities are about increasing collaboration. Don't replace your collaboration with GenAI. This is exactly why "GenAI can magically speed up refinement" is the [monster backlog refinement anti-pattern](/blog/how-many-of-these-backlog-refinement-anti-patterns-does-your-team-have/) of the year.

If you want a deeper, evidence-based walk through making GenAI work for your team instead of your team working for the AI, that's exactly what my [Surviving the AI Tsunami](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/) course covers.

[^1]: [*Research: Gen AI Makes People More Productive and Less Motivated*](https://hbr.org/2025/05/research-gen-ai-makes-people-more-productive-and-less-motivated), Harvard Business Review (May 2025). Discussed in [The Human Cost of GenAI](/blog/the-human-cost-of-genai/).

*Image attribution: © Agile Pain Relief Consulting (June 2026). Drawn with Linea Sketch.*

1	---
2	title: "Product Management with GenAI: What Changes and What Doesn't"
3	date: '2026-04-23'
4	categories:
5	  - 'artificial-intelligence'
6	  - 'product-ownership'
7	coverImage: '@/content/blog/product-management-and-genai/images/BottleGenAINarrowed.png'
8	excerpt: 'GenAI makes shipping cheap, not shipping right. Lean UX, Impact Mapping, and real-user experiments matter more when code is disposable.'
9	---
10	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
11	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
12	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
13	import bottleneckBeforeGenAI from '@/content/blog/product-management-and-genai/images/BottleneckBeforeGenAI.png';
14	import bottleneckWithGenAI from '@/content/blog/product-management-and-genai/images/BottleNeckWithGenAI.png';
15	import bottleneckGenAIWithErrors from '@/content/blog/product-management-and-genai/images/BottleGenAIWithErrors.png';
16	
17	I’m seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They’re full of features that don’t fit well together. Some of the products I’ve seen don’t solve a real problem.
18	
19	<HighlightBox variant="info">
20	“Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.”
21	</HighlightBox>
22	
23	At Product Camp Ottawa 2026, I asked 3 questions:
24	1. How many of you work in organizations that shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code? *About 1/3 to 1/2 of the people in the room*
25	2. How many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written? *Only 3 people raised their hands, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI*
26	3. How many of you have spoken to an actual end user, human to human, in the last month? *Nearly half, a good sign. However, this is different from what I see working with teams.*
27	
28	I learned that people at Product Camp are better than most at talking to their users. However, like the rest of the world, they’re struggling to ensure that the right thing is being built. (For Product Owners who want to work through this in depth, our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/) is an evidence-based, cohort-based course.)
29	
30	Before GenAI appeared, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance.
31	
32	<Figure
33	  src={bottleneckBeforeGenAI}
34	  alt="Diagram showing a bottleneck at Quality Assurance before GenAI"
35	  caption="Before GenAI: the bottleneck sits at Quality Assurance."
36	/>
37	
38	With GenAI, this problem doesn’t change. We still have more features than we can possibly test. If the bottleneck shifts, it’s only because we now have an even worse Code Review problem.
39	
40	<Figure
41	  src={bottleneckWithGenAI}
42	  alt="Diagram showing GenAI pushing more work into Code Review and Quality Assurance"
43	  caption="With GenAI: more code generated upstream of the same bottlenecks."
44	/>
45	
46	Worse, in many cases, features are getting rejected in the review process or fail in testing. The bottleneck is the place where we don’t have enough people to do the work. Failures discovered here are the most expensive because we wasted the time of the people doing the review and testing. Many of these failures are features that should never have been built or ones with a poor user experience.
47	
48	<Figure
49	  src={bottleneckGenAIWithErrors}
50	  alt="Diagram showing rejected features and failed tests accumulating at the bottleneck"
51	  caption="Failures found at the bottleneck are the most expensive."
52	/>
53	
54	Pressure to use GenAI everywhere it can be used is increasing. No one would suggest that putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck is a good idea. Yet that is exactly what we’re doing when we generate code. (Classic Theory of Constraints)
55	
56	You end up with [feature bloat](/blog/gen-ai-and-the-feature-factory-automating-away-collaboration/) that confuses users and feels unfinished. By increasing the number of features, we increase the attack surface and with it the security risk. (The more features we have, the more places an attacker can try to get in.)
57	
58	<HighlightBox variant="info">
59	“More features, faster, isn’t winning.”
60	</HighlightBox>
61	
62	## How should Product Management Respond?
63	Every feature that is built is a hypothesis: “If we build this feature, it will solve a specific problem for a group of users.”
64	
65	[Agile Product Management](/courses/certified-scrum-product-owner-cspo-training/) has long had a set of Discovery tools to help with this:
66	- Lean Startup: good for testing big hypotheses: should we build this product or feature?
67	- Lean UX: what version of the feature will solve the problem? (It also puts emphasis on improving usability and user experience)
68	- Continuous Discovery: what feature(s) are most important right now?
69	- Behaviour Driven Development: exploring the acceptance criteria for the feature before implementation, so that we build the right thing. Generating code without doing this is a big risk
70	- Impact Mapping: which feature will have the biggest impact for the business?
71	
72	Even without GenAI, all of these tools would help a team build the right product for the right users. GenAI makes these tools easier to use, but it’s not magic.
73	
74	### What changes with GenAI?
75	Across all of these tools, I see that GenAI helps:
76	- Make prototypes easier to build
77	- Faster to run Lean Startup type experiments: Wizard of Oz, Fake Door, etc.
78	- Possible to run multiple experiments at once
79	- Analysis of large amounts of user data: customer interviews, surveys, analytics, etc.
80	
81	GenAI also creates some risks:
82	
83	| Risk | Resolution |
84	| --- | --- |
85	| Prototypes seem polished and complete, so they get mistaken for certainty | Grayscale: build the prototype without colour. No one can mistake it for the real thing. *I learned about this over 30 years ago, doing usability work. When we show a UI that looks good, we get feedback about font and colour. When it is deliberately simple, we get far more information about the usability.* |
86	| [Outsourcing all analysis to GenAI](/blog/the-human-cost-of-genai/) risks missing important insights and introducing bias and hallucinations[^1] | Do your own analysis before getting the AI to do one. This way, you’ll have a better understanding of the data. Use the AI as a cross-check for your completed analysis, not to replace it. |
87	| Using AI agents to simulate real users | Don’t. Talk to real users, even if only three of them, instead. |
88	| Pressure to go faster means that we skip key validation steps | Remind the people pressuring you that going faster will [cost more later](/blog/the-real-cost-of-ai-generated-code-it-s-not-all-it-s-cracked-up-to-be/), when you need to revert a feature that doesn’t meet a user need or has poor usability. |
89	
90	The biggest risk is going through the motions: theatre, going through the discovery process without learning. **Ask**: what did we learn this week that changed our plan? If nothing, it’s theatre.
91	
92	### What doesn’t change?
93	The need for:
94	- Customer contact, real world conversations and testing with people
95	- Collaboration with the team building the product
96	
97	GenAI speeds up the mechanics of Discovery. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning.
98	
99	To compete in this market, stop promising to build features just because a stakeholder asked for them. Have a clear testable hypothesis. Building great products still comes down to the same things: talking to real users, running experiments, and listening to the feedback.
100	
101	What hypothesis will you test next? How will you use GenAI to help? What will you do to offset the risks?
102	
103	[^1]: AI Generated Personas are a very specific example of this: “[Generative AI personas considered harmful? Putting forth twenty challenges of algorithmic user representation in human-computer interaction](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1071581925002149)” Danial Amin, Joni Salminen, Bernard J. Jansen, Joongi Shin, Dae Hyun Kim

---
title: "Product Management with GenAI: What Changes and What Doesn't"
date: '2026-04-23'
categories:
  - 'artificial-intelligence'
  - 'product-ownership'
coverImage: '@/content/blog/product-management-and-genai/images/BottleGenAINarrowed.png'
excerpt: 'GenAI makes shipping cheap, not shipping right. Lean UX, Impact Mapping, and real-user experiments matter more when code is disposable.'
---
import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import bottleneckBeforeGenAI from '@/content/blog/product-management-and-genai/images/BottleneckBeforeGenAI.png';
import bottleneckWithGenAI from '@/content/blog/product-management-and-genai/images/BottleNeckWithGenAI.png';
import bottleneckGenAIWithErrors from '@/content/blog/product-management-and-genai/images/BottleGenAIWithErrors.png';

I’m seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They’re full of features that don’t fit well together. Some of the products I’ve seen don’t solve a real problem.

<HighlightBox variant="info">
“Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.”
</HighlightBox>

At Product Camp Ottawa 2026, I asked 3 questions:
1. How many of you work in organizations that shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code? *About 1/3 to 1/2 of the people in the room*
2. How many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written? *Only 3 people raised their hands, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI*
3. How many of you have spoken to an actual end user, human to human, in the last month? *Nearly half, a good sign. However, this is different from what I see working with teams.*

I learned that people at Product Camp are better than most at talking to their users. However, like the rest of the world, they’re struggling to ensure that the right thing is being built. (For Product Owners who want to work through this in depth, our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/) is an evidence-based, cohort-based course.)

Before GenAI appeared, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance.

<Figure
  src={bottleneckBeforeGenAI}
  alt="Diagram showing a bottleneck at Quality Assurance before GenAI"
  caption="Before GenAI: the bottleneck sits at Quality Assurance."
/>

With GenAI, this problem doesn’t change. We still have more features than we can possibly test. If the bottleneck shifts, it’s only because we now have an even worse Code Review problem.

<Figure
  src={bottleneckWithGenAI}
  alt="Diagram showing GenAI pushing more work into Code Review and Quality Assurance"
  caption="With GenAI: more code generated upstream of the same bottlenecks."
/>

Worse, in many cases, features are getting rejected in the review process or fail in testing. The bottleneck is the place where we don’t have enough people to do the work. Failures discovered here are the most expensive because we wasted the time of the people doing the review and testing. Many of these failures are features that should never have been built or ones with a poor user experience.

<Figure
  src={bottleneckGenAIWithErrors}
  alt="Diagram showing rejected features and failed tests accumulating at the bottleneck"
  caption="Failures found at the bottleneck are the most expensive."
/>

Pressure to use GenAI everywhere it can be used is increasing. No one would suggest that putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck is a good idea. Yet that is exactly what we’re doing when we generate code. (Classic Theory of Constraints)

You end up with [feature bloat](/blog/gen-ai-and-the-feature-factory-automating-away-collaboration/) that confuses users and feels unfinished. By increasing the number of features, we increase the attack surface and with it the security risk. (The more features we have, the more places an attacker can try to get in.)

<HighlightBox variant="info">
“More features, faster, isn’t winning.”
</HighlightBox>

## How should Product Management Respond?
Every feature that is built is a hypothesis: “If we build this feature, it will solve a specific problem for a group of users.”

[Agile Product Management](/courses/certified-scrum-product-owner-cspo-training/) has long had a set of Discovery tools to help with this:
- Lean Startup: good for testing big hypotheses: should we build this product or feature?
- Lean UX: what version of the feature will solve the problem? (It also puts emphasis on improving usability and user experience)
- Continuous Discovery: what feature(s) are most important right now?
- Behaviour Driven Development: exploring the acceptance criteria for the feature before implementation, so that we build the right thing. Generating code without doing this is a big risk
- Impact Mapping: which feature will have the biggest impact for the business?

Even without GenAI, all of these tools would help a team build the right product for the right users. GenAI makes these tools easier to use, but it’s not magic.

### What changes with GenAI?
Across all of these tools, I see that GenAI helps:
- Make prototypes easier to build
- Faster to run Lean Startup type experiments: Wizard of Oz, Fake Door, etc.
- Possible to run multiple experiments at once
- Analysis of large amounts of user data: customer interviews, surveys, analytics, etc.

GenAI also creates some risks:

| Risk | Resolution |
| --- | --- |
| Prototypes seem polished and complete, so they get mistaken for certainty | Grayscale: build the prototype without colour. No one can mistake it for the real thing. *I learned about this over 30 years ago, doing usability work. When we show a UI that looks good, we get feedback about font and colour. When it is deliberately simple, we get far more information about the usability.* |
| [Outsourcing all analysis to GenAI](/blog/the-human-cost-of-genai/) risks missing important insights and introducing bias and hallucinations[^1] | Do your own analysis before getting the AI to do one. This way, you’ll have a better understanding of the data. Use the AI as a cross-check for your completed analysis, not to replace it. |
| Using AI agents to simulate real users | Don’t. Talk to real users, even if only three of them, instead. |
| Pressure to go faster means that we skip key validation steps | Remind the people pressuring you that going faster will [cost more later](/blog/the-real-cost-of-ai-generated-code-it-s-not-all-it-s-cracked-up-to-be/), when you need to revert a feature that doesn’t meet a user need or has poor usability. |

The biggest risk is going through the motions: theatre, going through the discovery process without learning. **Ask**: what did we learn this week that changed our plan? If nothing, it’s theatre.

### What doesn’t change?
The need for:
- Customer contact, real world conversations and testing with people
- Collaboration with the team building the product

GenAI speeds up the mechanics of Discovery. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning.

To compete in this market, stop promising to build features just because a stakeholder asked for them. Have a clear testable hypothesis. Building great products still comes down to the same things: talking to real users, running experiments, and listening to the feedback.

What hypothesis will you test next? How will you use GenAI to help? What will you do to offset the risks?

[^1]: AI Generated Personas are a very specific example of this: “[Generative AI personas considered harmful? Putting forth twenty challenges of algorithmic user representation in human-computer interaction](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1071581925002149)” Danial Amin, Joni Salminen, Bernard J. Jansen, Joongi Shin, Dae Hyun Kim

1	---
2	title: "Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster (and probably never will)"
3	date: "2025-05-21"
4	lastUpdated: '2026-05-22'
5	draft: false
6	categories:
7	  - "artificial-intelligence"
8	coverImage: '@/content/blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/images/ai-does-not-replace-scrummaster.jpg'
9	excerpt: 'Practical AI insights for ScrumMasters and Agile Coaches. See how it works and where it falls short. Avoid the hype.'
10	---
11	
12	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
13	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
14	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
15	import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro'
16	import aiScrumMaster from '@/content/blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/images/ai-does-not-replace-scrummaster.jpg';
17	
18	AI's superpower is speed—its ability to churn out text faster than any human. But there's a catch: it sounds too confident for what it actually "knows".
19	ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers frequently ask me how they can use GenAI effectively, and they wonder if it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most questions come from misunderstandings of how the current generation of tools work.
20	
21	This post is the starting point for our work on GenAI and Agile teams. If you want to go deeper with practice and coaching alongside other ScrumMasters and Product Owners, our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/) is an evidence-based, cohort-based course where we work through these problems with real teams.
22	
23	## GenAI Doesn't Think
24	Marketing hype for the current generation of tools that we call AIs makes it seem like these tools are on the verge of replacing people at work, implying that you won't need a ScrumMaster because the AI will be your coach, and there's no need for a Product Owner when User Stories write themselves.
25	
26	The hype claims that Generative AIs (or GenAI), such as Google Gemini, Claude Sonnet, and ChatGPT, can think and reason, but don't be fooled by the marketing language. Here's the reality:
27	-	Learning - They don't learn, they're limited to the data they were trained on.
28	-	Reasoning and Thinking - Even when asked to think step-by-step, it's just faking the process. It doesn't actually understand.
29	-	Context Window - The models we use today have limited memory for the current conversation. Once that memory is exceeded, they forget the beginning of the conversation.
30	-	Training Data - AIs have been trained on all of the text on the internet. So their output is just the average of the internet which, of course, is unregulated.
31	
32	GenAI (properly called Large Language Models) takes the text you give it in the prompt and predicts the next word that should come in the conversation. That word is added to the text after your original prompt, and the revised text is fed back to the model to predict the next word. This continues, building responses one word at a time, until it predicts that enough words have been generated.
33	
34	This is not how a human works. We consider what we want to express and then find the best way to say it. By giving GenAI human attributes—reason, thinking, conversation—we build a model in our heads that implies they're like humans. Except they're not, so we must keep clear in mind their strengths and weaknesses.
35	
36	## GenAI Strengths and Weaknesses
37	Their core strength is dealing quickly with a large amount of information. Their weaknesses centre around errors. The greatest danger is that, as demonstrated in "The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking"[^1], the more confident the AI sounds, the more likely we are to believe it[^2] even though there is no correlation between that and whether or not the information is good.
38	
39	### Strengths
40	- Sifting through a large quantity of information quickly
41	- Finding patterns in data
42	- Generating a large number of different ideas quickly in response to a question (also a weakness if done too early in our work process, as it will bias our creative thinking and the likelihood of spotting missed cases)
43	- Summarization
44	- Analyzing our existing work for what we might have missed
45	
46	### Weaknesses
47	-	Patterns - false positives, it will find a signal in noise even when there is no signal
48	-	Sounds confident even when providing inaccurate information
49	-	Sycophantic – The tool's response to a prompt often starts with "That's a great idea"
50	-	Risk of errors (from misinterpretations) and hallucination (completely false information) with new models may worsen as new models are increasingly trained with limited supervision on "synthetic data" (generated by other models)
51	
52	GenAI can be beneficial, however, we need guardrails.
53	## Guidelines for GenAI Use
54	Key considerations:
55	1.	Collaboration - Much of Scrum's success is getting team members to collaborate
56	2.	Bottlenecks - The theory of constraints shows that improvements that aren't at a system's bottleneck are waste (usually making the bottleneck worse).
57	
58	Scrum and Agile teams can use the following questions to help distinguish between healthy and harmful uses of GenAI.
59	<CalloutBox heading="Before using GenAI in your Scrum team, evaluate:">
60	-	**Collaboration**: Does this enhance team collaboration?
61	-	**Bottlenecks/Value**: Is it addressing the team's bottleneck or significantly speeding up a time-consuming task? (Hint: shaving 5 minutes off a 10-minute task is not a win.)
62	-	**Risk Tolerance**: Can we afford the errors the tool will make? Do we know the subject area well enough to sufficiently review and identify errors in the generated work?
63	-	**Complexity & Sustainability**: Can we manage the added complexity from adopting the tool? Does the time savings account for error detection, correction, and long-term maintenance?
64	-	**Enabling**: Does it make it possible to do something new and novel
65	</CalloutBox>
66	## Evaluating Tools Using Our Questions
67	I've surveyed many tools across the internet to find a representative sample of the promises the tool vendors make about helping your team. But there's an inherent problem as I offer my opinions. No website or marketing copy captures what a product actually does behind the scenes. I interpret content and then share the information with you, and you will in turn interpret what you think I'm saying. Think of the child's game of "Telephone". Communication, no matter how careful and responsible, leaves room for error.
68	
69	### AI for a Sprint Retrospectives
70	Many GenAI models promise to connect with tools like Jira, Slack, GitHub, and calendars to automatically gather and analyze sprint data (e.g. completed tasks, communication patterns, roadblocks). They pitch:
71	
72	- **AI-Suggested Talking Points:** Generates relevant discussion topics based on the analyzed data, helping teams focus on impactful issues.
73	- **AI Grouping** and **AI generated Action Items:** Help you easily streamline your retrospective.
74	- **Sentiment Analysis:** Analyzes team communications and feedback to gauge sentiment and identify underlying emotions or concerns.
75	- **Facilitation Assistance:** The AI can act as a co-facilitator, guiding the conversation and covering all key areas.
76	- **Team Members Accountability:** Helps identify, assign, and track action items that arise from the retrospective.
77	
78	#### My Take
79	This is a bit of a mix.
80	
81	The good: **Automated data collection** makes it more likely that valuable data comes to the Retrospective.
82	
83	Only 'okay': **Analysis**, if used to augment and not replace human thinking, might spot hidden patterns. **Sentiment Analysis** of the team's conversations might spot overlooked patterns. However, the harm caused to Psychological Safety, knowing that an AI overlord always looks over our shoulders, exceeds the value.
84	
85	Outright bad: Grouping exercises in Retrospectives are designed to start a conversation among team members about how problems are related. So **AI Grouping** and, worse, **AI generated Action Items** are replacing human insight, which is ironic since the humans still need to understand and solve the problem.
86	
87	Baked into the tools, I looked at? The assumption that all of the meaningful interactions occur inside a JIRA, Asana or KanbanZone. Email, Slack, or real-world conversations are far more important in most teams.
88

90	  src={aiScrumMaster}

92	  caption="sketch of GenAI assigning tasks to team members"
93	/>
94	### AI Daily Scrum
95	You just can't make this up. One vendor promises to replace Daily Scrum with text, voice and video messages, then run reports on a schedule and share the reports with multiple Admins.
96	
97	#### My Take
98	A Daily Scrum is an event to give the team time to understand what their peers are working on, hear about impediments others face, and to spark collaboration. None of this is served by an automated tool. This tool has nothing to do with Scrum, except that it stole the language. I can only imagine that a team using a tool like this will have low psychological safety and also be [micromanaged](/blog/scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement/) to the brink of extinction.
99	
100	Not surprisingly, this same vendor, who completely misses the point of Scrum, pitched the ability of the tool to also run Retrospectives on autopilot by gathering notes and feedback from individual team member submissions and "Replace retrospective meetings with scheduled team surveys. …. Run retrospectives consistently on schedule". Is replacing human interaction with writing to an AI the way to build effective teams and positive work environments? Is keeping to a schedule the most important thing in a Retrospective?
101	
102	### Generate Meeting Agendas and Take Notes
103	Several tools are offered to generate meeting agendas (planning, reviewing, and retrospectives) based on the current sprint's needs, and claim to make meetings more purposeful, efficient, and less time-consuming.
104	
105	An AI meeting assistant auto joins, auto shares, and auto summarizes meetings. AI-powered meeting assistants help save professionals and teams an average of 4 hours a week and increase productivity by automatically generating action items, summaries, and follow-up emails.

---
title: "Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster (and probably never will)"
date: "2025-05-21"
lastUpdated: '2026-05-22'
draft: false
categories:
  - "artificial-intelligence"
coverImage: '@/content/blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/images/ai-does-not-replace-scrummaster.jpg'
excerpt: 'Practical AI insights for ScrumMasters and Agile Coaches. See how it works and where it falls short. Avoid the hype.'
---

import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro'
import aiScrumMaster from '@/content/blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/images/ai-does-not-replace-scrummaster.jpg';

AI's superpower is speed—its ability to churn out text faster than any human. But there's a catch: it sounds too confident for what it actually "knows".
ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers frequently ask me how they can use GenAI effectively, and they wonder if it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most questions come from misunderstandings of how the current generation of tools work.

This post is the starting point for our work on GenAI and Agile teams. If you want to go deeper with practice and coaching alongside other ScrumMasters and Product Owners, our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/) is an evidence-based, cohort-based course where we work through these problems with real teams.

## GenAI Doesn't Think
Marketing hype for the current generation of tools that we call AIs makes it seem like these tools are on the verge of replacing people at work, implying that you won't need a ScrumMaster because the AI will be your coach, and there's no need for a Product Owner when User Stories write themselves.

The hype claims that Generative AIs (or GenAI), such as Google Gemini, Claude Sonnet, and ChatGPT, can think and reason, but don't be fooled by the marketing language. Here's the reality:
-	Learning - They don't learn, they're limited to the data they were trained on.
-	Reasoning and Thinking - Even when asked to think step-by-step, it's just faking the process. It doesn't actually understand.
-	Context Window - The models we use today have limited memory for the current conversation. Once that memory is exceeded, they forget the beginning of the conversation.
-	Training Data - AIs have been trained on all of the text on the internet. So their output is just the average of the internet which, of course, is unregulated.

GenAI (properly called Large Language Models) takes the text you give it in the prompt and predicts the next word that should come in the conversation. That word is added to the text after your original prompt, and the revised text is fed back to the model to predict the next word. This continues, building responses one word at a time, until it predicts that enough words have been generated.

This is not how a human works. We consider what we want to express and then find the best way to say it. By giving GenAI human attributes—reason, thinking, conversation—we build a model in our heads that implies they're like humans. Except they're not, so we must keep clear in mind their strengths and weaknesses.

## GenAI Strengths and Weaknesses
Their core strength is dealing quickly with a large amount of information. Their weaknesses centre around errors. The greatest danger is that, as demonstrated in "The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking"[^1], the more confident the AI sounds, the more likely we are to believe it[^2] even though there is no correlation between that and whether or not the information is good.

### Strengths
- Sifting through a large quantity of information quickly
- Finding patterns in data
- Generating a large number of different ideas quickly in response to a question (also a weakness if done too early in our work process, as it will bias our creative thinking and the likelihood of spotting missed cases)
- Summarization
- Analyzing our existing work for what we might have missed

### Weaknesses
-	Patterns - false positives, it will find a signal in noise even when there is no signal
-	Sounds confident even when providing inaccurate information
-	Sycophantic – The tool's response to a prompt often starts with "That's a great idea"
-	Risk of errors (from misinterpretations) and hallucination (completely false information) with new models may worsen as new models are increasingly trained with limited supervision on "synthetic data" (generated by other models)

GenAI can be beneficial, however, we need guardrails.
## Guidelines for GenAI Use
Key considerations:
1.	Collaboration - Much of Scrum's success is getting team members to collaborate
2.	Bottlenecks - The theory of constraints shows that improvements that aren't at a system's bottleneck are waste (usually making the bottleneck worse).

Scrum and Agile teams can use the following questions to help distinguish between healthy and harmful uses of GenAI.
<CalloutBox heading="Before using GenAI in your Scrum team, evaluate:">
-	**Collaboration**: Does this enhance team collaboration?
-	**Bottlenecks/Value**: Is it addressing the team's bottleneck or significantly speeding up a time-consuming task? (Hint: shaving 5 minutes off a 10-minute task is not a win.)
-	**Risk Tolerance**: Can we afford the errors the tool will make? Do we know the subject area well enough to sufficiently review and identify errors in the generated work?
-	**Complexity & Sustainability**: Can we manage the added complexity from adopting the tool? Does the time savings account for error detection, correction, and long-term maintenance?
-	**Enabling**: Does it make it possible to do something new and novel
</CalloutBox>
## Evaluating Tools Using Our Questions
I've surveyed many tools across the internet to find a representative sample of the promises the tool vendors make about helping your team. But there's an inherent problem as I offer my opinions. No website or marketing copy captures what a product actually does behind the scenes. I interpret content and then share the information with you, and you will in turn interpret what you think I'm saying. Think of the child's game of "Telephone". Communication, no matter how careful and responsible, leaves room for error.

### AI for a Sprint Retrospectives
Many GenAI models promise to connect with tools like Jira, Slack, GitHub, and calendars to automatically gather and analyze sprint data (e.g. completed tasks, communication patterns, roadblocks). They pitch:

- **AI-Suggested Talking Points:** Generates relevant discussion topics based on the analyzed data, helping teams focus on impactful issues.
- **AI Grouping** and **AI generated Action Items:** Help you easily streamline your retrospective.
- **Sentiment Analysis:** Analyzes team communications and feedback to gauge sentiment and identify underlying emotions or concerns.
- **Facilitation Assistance:** The AI can act as a co-facilitator, guiding the conversation and covering all key areas.
- **Team Members Accountability:** Helps identify, assign, and track action items that arise from the retrospective.

#### My Take
This is a bit of a mix.

The good: **Automated data collection** makes it more likely that valuable data comes to the Retrospective.

Only 'okay': **Analysis**, if used to augment and not replace human thinking, might spot hidden patterns. **Sentiment Analysis** of the team's conversations might spot overlooked patterns. However, the harm caused to Psychological Safety, knowing that an AI overlord always looks over our shoulders, exceeds the value.

Outright bad: Grouping exercises in Retrospectives are designed to start a conversation among team members about how problems are related. So **AI Grouping** and, worse, **AI generated Action Items** are replacing human insight, which is ironic since the humans still need to understand and solve the problem.

Baked into the tools, I looked at? The assumption that all of the meaningful interactions occur inside a JIRA, Asana or KanbanZone. Email, Slack, or real-world conversations are far more important in most teams.

<Figure
  src={aiScrumMaster}
  alt="sketch of GenAI assigning tasks to team members"
  caption="sketch of GenAI assigning tasks to team members"
/>
### AI Daily Scrum
You just can't make this up. One vendor promises to replace Daily Scrum with text, voice and video messages, then run reports on a schedule and share the reports with multiple Admins.

#### My Take
A Daily Scrum is an event to give the team time to understand what their peers are working on, hear about impediments others face, and to spark collaboration. None of this is served by an automated tool. This tool has nothing to do with Scrum, except that it stole the language. I can only imagine that a team using a tool like this will have low psychological safety and also be [micromanaged](/blog/scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement/) to the brink of extinction.

Not surprisingly, this same vendor, who completely misses the point of Scrum, pitched the ability of the tool to also run Retrospectives on autopilot by gathering notes and feedback from individual team member submissions and "Replace retrospective meetings with scheduled team surveys. …. Run retrospectives consistently on schedule". Is replacing human interaction with writing to an AI the way to build effective teams and positive work environments? Is keeping to a schedule the most important thing in a Retrospective?

### Generate Meeting Agendas and Take Notes
Several tools are offered to generate meeting agendas (planning, reviewing, and retrospectives) based on the current sprint's needs, and claim to make meetings more purposeful, efficient, and less time-consuming.

An AI meeting assistant auto joins, auto shares, and auto summarizes meetings. AI-powered meeting assistants help save professionals and teams an average of 4 hours a week and increase productivity by automatically generating action items, summaries, and follow-up emails.
<HighlightBox heading="Feel stuck for ideas?" float="right" variant="warning">
  FWIW, if you want more creative ideas for retrospectives, see the Retromat: [http://retromat.org/en](http://retromat.org/en)
</HighlightBox>
#### My Take
- How much time do we spend writing agendas? Minutes? Speed-ups in creating agendas seem to be of low value.
- Meeting summary and action items might be useful. It saves time, and the risk of errors seems low as long as the participants review the notes/actions immediately afterwards.

## Conclusion
So many tools out there promise to provide AI, making promises to solve all of your team's problems. I could write another five pages reviewing tools. Like any other Scrum-related improvement, take the time to breathe. Before we rush to adopt AI, take the time to look:
- Where is your team bottlenecked?
- Where would applying a GenAI help make the lives of all team members easier?
- Have we considered all the consequences, not just the hype the tool vendor is selling us?

GenAI is a valuable tool. However, it is not the only tool in a ScrumMaster's tool chest. In our [Certified ScrumMaster workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), we practice the collaboration, facilitation, and critical thinking skills that no AI can replace.

Good tools help you better understand your team and current circumstance. The real work of understanding a team and their work can't be automated.

Where have you found GenAI helping or harming your team?
<CalloutBox heading="Your Pain is Real">
Knowing how and when to use AI for your team's benefit is just one of many issues for Scrum teams today. Use [Effective Scrum](/effective-scrum/) to help improve your team, in a world that is increasingly challenging.
</CalloutBox>
