1	---
2	title: "The Jenga Effect: Why Clients Don't Make Good Product Owners"
3	date: "2025-06-10"
4	lastUpdated: '2025-06-10'
5	draft: false
6	categories: 
7	  - "product-ownership"
8	coverImage: '@/content/blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/images/client-as-product-owner.jpg'
9	excerpt: 'How having the client as Product Owner is a bit like playing Jenga with a blind fold. Entertaining to watch, painful to play.'
10	---
11	
12	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
13	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
14	import clientAsPO from '@/content/blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/images/client-as-product-owner.jpg';
15	
16	I recently met with a team where the client was the Product Owner. The team kept saying that their product backlog didn’t make sense. They didn’t understand the product they were trying to build, and they had never seen a vision or strategy. Despite all this, their PO was focused on more features, faster, now, please.
17	
18	Their product looked like a Jenga tower just before it was about to topple. This impacted quality, usability and, worse, the team was on the verge of burnout. They were getting whiplash from the number of misunderstandings the client had about how products get built.
19	<Figure
20	  src={clientAsPO}
21	  alt="illustration of client acting as product owner and the unstable product that results"
22	  caption="illustration of client acting as product owner and the unstable product that results"
23	/>
24	Let's think about the Product Owner role and how things could go sideways...
25	## Product Owner Responsibilities
26	- The Product Owner owns the vision - *why* are we building this product? Clients are the initial source for the vision information, but so, too, are ends users. Relying solely on the client's vision can easily lead to cognitive bias and have a team building the wrong thing at the wrong time.
27	- The PO owns the strategy - *how* we are getting there? Unless the client is fully experienced and informed, not only in the technology but also in the team, then they have no idea of the *how* and shouldn't be weighing in on it. 
28	- And the PO also owns prioritization - *what* do we work on next, and how can I justify it? Clients typically want everything now, or as soon as inhumanly possible, with no experience in matching priority to the team's capacity.
29	- Along with the product itself, Product Owners also need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security. Clients typically just want to know that it works. 
30	- POs collaborate with developers to agree on what a feature or user story is. (Sometimes with pencil sketches or discussions around acceptance criteria.) Clients would struggle to understand both the terminology and the techniques.
31	- POs balance stakeholder needs. If the client is acting as product owner, how unbiased do you think they would be able to be about multiple stakeholder requests?
32	
33	The PO needs to be empowered to make product decisions. A great Product Owner understands the big picture of product management, and they help Developers (i.e. team members) to understand all of the above. 
34	
35	POs also need to have ability to interview a variety of end users, digest the information, design and run experiments. And they need to develop a relationship with, and understanding of, the team so they can find a rhythm together (e.g. How much detail does the team need? What decisions can they handle independently?) Clients don't have the time, experience, or relationships to be able to do these. 
36	
37	
38	This only scratches the surface of a good PO's role. Many people, on discovering the work involved in being a PO, run away after a few months. In government, some people rotate out of their jobs every 6-12 months. That's not conducive to acting as product owner.
39	
40	What happens when someone without expertise steps into the product owner role?
41	
42	## Client as a Product Owner
43	People from the client side understand the business problem well, but not the product build.
44	
45	**Weaknesses**
46	- Don’t understand how product development works
47	- Don’t have experience working with a team
48	- Limited experience with all of the responsibilities mentioned above
49	- Not prepared to make it a full-time role
50	- … they’re missing almost all the skills and responsibilities mentioned above
51	
52	The main issue is that most clients lack the background in product work to play the role effectively. Instead of the client as PO, we’re better off with the client as a stakeholder. The Product Owner ensures the product solves their problem, but they do it while considering the big picture, not just the next feature. 
53	
54	## Conclusion
55	Effective Product Owners have a background in product management. In areas where they’re weak, they take time to learn, as it is their trade craft. Your client makes a good stakeholder, not a good Product Owner.
56	
57	Because the PO role takes ongoing investment, I keep a running list of [recommended books for Product Owners](/blog/recommended-books-for-product-owners/) to help POs keep building the craft.

I recently met with a team where the client was the Product Owner. The team kept saying that their product backlog didn’t make sense. They didn’t understand the product they were trying to build, and they had never seen a vision or strategy. Despite all this, their PO was focused on more features, faster, now, please.

Their product looked like a Jenga tower just before it was about to topple. This impacted quality, usability and, worse, the team was on the verge of burnout. They were getting whiplash from the number of misunderstandings the client had about how products get built.
<Figure
  src={clientAsPO}
  alt="illustration of client acting as product owner and the unstable product that results"
  caption="illustration of client acting as product owner and the unstable product that results"
/>
Let's think about the Product Owner role and how things could go sideways...
## Product Owner Responsibilities
- The Product Owner owns the vision - *why* are we building this product? Clients are the initial source for the vision information, but so, too, are ends users. Relying solely on the client's vision can easily lead to cognitive bias and have a team building the wrong thing at the wrong time.
- The PO owns the strategy - *how* we are getting there? Unless the client is fully experienced and informed, not only in the technology but also in the team, then they have no idea of the *how* and shouldn't be weighing in on it. 
- And the PO also owns prioritization - *what* do we work on next, and how can I justify it? Clients typically want everything now, or as soon as inhumanly possible, with no experience in matching priority to the team's capacity.
- Along with the product itself, Product Owners also need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security. Clients typically just want to know that it works. 
- POs collaborate with developers to agree on what a feature or user story is. (Sometimes with pencil sketches or discussions around acceptance criteria.) Clients would struggle to understand both the terminology and the techniques.
- POs balance stakeholder needs. If the client is acting as product owner, how unbiased do you think they would be able to be about multiple stakeholder requests?

The PO needs to be empowered to make product decisions. A great Product Owner understands the big picture of product management, and they help Developers (i.e. team members) to understand all of the above. 

POs also need to have ability to interview a variety of end users, digest the information, design and run experiments. And they need to develop a relationship with, and understanding of, the team so they can find a rhythm together (e.g. How much detail does the team need? What decisions can they handle independently?) Clients don't have the time, experience, or relationships to be able to do these. 


This only scratches the surface of a good PO's role. Many people, on discovering the work involved in being a PO, run away after a few months. In government, some people rotate out of their jobs every 6-12 months. That's not conducive to acting as product owner.

What happens when someone without expertise steps into the product owner role?

## Client as a Product Owner
People from the client side understand the business problem well, but not the product build.

**Weaknesses**
- Don’t understand how product development works
- Don’t have experience working with a team
- Limited experience with all of the responsibilities mentioned above
- Not prepared to make it a full-time role
- … they’re missing almost all the skills and responsibilities mentioned above

The main issue is that most clients lack the background in product work to play the role effectively. Instead of the client as PO, we’re better off with the client as a stakeholder. The Product Owner ensures the product solves their problem, but they do it while considering the big picture, not just the next feature. 

## Conclusion
Effective Product Owners have a background in product management. In areas where they’re weak, they take time to learn, as it is their trade craft. Your client makes a good stakeholder, not a good Product Owner.

Because the PO role takes ongoing investment, I keep a running list of [recommended books for Product Owners](/blog/recommended-books-for-product-owners/) to help POs keep building the craft.

2	title: "Scrum by Example – Don't Let Sprint Review be a Missed Opportunity"
3	date: "2021-10-12"

9	excerpt: 'Replace Show and Tell with Show and Play. Saving Boring Sprint Reviews one Step at a Time'
10	---
11	
12	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
13	import APRStoryOfASprintBoard121024x576 from '@/content/blog/dont-let-sprint-review-be-a-missed-opportunity/images/APR-Story-of-a-Sprint-board-12-1024x576.png';
14	import SbEWSOBSBuyerReviewsUnverifiedBuyer from '@/content/blog/dont-let-sprint-review-be-a-missed-opportunity/images/SbE-WSOBS-buyer-reviews-unverified-buyer.png';
15	import SbEWSOBSBuyerReviewsHelpfulVote from '@/content/blog/dont-let-sprint-review-be-a-missed-opportunity/images/SbE-WSOBS-buyer-reviews-helpful-vote.png';
16	
17	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
18	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
19	
20	<HighlightBox heading="Dramatis Personae" variant="caseStudy">
21	**Steve:**
22	A scrumMaster and the hero of our story
23	
24	**Paula:**
25	The Product Owner of Steve's team
26	</HighlightBox>
27	
28	When last we left our World's Smallest Online Bookstore team, their Sprint was rocky. To have an effective Sprint Review story, let's assume that they magically wound back the clock (shazam!) and implemented the changes. As a result, they had the more effective Sprint Planning that we discussed [in the last blog post](/blog/how-sprint-planning-mistakes-can-derail-a-team/).
29	
30	So let's quickly recap that last episode. The team set "Have basic reader review system in place so book buyers can see a variety of opinions about a book" as their Sprint Goal. (They had a weak Goal initially but, after they magically went back in time and did things different, that was the improved result.)
31	
32	They then selected the following Product Backlog Items:
33	
34	- Reader can add star ratings to a book
35	- Reader can write a review of a book (plain text only)
36	- Reader can add pictures to their reviews
37	- When a review is written by someone who purchased the book through our store, the system highlights their review as a "verified buyer"
38	- Registered site users can click a button to vote that a review is helpful
39	- Reader can format the text of their review
40	- Reviews feature the date they were written and the location of the author
41	- They also planned to fix two bugs that affect how books are displayed to buyers.
42	
43	The Sprint went surprisingly well. They finished the top five of seven items and fixed one bug. (_By the standards of many teams this is remarkably good._) They are now ready to hold a Sprint Review.
44	
45	Steve, being a well-organized ScrumMaster, has an agenda in place:
46	
47	- Remind the audience that the Sprint Review has a focus on the Product
48	- Restate the Sprint Goal and review if it has been met
49	- For each feature:
50	    - Team members demonstrate the features they worked on
51	    - Team checks features against the Definition of 'Done'
52	    - PO accepts or rejects an item[^1]
53	- PO, Stakeholders, and Team members discuss the Product Backlog and the Product Map (often a Story Map or Impact Map)
54	
55	Steve has invited all stakeholders to attend, which include the Team's Director, and the Directors of Support and Marketing.
56	
57	<Figure
58	  src={APRStoryOfASprintBoard121024x576}
59	  alt="Illustration of Scrum team meeting with shareholders, with the Product Owner moderating discussion."
60	  caption="Illustration of Scrum team meeting with shareholders, with the Product Owner moderating discussion."
61	/>
62	
63	
64	At the start of the Review, Steve reminds everyone of their Sprint Goal: "Have basic reader review system ….".
65	
66	Paula reports, "The team achieved the core of that goal, with a reader review system ready on staging server. All I have to do is press a button and the new version is live on the site."
67	
68	She then hands over the stage to team member Ian to start walking through the features that the team have built.
69	
70	Director of Support Eric's phone starts buzzing and he disappears into it, apologizing to the room. "Sorry, we have a problem with some users not being able to see their account order history."
71	
72	The first few features that Ian demonstrates garner almost no feedback except people saying vague things like "Good job" and "I like that". There are no substantive questions or suggestions offered.
73	
74	When Ian demonstrates the Product Backlog Item "Reviews from a verified buyer are highlighted and displayed above other reviews", Paula asks a few questions about the behaviour of the feature. She also checks the Definition of Done and learns from the team it is Done except for testing the text-only book review in Safari on MacOS and iPad.
75	
76	<Figure
77	  src={SbEWSOBSBuyerReviewsUnverifiedBuyer}
78	  alt="Placeholder example of an online review with a 1-5 star rating"
79	  caption="Placeholder example of an online review with a 1-5 star rating"
80	/>
81	
82	
83	Jan, the Director of Marketing, asks, "How are we handling fraudulent reviews? Our reviews have always been from staff. That has been a differentiator. If we take this feature live, we lose our ability to differentiate on that."
84	
85	Paula replies, "But we've verified that the buyer bought the book, so their review is legitimate."
86	
87	"There is a black market for reviews, and the book seller might pay the reviewer $10 for a good review and reimburse them the cost of the book," explains Jan. "Although we verified that they bought the book, we haven't verified that they read the book or that this is their honest opinion."
88	
89	After a lot more discussion it's agreed that it's okay to leave the verified buyer tag on the reviews since most are legitimate. However, they won't be featured or placed higher on the page. They will just appear in the normal sort order.
90	
91	Ian is almost afraid to bring up the next feature, "Registered site users can click a button to vote that a review is helpful". He wonders what unexpected problem will be found next.
92	
93	As he shows the feature, Jan interrupts. "We can't have that at all. It's another source of fraud. Sellers will often pay for many users to click the helpful review button on any review that has 4+ star rating. Their goal is to bury critical reviews."
94	
95	<Figure
96	  src={SbEWSOBSBuyerReviewsHelpfulVote}
97	  alt="A placeholder example of an online review from a verified buyer of a product"
98	  caption="A placeholder example of an online review from a verified buyer of a product"
99	/>
100	
101	
102	At this point Paula can't contain her frustration. "Why didn't you tell us this before? Why wait until we wasted the team's effort on implementing these features?"
103	
104	Jan snaps back, "I tried to warn you about fraud weeks ago, but you didn't listen."
105	
106	Realizing that the event has spiralled out beyond his ability to facilitate, ScrumMaster Steve asks for a ten-minute break. When everyone returns to the room, he suggests that they wind down the Sprint Review early, since they now have the list of features that were accepted and the ones that need more work.
107	
108	As they leave, Ian mutters under his breath, "That was a ton of fun. Next time I'm asked to do the demo, the answer is NO!"
109	
110	### Analysis
111	
112	What happened? Steve was exceptionally well-prepared. He had a thoughtful agenda and yet most features got no feedback. Of the people present, some (like Eric) were engaged only with their phone and they never participated in discussing upcoming product priorities.
113	
114	Done well, a Sprint Review is a point of pride for the team. This one was a downer for their morale, even though some of the work that was completed made the product better.
115	
116	#### Challenges:
117	
118	- The Sprint Review was a Show and _Tell_. The goal is to increase engagement with stakeholders and end-users, not _decrease_ it. If you ask the team members who worked on each feature to demo it, it's likely to result in an unnecessarily long, tedious monologue, or demonstration of every nook and cranny of the feature, putting attendees to sleep. Having Paula demo alone would be just as bad. She might script a better story and make it seem more fun, but "Telling" — aka talking at other people — decreases engagement.
119	- The Definition of Done wasn't checked _before_ the Sprint Review. This is critical. It is the way the team and the Product Owner know that they're on the same page with respect to quality. However, much of the "Done" is just going to put the audience to sleep, so going through the process during the Sprint Review isn't practical.
120	- The Director of Support was more engaged with his phone than in participating in the Review. We missed the opportunity for his feedback and we don't know if his team's needs are being well represented.
121	- The surprise around the two features and how fraud mitigation wasn't included indicates that the Marketing Director wasn't involved enough in the Roadmap (hint: StoryMap) or Ongoing Backlog Refinement.
122	- No end users were involved in the Sprint Review. Without their input, all of the feedback that was delivered was theoretical and from people who are involved day-to-day with the Product, so hardly objective.
123	- Underdeveloped facilitation skills showed through. As Steve grows in the role of ScrumMaster over time, he might prepare in advance for conflict. Knowing that it will or might happen, he could have a short reset exercise ready to go that will cool tempers and improve relations so the Review can continue and the conflict can get resolved, rather than postponed. _In the early stages of a ScrumMaster's journey, it is a little unfair to expect them to know how to facilitate through conflict._
124	
125	### What could they do differently next time?
126	
127	It starts long before the Sprint Review meeting. When the strategic work is done in Product Backlog Refinement, ScrumMaster Steve and Product Owner Paula need to make sure that key stakeholders, like Jan (Marketing) and Eric (Support), are involved. ScrumMaster and Product Owner should also commit to spending a couple of hours a month reviewing the strategy and looking for things that might turn into surprises. When there are items that represent more risk or challenge, Paula can invite the Stakeholders to the Backlog Refinement session so they can provide input and clarity. These two actions will go a long way toward reducing surprises in the Sprint Review.
128	
129	Seeing a feature get reviewed by the PO and checked against the Definition of Done has never been a recipe to increase engagement. As an alternative, Paula could review features as fully completed, having already checked them against "Done" prior to the Sprint Review. This approach fits well in a world of Continuous Delivery, something many modern teams are already employ. As a good final check just before Sprint Review, Paula could recheck all features to make sure they work well together.
130	
131	Get End Users in the room. Where humanly possible involve actual users of the product to get feedback, to learn more about their needs, and generate enthusiasm. _There are clear limits as most users won't have the time or energy to participate every Sprint._
132	
133	Replace Show and Tell with Show and Play. Have someone who knows the product well show the high-level features. Have each developer pair with a stakeholder/end-user and invite them to play with the product. As much as possible they should focus only on the work completed in this Sprint. Show and Play helps the users and other stakeholders discover how the product actually works, it generates a much deeper level of feedback, and it helps team members learn more about the needs of real users.
134	
135	A good Sprint Review gets features accepted and deployed. A **great** Sprint Review engages the attendees and creates productive discussion around product direction and business priorities.
136	
137	<CalloutBox heading="Learn more about how to hold great Sprint Reviews">
138	
139	Consider attending one of our [Certified ScrumMaster workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), where we discuss the _how_ and _why_ of Scrum, not just the _what_.  You'll get hands-on practical experience, and learn about some of the challenges – and solutions – along with tips on how to help your Team learn and grow to realize their potential.
140	
141	</CalloutBox>
142	
143	[^1]: Hint: this shouldn't be the first time the PO sees a feature

1	---
2	title: 'Psychological Safety'
3	date: '2021-03-25'
4	lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
5	relatedTerms: ['blame-chet', 'failure-bow', 'scrum-team', 'self-organization']
6	excerpt: 'Psychological safety is about being part of a team and knowing that you can share'
7	---
8	
9	import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
10	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
11	
12	**Psychological safety** is about being part of a team and knowing that you can share ideas and information without fear. Psychological safety isn’t the avoidance of conflict, rather it is knowing that we can share information inside a team instead of focusing on protecting ourselves.
13	
14	> "The belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes, and that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking" - Amy Edmondson, 1999
15	
16	It isn't just trust. We can trust each other and not be safe. Psychological safety requires that we know that if we take a chance or make a mistake, that we will be supported and not punished.
17	
18	As safety increases, communication within the team becomes more open. This openness leads to better awareness of what is really happening in the work environment.
19	
20	As communication improves, mistakes are reported and fixed more rapidly.
21	
22	It is a virtuous circle.
23	
24	## What psychological safety isn't
25	
26	Psychological safety isn't agreement for the sake of agreement. Rather, it's an environment where we know we can be honest about what we have seen and not be punished for it. Warning: safety isn't an excuse to highlight the mistakes we see in other people on our team. It is about being able to acknowledge our own mistakes and what we learned without repercussions.
27	
28	Amy Edmonsen, who has written the book on the subject, uses the following survey to test a team’s level of safety:
29	
30	1. If you make a mistake on this team, it is often held against you.
31	2. Members of this team are able to bring up problems and tough issues.
32	3. People on this team sometimes reject others for being different.
33	4. It is safe to take a risk on this team.
34	5. It is difficult to ask other members of this team for help.
35	6. No one on this team would deliberately act in a way that undermines my efforts.

title: 'Psychological Safety'
date: '2021-03-25'
lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
relatedTerms: ['blame-chet', 'failure-bow', 'scrum-team', 'self-organization']
excerpt: 'Psychological safety is about being part of a team and knowing that you can share'
---

import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';

**Psychological safety** is about being part of a team and knowing that you can share ideas and information without fear. Psychological safety isn’t the avoidance of conflict, rather it is knowing that we can share information inside a team instead of focusing on protecting ourselves.

> "The belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes, and that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking" - Amy Edmondson, 1999

It isn't just trust. We can trust each other and not be safe. Psychological safety requires that we know that if we take a chance or make a mistake, that we will be supported and not punished.

As safety increases, communication within the team becomes more open. This openness leads to better awareness of what is really happening in the work environment.

As communication improves, mistakes are reported and fixed more rapidly.

It is a virtuous circle.

## What psychological safety isn't

Psychological safety isn't agreement for the sake of agreement. Rather, it's an environment where we know we can be honest about what we have seen and not be punished for it. Warning: safety isn't an excuse to highlight the mistakes we see in other people on our team. It is about being able to acknowledge our own mistakes and what we learned without repercussions.

Amy Edmonsen, who has written the book on the subject, uses the following survey to test a team’s level of safety:

1. If you make a mistake on this team, it is often held against you.
2. Members of this team are able to bring up problems and tough issues.
3. People on this team sometimes reject others for being different.
4. It is safe to take a risk on this team.
5. It is difficult to ask other members of this team for help.
6. No one on this team would deliberately act in a way that undermines my efforts.
7. Working with members of this team, my unique skills and talents are valued and utilized.

People answer on a scale of Strongly Agree -> Strongly Disagree. Once the survey has been run, the team can use the data to help themselves see how they might evolve.

Timothy Clark - 2020 - has extended the concept to four levels: included; safe environment to learn; safe to contribute; safe to challenge the status quo.

1	---
2	title: 'Impediments'
3	date: '2023-11-10'
4	lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
5	relatedTerms: ['anti-patterns','interruptions', 'scrummaster-role']
6	excerpt: 'Anything that slows the teams progress towards, it's goals is an impediment. Missing knowledge or skills, stuck waiting for a decision, ...'
7	---
8	
9	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
10	import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
11	
12	In the context of a Scrum team, **anything that slows the team’s progress towards the Sprint Goal is an impediment.** And since one of the primary responsibilities in the role as Scrum Master is removing impediments to the Scrum team’s progress, it’s important to have a clear understanding on this point.
13	
14	All too often I hear Developers in [Daily Scrum](/blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/) mention the same chunk of work 4-5 days running and say, “No Blockers.” Why is that? Experience tells me there is a heap of factors, but the biggest seems to be that we don’t have a common understanding of **what an impediment is**.
15	
16	## Understanding what is an impediment in Scrum
17	
18	According to the _Cambridge Dictionary_, an impediment is “something that makes progress, movement, or achieving something difficult or impossible”[^1].
19	
20	But in Scrum, it goes further. And until our teams recognize what impediments are, they can’t get resolved. For example, these are all Scrum impediments:
21	- Low bandwidth connection while working from home
22	- Email interruptions
23	- Slack or MS teams scrolling messages at an alarming rate
24	- Interruptions - People outside the team asking for help (either other teams or management)
25	- Lack of information (e.g.. interacting with a poorly understood legacy system)
26	- Missing technical knowledge or skills
27	- Waiting for another team
28	- Waiting for a third-party vendor
29	- Team member out sick
30	- Access or permissions problems that prevent team members from accessing a server or making database changes
31	- Language or cultural barriers with an offshore team
32	- Poorly understood Product Backlog Item/User Story
33	- Low understanding how this Product Backlog Item fits into the overall product and delivers value to the customer
34	- Slow computer
35	- Frequent broken builds
36	- Poor quality chair or desk, small computer monitor
37	- Slow decision-making
38	- Changing requirement mid-Sprint
39	- Bottlenecks in the Team (e.g. worked piled in front of Business Analysts, Developers or QA)
40	- Too many cat photos in the team's Slack stream 🙂
41	- …
42	
43	Anything that slows the team’s progress towards the Sprint Goal is an impediment.
44	
45	### Spot the Problem
46	
47	There are a couple of tricks and tips that I’ve found to help make impediments more apparent. First, change the word to “slowdowns” – it’s a lot easier to admit to being slowed by something,  than it is being impeded (which suggests stopped). Go deeper as the Certified ScrumMaster, and look at [the Sprint Backlog](/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/) or Kanban board to spot items that have spent several days in the same state (e.g. “In Progress”, “waiting for test” etc.). These items are likely impeded by something.
48	
49	Is work piling up? Sometimes bottlenecks or missing skills create impediments. Too many teams don’t even notice that they have bottlenecks, but they’re great indicators of areas where cross-skilling will be a benefit and make the team more efficient.
50	
51	## How to remove impediments in Scrum
52	
53	The _Scrum Guide_ says the Scrum Master can act as an impediment remover by “causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress”. This sounds comically obvious and simple on the surface, and yet it gets misinterpreted. Too many teams think that it’s the Scrum Master’s job to directly remove the impediments. “Scrum Master, I’m out of coffee (or sticky notes), can you get me more?” This is clearly ridiculous. A good ScrumMaster helps the team learn to remove their own impediments. They aren’t a magician who waves a wand and does it all for you.
54	
55	Even if the Scrum Master were to remove all impediments, the team would only learn that when they had a problem the Scrum Master would solve it for them. The Scrum Master would turn into a babysitter – an unwelcome prospect.
56	
57	So what’s effective? This is where the ScrumMaster role can have a huge beneficial impact by promoting self-organization, and striking a balance between firefighting problems that crop up and preventing the impediments in the first place.
58	
59	When there is a problem, I encourage Scrum Masters to ask their team member(s):
60	- what they already tried toward solving the impediment
61	- if they asked the rest of the team for help
62	- whether they ever had similar problems before and what worked in resolving those
63	
64	### Tougher than it looks
65	
66	If all of the above has been explored and the impediment to the Scrum team still remains, the problem is probably beyond the capacity of the team to solve on their own. However, before running around problem-solving, there is still more work for our Scrum Master to do, to be able to fix anything effectively. They should explore:
67	- Is this the first time we’ve had an impediment like this?
68	- If this is a repeated impediment, why has it reoccurred? (Hint: often because the last solution was a band-aid fix.)
69	- Do we need to address this immediately or can the challenge become a learning opportunity for the team?
70	- What else is going on here?
71	
72	That last point is probably the most important, but hardest, one to deal with. Instead of using the popular but weaker techniques of 5 Whys or Root Cause Analysis[^2], dig into Systems Thinking to find the underlying issues. Use this understanding to address the real issues in the system, and not just the surface-level problems.
73	
74	## The Scrum Master role when impediments occur
75	
76	The Scrum Master shouldn’t solve impediments on their own. It’s important that they give the team autonomy and let them self-organize. Encourage them to take ownership and find their own solution to many impediments.
77	
78	When an impediment is one that the team can’t solve themselves, then the Scrum Master’s responsibility is to step in. Review team history for similar impediments. How were they resolved (or not)? What were the underlying causes? By identifying the real problem, and not just the surface issue, the impediment can be removed permanently, and not affect the team’s progress again in the future.
79	
80	[^1]: [Cambridge Dictionary](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/impediment)
81	[^2]: These approaches are weaker because they tend to find recent things and not the deeper problems.
82	
83	<LinkList heading="Agile Pain Relief Blog Entries">
84	    - [Beyond the Surface: GenAI-Powered Critical Thinking for Deep Team Issues](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/)

---
title: 'Impediments'
date: '2023-11-10'
lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
relatedTerms: ['anti-patterns','interruptions', 'scrummaster-role']
excerpt: 'Anything that slows the teams progress towards, it's goals is an impediment. Missing knowledge or skills, stuck waiting for a decision, ...'
---

import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';

In the context of a Scrum team, **anything that slows the team’s progress towards the Sprint Goal is an impediment.** And since one of the primary responsibilities in the role as Scrum Master is removing impediments to the Scrum team’s progress, it’s important to have a clear understanding on this point.

All too often I hear Developers in [Daily Scrum](/blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/) mention the same chunk of work 4-5 days running and say, “No Blockers.” Why is that? Experience tells me there is a heap of factors, but the biggest seems to be that we don’t have a common understanding of **what an impediment is**.

## Understanding what is an impediment in Scrum

According to the _Cambridge Dictionary_, an impediment is “something that makes progress, movement, or achieving something difficult or impossible”[^1].

But in Scrum, it goes further. And until our teams recognize what impediments are, they can’t get resolved. For example, these are all Scrum impediments:
- Low bandwidth connection while working from home
- Email interruptions
- Slack or MS teams scrolling messages at an alarming rate
- Interruptions - People outside the team asking for help (either other teams or management)
- Lack of information (e.g.. interacting with a poorly understood legacy system)
- Missing technical knowledge or skills
- Waiting for another team
- Waiting for a third-party vendor
- Team member out sick
- Access or permissions problems that prevent team members from accessing a server or making database changes
- Language or cultural barriers with an offshore team
- Poorly understood Product Backlog Item/User Story
- Low understanding how this Product Backlog Item fits into the overall product and delivers value to the customer
- Slow computer
- Frequent broken builds
- Poor quality chair or desk, small computer monitor
- Slow decision-making
- Changing requirement mid-Sprint
- Bottlenecks in the Team (e.g. worked piled in front of Business Analysts, Developers or QA)
- Too many cat photos in the team's Slack stream 🙂
- …

Anything that slows the team’s progress towards the Sprint Goal is an impediment.

### Spot the Problem

There are a couple of tricks and tips that I’ve found to help make impediments more apparent. First, change the word to “slowdowns” – it’s a lot easier to admit to being slowed by something,  than it is being impeded (which suggests stopped). Go deeper as the Certified ScrumMaster, and look at [the Sprint Backlog](/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/) or Kanban board to spot items that have spent several days in the same state (e.g. “In Progress”, “waiting for test” etc.). These items are likely impeded by something.

Is work piling up? Sometimes bottlenecks or missing skills create impediments. Too many teams don’t even notice that they have bottlenecks, but they’re great indicators of areas where cross-skilling will be a benefit and make the team more efficient.

## How to remove impediments in Scrum

The _Scrum Guide_ says the Scrum Master can act as an impediment remover by “causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress”. This sounds comically obvious and simple on the surface, and yet it gets misinterpreted. Too many teams think that it’s the Scrum Master’s job to directly remove the impediments. “Scrum Master, I’m out of coffee (or sticky notes), can you get me more?” This is clearly ridiculous. A good ScrumMaster helps the team learn to remove their own impediments. They aren’t a magician who waves a wand and does it all for you.

Even if the Scrum Master were to remove all impediments, the team would only learn that when they had a problem the Scrum Master would solve it for them. The Scrum Master would turn into a babysitter – an unwelcome prospect.

So what’s effective? This is where the ScrumMaster role can have a huge beneficial impact by promoting self-organization, and striking a balance between firefighting problems that crop up and preventing the impediments in the first place.

When there is a problem, I encourage Scrum Masters to ask their team member(s):
- what they already tried toward solving the impediment
- if they asked the rest of the team for help
- whether they ever had similar problems before and what worked in resolving those

### Tougher than it looks

If all of the above has been explored and the impediment to the Scrum team still remains, the problem is probably beyond the capacity of the team to solve on their own. However, before running around problem-solving, there is still more work for our Scrum Master to do, to be able to fix anything effectively. They should explore:
- Is this the first time we’ve had an impediment like this?
- If this is a repeated impediment, why has it reoccurred? (Hint: often because the last solution was a band-aid fix.)
- Do we need to address this immediately or can the challenge become a learning opportunity for the team?
- What else is going on here?

That last point is probably the most important, but hardest, one to deal with. Instead of using the popular but weaker techniques of 5 Whys or Root Cause Analysis[^2], dig into Systems Thinking to find the underlying issues. Use this understanding to address the real issues in the system, and not just the surface-level problems.

## The Scrum Master role when impediments occur

The Scrum Master shouldn’t solve impediments on their own. It’s important that they give the team autonomy and let them self-organize. Encourage them to take ownership and find their own solution to many impediments.

When an impediment is one that the team can’t solve themselves, then the Scrum Master’s responsibility is to step in. Review team history for similar impediments. How were they resolved (or not)? What were the underlying causes? By identifying the real problem, and not just the surface issue, the impediment can be removed permanently, and not affect the team’s progress again in the future.

[^1]: [Cambridge Dictionary](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/impediment)
[^2]: These approaches are weaker because they tend to find recent things and not the deeper problems.

content.thinking:
I've gathered all nine sources and need to decide how to deliver the ten drafts. The skill defaults to chat, but that's a lot of content for a single message. Mark hasn't explicitly asked for a file, though his memory indicates drafts should go to the vault in APR/Efforts/Social Media/ with filenames ending in -drafts when he does request that format. I'm weighing whether the volume warrants a file despite no direct request.

The no-unsolicited-files rule is strong, so I'll deliver in chat but structure it efficiently—organizing the ten drafts across five days with two posts each, mixing the sources strategically and providing the angle, draft, and source for each post. I'm starting to draft the first post about how GenAI won't speed up Scrum events, using Mark's own language heavily. The angle is that rushing through these events misses their real purpose—they're not just about planning outcomes, but about building deep team understanding. I'll include a link to the source and wrap it with a practitioner takeaway that gives readers something actionable to take back to their teams.

The key reframe I'm making is shifting from "how can GenAI make this faster?" to "how can GenAI help us collaborate better and catch what we'd otherwise miss?" That changes what's actually worth doing with the tool in these contexts.

GenAI can genuinely help stress-test a Sprint plan or validate work against your Definition of Done, but it's a mistake to let it write your Sprint Goal or break down tasks for you—that's where the critical thinking happens. The real risk is that GenAI amplifies whatever you're already doing, good or bad, so you need to make sure your events are actually valuable before you introduce it.

Now I'm thinking about the next post on product management. The core insight is that building has become cheap, but figuring out what to build hasn't. I noticed at Product Camp that when I asked about shipping AI-generated features, roughly a third to half the room had done it—but when I dug into whether those features were based on user-tested hypotheses first, the hands went down significantly.

The real bottleneck isn't code generation anymore; it's still quality assurance and validation. We're generating more features than we can test, which is like adding more cars to a highway that's already congested upstream. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of discovery and prototyping, but that should mean we spend more time thinking and learning about what users actually need, not less. The danger is going through the motions of building without that deeper understanding.

Now I'm thinking about a different angle for the next post—how GenAI creates this confidence gap where it sounds most certain about things you should trust least.

The core issue is that these language models work by predicting the next word sequentially, which is fundamentally different from how humans think through problems. Research shows that the more confident the tool sounds, the more we believe it, regardless of whether the information is actually accurate. It'll find patterns in noise and present them with complete certainty, even when there's no real signal there.

That doesn't mean avoiding GenAI entirely—it means using it thoughtfully. Before introducing it to a team, I consider whether it genuinely improves how we work together, whether it's solving a real bottleneck or just trimming minutes off a task that's already quick, and whether we have enough expertise to spot when it gets things wrong. GenAI is useful, but it's one tool among many, and the actual work of understanding a team's needs still requires human judgment.

I'm thinking through a situation where a client served as the Product Owner, and things fell apart. They didn't grasp their own product, had no clear vision or strategy, yet kept demanding more features faster. The team's work resembled a Jenga tower on the verge of collapse—quality suffered, usability tanked, and the constant whiplash from the client's misunderstandings about product development was burning everyone out. The real issue was that the PO role wasn't being fulfilled properly. A Product Owner needs to own the vision and the why, the strategy and the how, and the prioritization decisions with clear reasoning behind them.

The client understood their business problem but lacked the product development background to do the role justice. They weren't prepared to commit full-time, and in government settings they'd rotate out every six to twelve months—the opposite of what the role demands. The better approach is to keep clients as stakeholders rather than Product Owners. A strong Product Owner ensures the product solves the client's problem while maintaining the broader vision, not just chasing the next feature request.

I'm thinking about how teams can wobble like a Jenga tower when this dynamic isn't managed well.

---

Now I'm working on the next post about Sprint Reviews. The problem is that most of them become passive presentations where stakeholders just nod along without offering real feedback. I watched one recently where early features got vague praise and no substantive questions, while the Director of Support checked his phone. Then later features got heavily criticized—the timing and engagement were completely off.

The real issue is that these concerns should surface during Backlog Refinement when Marketing and Support are actually at the table, not explode during the Review itself. The solution is shifting from Show and Tell to Show and Play: walk through the high-level work, then pair developers with stakeholders and end users to actually interact with the product hands-on. This generates much richer feedback than passive demos ever could.

A solid Sprint Review gets features accepted and deployed, but a truly great one engages people and sparks meaningful conversation about where the product should go next.

Psychological safety gets misunderstood in two ways. First, people confuse it with trust—but you can trust someone and still not feel safe speaking up. Safety, as Edmondson defines it, is the belief that you won't be punished or humiliated for sharing ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes. Second, people think it means avoiding conflict or enforcing agreement, when really it's the opposite—higher safety actually produces more honest disagreement, not less. When safety increases, communication opens up, people become more aware of what's actually happening in the work, and mistakes get caught and fixed faster. It's a reinforcing cycle.

But there's an important caveat: safety isn't a free pass to criticize everyone else. It's about being able to own your own mistakes and what you learned from them without fear of repercussions. Edmondson has a short survey to measure where a team actually stands—questions like "If you make a mistake on this team, is it held against you?" and "Is it safe to take a risk on this team?" can help teams see where they are and how they might improve.

---

A Sprint Goal isn't just "complete all the stories we committed to" or "finish seven stories"—that completely misses the point. A real Sprint Goal is a single product objective that the whole team shares, describing why the Sprint matters and keeping everyone aligned. Process-oriented goals like "finish the stories" don't explain why the work matters; a good goal helps the team understand the business objective so they're doing more than just checking off tasks. The Product Owner doesn't impose it either—they explain the business objective, then the team collaborates with them to figure out what's actually feasible.

Because everyone helps create the goal, everyone feels more ownership and purpose during the Sprint. Once you have one, it pays dividends: a clear goal makes it easier to prioritize backlog items, judge whether feedback is relevant, and explain the work to stakeholders. Some teams even add "Do we still believe in our Sprint Goal?" to their Daily Scrum, which is a solid habit.

When a team struggles to set a goal, it's usually a sign that the underlying business strategy is unclear—that's worth investigating rather than giving up on the goal entirely. Sprint Goals are genuinely hard and often misunderstood, so many teams just skip them quietly, which is a real missed opportunity.

I'm also thinking about whether teams are actually setting goals around outcomes or just tracking story counts, and then moving into a discussion about impediments—specifically how "no blockers" for days in a row often means the team doesn't share a common definition of what an impediment actually is. The real issue is that anything slowing progress toward the Sprint Goal counts as an impediment, not just the dramatic blockers.

I'm noting that reframing "impediment" as "slowdown" makes it easier for people to acknowledge when they're being slowed by something—whether that's a poor connection, constant interruptions, waiting on another team, unclear requirements, broken builds, slow decisions, or changing requirements mid-Sprint. Looking at items stuck in the same state on the board for days is usually a sign something's impeding them. There's also a misconception about whose job it is to remove impediments—many teams think the ScrumMaster should directly fix every single one.

A good ScrumMaster actually helps the team learn to solve their own problems and only steps in when it's truly beyond them. When the same impediment keeps recurring, I should avoid the 5 Whys approach since it tends to surface only recent and shallow causes. Instead, I'd use Systems Thinking to find the root issue and fix that. The real question is what impediment has the team stopped noticing because it's just become normal.

Now I'm drafting a newsletter angle about how Canada's AI strategy measures adoption as a proxy for productivity, which misses the point entirely. Using AI to quickly generate a presentation from bullet points might be faster, but that's not productivity if nobody wanted the presentation in the first place or if the person creating it learned nothing. The strategy focuses on five key areas including healthcare, but measuring adoption this way is fundamentally measuring the wrong thing.

The real issue is an old measurement trap in new clothes: when you optimize for tool adoption instead of actual outcomes, you get more tool usage and no improvement in what actually matters. Healthcare systems won't improve just because AI adoption numbers go up on a dashboard. Teams fall into this constantly, counting story points or shipped features as if those equal value. I'm also predicting we'll see a lot of "AI washing" where standard machine learning gets rebranded as AI over the next few years.

So if someone asks you to measure GenAI adoption on your team, the better question is what outcome you're actually trying to improve instead.

Now I'm thinking about a different angle—whether having more agents in a system automatically makes it better. I ran an experiment asking Claude to do deep research on newsletter lead magnets, and it spawned a whole swarm of agents to handle the task, which turned out to be a mistake.

The system created 150 agents analyzing 50 different claims with a three-vote consensus rule, and it consumed my entire daily token limit just to produce three pages with only two genuinely useful insights. The real takeaway is that people often assume you can use multiple agents to cancel out each other's mistakes, but that doesn't work—if each agent is imperfect, stacking them together just multiplies the problems rather than solving them.

More compute and more agents isn't the same as actually making the tool smarter. One of the two insights that did land was solid though: direct recommendations from existing readers are the most effective way to grow a newsletter. I'm now thinking about the links I need to add for the newsletter posts, particularly connecting to the Canada AI Strategy piece. I'll complete the URL list with the remaining posts and then consider whether to use emoji in the content, leaning toward Mark's more understated style.

For hashtags, I'm thinking minimal usage—maybe #EffectiveScrum on a couple of the Scrum-focused posts, but keeping the GenAI content clean without tags. Once these drafts are actually posted, I'll need to log them in the launch promotion table as the skill requires.

I'll organize these 10 drafts by day with clean formatting, noting the angle and source for each one.

content.text:
All nine sources read. Here are 10 drafts across 5 days, built mostly from your own sentences. Structure follows your batch recipe: 2 recent blog + 3 older blog + 3 glossary + 1 newsletter (A/B from the 2026-07-21 issue). Each is ready to edit, not finished. Pick any to sharpen and I'll drop into review mode.

---

## Day 1

### Post 1 - Recent blog: [GenAI Won't Speed Up Your Scrum Events](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/)
**Angle:** The pull toward speed skips the understanding the event exists to build.

> Shortly after ChatGPT 4o came out, I saw people talking about doing Backlog Refinement in minutes with GenAI. Most people have realized that's just not a good idea.
>
> Here's why speeding through the events doesn't help. At surface level it looks like we hold Sprint Planning to plan the outcome for the Sprint. That's true, but the real story is much deeper. Sprint Planning is really about the team having a deep conversation to understand the Sprint Goal, their capacity, and how they'll actually get there. The benefit isn't a Sprint Backlog that looks like a Tetris board. It's a team that has a good understanding of what they're working toward.
>
> The pull with GenAI is always toward speed. But a faster event doesn't build that understanding, it skips it. So instead of asking how GenAI can make the event quicker, ask a different question: how can the tool help team members spot details that might get missed, look at deeper issues, and improve collaboration?
>
> That reframe changes what's worth doing. GenAI is genuinely useful for stress-testing a Sprint plan, checking Product Backlog Items against the Definition of Done, or digging deeper on an impediment. It's a poor idea for writing your Sprint Goal or breaking work into tasks for you, because that's exactly where you shut down the critical thinking that good judgement needs.
>
> If you can significantly speed up any of these events with GenAI, then you're probably not getting the value out of them in the first place. In my experience GenAI amplifies what you're already doing, both good and bad. So before you introduce it, make sure you're already facilitating events people actually want to participate in.
>
> Where has GenAI helped or hurt your Scrum events?
>
> https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/

**Source lines:** "doing Backlog Refinement in minutes"; "The benefit of Sprint Planning isn't a Sprint Backlog that looks like a Tetris board"; "a faster event doesn't build that understanding; it skips it"; "shut down the critical thinking required for good judgement"; "If you can significantly speed up any of these events... you're probably not getting the value out of it"; "GenAI amplifies what you're already doing. Both good and bad."

### Post 2 - Recent blog: [Product Management with GenAI](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/product-management-and-genai/)
**Angle:** Building is cheap now; building the right thing is not. Discovery matters more, not less.

> I'm seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They're full of features that don't fit well together, and some of them don't solve a real problem.
>
> Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.
>
> At Product Camp Ottawa I asked a room how many had shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code. About a third to a half put their hands up. Then I asked how many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written. Only three people, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI.
>
> Here's the mechanism. Before GenAI, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance. With GenAI that problem doesn't change; we still have more features than we can possibly test. No one would suggest putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck, yet that's exactly what we're doing when we generate more code. (Classic Theory of Constraints.)
>
> So what should Product Management do? Every feature is a hypothesis: if we build this, it will solve a specific problem for a group of users. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of Discovery, running experiments, building prototypes, analyzing user data. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning, not less.
>
> The biggest risk is going through the motions: theatre, running the discovery process without learning anything. Ask one question this week: what did we learn that changed our plan? If nothing, it's theatre.
>
> Building great products still comes down to the same things: talking to real users, running experiments, and listening to the feedback.
>
> https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/product-management-and-genai/

**Source lines:** "Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive"; the three Product Camp questions and "roughly 15%"; "putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck... Classic Theory of Constraints"; "Every feature that is built is a hypothesis"; "what did we learn this week that changed our plan? If nothing, it's theatre"; "talking to real users, running experiments, and listening to the feedback."

---

## Day 2

### Post 3 - Older blog: [Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/)
**Angle:** The confidence gap - GenAI sounds most sure exactly when you should trust it least.

> GenAI's superpower is speed, its ability to churn out text faster than any human. But there's a catch: it sounds too confident for what it actually "knows".
>
> ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers keep asking me whether it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most of those questions come from a misunderstanding of how the current tools actually work. GenAI, properly called a Large Language Model, takes the text in your prompt and predicts the next word, then feeds the result back in and predicts the next, one word at a time. That is not how a human works. We consider what we want to express and then find the best way to say it.
>
> The greatest danger sits right there. Research on the impact of GenAI on critical thinking found that the more confident the tool sounds, the more likely we are to believe it, even though there's no correlation between that confidence and whether the information is any good. It will find a signal in noise even when there's no signal. It starts its reply with "that's a great idea" whether or not it is.
>
> None of that means don't use it. It means use it with guardrails. Before reaching for GenAI in your team, I ask a few questions: does this enhance collaboration? Is it addressing the team's actual bottleneck, or just shaving five minutes off a ten-minute task? Can we afford the errors it will make, and do we know the subject well enough to catch them?
>
> GenAI is a valuable tool. It just isn't the only tool in a ScrumMaster's tool chest, and the real work of understanding a team and their situation can't be automated.
>
> Where have you found GenAI helping or harming your team?
>
> https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/

**Source lines:** "AI's superpower is speed... it sounds too confident for what it actually 'knows'"; the next-word prediction description; "the more confident the AI sounds, the more likely we are to believe it"; "it will find a signal in noise even when there is no signal"; "shaving 5 minutes off a 10-minute task is not a win"; "not the only tool in a ScrumMaster's tool chest"; "The real work of understanding a team and their work can't be automated."

### Post 4 - Older blog: [The Jenga Effect](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/)
**Angle:** Client-as-PO looks efficient and quietly topples the product.

> I recently met a team where the client was the Product Owner. They kept saying their Product Backlog didn't make sense. They didn't understand the product they were trying to build, and they'd never seen a vision or a strategy. Despite all that, their PO wanted more features, faster, now, please.
>
> Their product looked like a Jenga tower just before it topples. It hit quality and usability, and worse, the team was on the verge of burnout from the whiplash of the client's misunderstandings about how products actually get built.
>
> It helps to be clear about what the role involves. The Product Owner owns the vision, the why behind the product. They own the strategy, the how of getting there. They own prioritization, the what we work on next and the reason for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, and build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together. Clients typically just want to know that it works.
>
> People from the client side understand the business problem well, but not the product build. That's not a character flaw, it's a different trade. Most clients lack the background in product work to play the role effectively, aren't prepared to make it a full-time job, and in government often rotate out every 6 to 12 months, which is the opposite of what the role needs.
>
> So don't make your client the Product Owner. Make them a stakeholder. A good Product Owner ensures the product solves the client's problem, but does it while holding the big picture, not just the next feature.
>
> Have you watched the Jenga tower wobble on a team you've worked with?
>
> https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/

**Source lines:** the opening client-as-PO story verbatim; "Jenga tower just before it was about to topple"; the vision/strategy/prioritization (why/how/what) breakdown; "Clients typically just want to know that it works"; "rotate out of their jobs every 6-12 months"; "client as a stakeholder... not just the next feature."

---

## Day 3

### Post 5 - Older blog: [Don't Let Sprint Review be a Missed Opportunity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/dont-let-sprint-review-be-a-missed-opportunity/)
**Angle:** Show and Tell puts everyone to sleep; Show and Play gets real feedback.

> Too many Sprint Reviews are a Show and Tell. Someone demos every nook and cranny of a feature while the room nods along, says "good job", and offers nothing substantive. The goal of the event is to increase engagement with stakeholders and end users, not decrease it, and talking at people does the opposite.
>
> I watched one go sideways recently. Every early feature drew vague praise and no real questions. The Director of Support spent the meeting on his phone. Then two features got torn apart late, once for a fraud risk that Marketing had apparently flagged weeks earlier, and the whole thing spiralled until the ScrumMaster called an early stop. By the end the developer doing the demo muttered that next time he's asked, the answer is no.
>
> Two things would have changed that day. First, it starts long before the meeting: when the strategic work happens in Product Backlog Refinement, make sure key stakeholders like Marketing and Support are actually involved, so their concerns surface early instead of exploding in the Review. Second, replace Show and Tell with Show and Play. ## Day 1

### Post 1 - Recent blog: GenAI Won't Speed Up Your Scrum Events
**Angle:** The pull toward speed skips the understanding the event exists to build.

Shortly after ChatGPT 4o came out, I saw people talking about doing Backlog Refinement in minutes with GenAI. Most people have realized that's just not a good idea.

The benefit isn't a Sprint Backlog that looks like a Tetris board. It's a team that has a good understanding of what they're working toward.

The pull with GenAI is always toward speed. But a faster event doesn't build that understanding, it skips it. So instead of asking how GenAI can make the event quicker, ask a different question: how can the tool help team members spot details that might get missed, look at deeper issues, and improve collaboration?

That reframe changes what's worth doing. GenAI is genuinely useful for stress-testing a Sprint plan, checking Product Backlog Items against the Definition of Done, or digging deeper on an impediment. It's a poor idea for writing your Sprint Goal or breaking work into tasks for you, because that's exactly where you shut down the critical thinking that good judgement needs.

If you can significantly speed up any of these events with GenAI, then you're probably not getting the value out of them in the first place. In my experience GenAI amplifies what you're already doing, both good and bad. So before you introduce it, make sure you're already facilitating events people actually want to participate in.

### Post 2 - Recent blog: Product Management with GenAI
**Angle:** Building is cheap now; building the right thing is not. Discovery matters more, not less.

I'm seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They're full of features that don't fit well together, and some of them don't solve a real problem.

Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.

At Product Camp Ottawa I asked a room how many had shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code. About a third to a half put their hands up. Then I asked how many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written. Only three people, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI.

Here's the mechanism. Before GenAI, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance. With GenAI that problem doesn't change; we still have more features than we can possibly test. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning, not less.

The biggest risk is going through the motions: theatre, running the discovery process without learning anything. Ask one question this week: what did we learn that changed our plan? If nothing, it's theatre.

Building great products still comes down to the same things: talking to real users, running experiments, and listening to the feedback.

## Day 2

### Post 3 - Older blog: Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster
**Angle:** The confidence gap - GenAI sounds most sure exactly when you should trust it least.

GenAI's superpower is speed, its ability to churn out text faster than any human. But there's a catch: it sounds too confident for what it actually "knows".

ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers keep asking me whether it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most of those questions come from a misunderstanding of how the current tools actually work. GenAI, properly called a Large Language Model, takes the text in your prompt and predicts the next word, then feeds the result back in and predicts the next, one word at a time. That is not how a human works. We consider what we want to express and then find the best way to say it.

The greatest danger sits right there. Research on the impact of GenAI on critical thinking found that the more confident the tool sounds, the more likely we are to believe it, even though there's no correlation between that confidence and whether the information is any good. It will find a signal in noise even when there's no signal. It starts its reply with "that's a great idea" whether or not it is.

None of that means don't use it. It means use it with guardrails. Before reaching for GenAI in your team, I ask a few questions: does this enhance collaboration? Is it addressing the team's actual bottleneck, or just shaving five minutes off a ten-minute task? Can we afford the errors it will make, and do we know the subject well enough to catch them?

GenAI is a valuable tool. It just isn't the only tool in a ScrumMaster's tool chest, and the real work of understanding a team and their situation can't be automated.

### Post 4 - Older blog: The Jenga Effect
**Angle:** Client-as-PO looks efficient and quietly topples the product.

I recently met a team where the client was the Product Owner. They kept saying their Product Backlog didn't make sense. They didn't understand the product they were trying to build, and they'd never seen a vision or a strategy. Despite all that, their PO wanted more features, faster, now, please.

Their product looked like a Jenga tower just before it topples. It hit quality and usability, and worse, the team was on the verge of burnout from the whiplash of the client's misunderstandings about how products actually get built.

It helps to be clear about what the role involves. The Product Owner owns the vision, the why behind the product. They own the strategy, the how of getting there. They own prioritization, the what we work on next and the reason for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, and build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together. Clients typically just want to know that it works.

People from the client side understand the business problem well, but not the product build. That's not a character flaw, it's a different trade. Most clients lack the background in product work to play the role effectively, aren't prepared to make it a full-time job, and in government often rotate out every 6 to 12 months, which is the opposite of what the role needs.

So don't make your client the Product Owner. Make them a stakeholder. A good Product Owner ensures the product solves the client's problem, but does it while holding the big picture, not just the next feature.

23	## 1. Blog — Canada's AI Strategy (recent, touch 4)
24	**URL:** /blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/
25	*Prior touches used AI-washing, adoption-isn't-productivity, ER-triage-vs-beds. These two open fresh veins.*
26	
27	### Option A — the family-doctor symptom (most distinct)
28	🩺 Here's a piece of Canada's AI story you don't hear in the strategy documents. After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour: the doctor is paid for the visit, and the documentation is treated as overhead.
29	
30	To reduce that unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both diagnoses and medications, yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive without making a big difference.
31	
32	Because even where GenAI helps, we've only solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses, which isn't their training, and to handle a large pile of administrative tasks on top of seeing patients. That burden is a major factor in their burnout, and burnout is a big reason there aren't enough family doctors, which pushes more people into overflowing emergency rooms.
33	
34	Transcription tools may help, but they don't touch the underlying problem. We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.
35	
36	Where in your organization is GenAI quietly making a symptom feel better while the real bottleneck stays put?
37	
38	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
39	
40	### Option B — measure outcome, not adoption
41	📉 Canada has a real productivity problem, and we have for decades. In 1984 the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked; by 2022 it had fallen to 71%. The new national AI strategy promises to fix that with a 3 percent GDP boost by raising business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034.
42	
43	Notice what's being measured: adoption. And adoption of AI doesn't make an organization more productive. Dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. Worse, a target built on an adoption rate invites AI washing, because when success is measured by how many organizations are "doing AI," they'll claim they are to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.
44	
45	Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn't make it so. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottleneck, and focus on eliminating that bottleneck. That's slower and less headline-friendly than an adoption target, and it's the only thing that actually moves the number.
46	
47	What would it take for your organization to measure the outcome instead of the adoption rate?
48	
49	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

53	## 2. Blog — Backlog Refinement Anti-Patterns (recent, touch 1)
54	**URL:** /blog/how-many-of-these-backlog-refinement-anti-patterns-does-your-team-have/
55	
56	### Option A (i) — assigned work
57	🗂️ How many of these backlog refinement anti-patterns does your team have? Here's the one I see most: assigned work. During refinement, the team decides who will work on which item. But refinement is about understanding the work, not assigning it. In Scrum there is no assigned work, period.
58	
59	It usually travels with a sibling: drifting into Sprint Planning. Instead of shaping the work and building shared understanding, the session turns into deciding who does what and committing to it. The conversation that was supposed to give everyone a common picture of the work has quietly become a scheduling exercise.
60	
61	A couple more worth naming, because they're common and quiet. Refining too far ahead, detailing items six or more Sprints out that may never get built. Acceptance-criteria gold-plating, where the Product Owner writes 15 criteria covering every edge case and kills the conversation (I delay detailed acceptance criteria until after Sprint Planning). And "present but absent," where people attend while buried in laptops and Slack.
62	
63	None of these is fatal on its own. Stacked together, they turn refinement into theatre.
64	
65	Which one is your team's most stubborn? I'd like to hear about it.
66	
67	#Scrum #ProductOwner
68	
69	### Option A (ii) — the shared-understanding illusion
70	🗂️ Product Backlog Refinement has a quiet failure mode: everyone nods that they understand the item, and yet each person is holding a different picture in their head. It looks like agreement. It isn't. The gap only surfaces mid-Sprint, when the work turns out to mean three different things to three different people.
71	
72	A couple of anti-patterns feed that. Jumping to the solution, where the team designs the "how" before anyone has agreed on the "why" and the "what." And forgetting the user and the why altogether, treating refinement as a queue of tickets to process rather than problems to solve for real people. The people and their needs should be front and centre.
73	
74	When you're stuck and don't have agreement about a feature, write an example. In adult life, when two people get stuck in a conversation, we reach for an example to break the logjam, then somehow forget to do it as a team. It can be a pencil sketch of the interface, or a quick happy path showing how someone would actually use the feature. My rule is just enough detail to get everyone on the same page, and I delay the detailed acceptance criteria until after Sprint Planning.
75	
76	The goal isn't a tidy backlog. It's a team that leaves the conversation holding the same picture.
77	
78	Which item on your board does everyone "understand" in a slightly different way?
79	
80	#Scrum #ProductOwner

84	## 3. Blog — Recommended Scrum Team Size (older)
85	**URL:** /blog/scrum-team-size/
86	
87	### Option A — the relationships math
88	👥 What's the optimal Scrum team size? My honest answer is that there's no single right number, but there's a lot of signal in how relationships grow. On a team of 5 there are 10 relationships to form. A team of 7 has 21, and a team of 9 has 36. Each new person adds some individual productivity, but they also add an exponentially growing number of relationships to maintain.
89	
90	That's why bigger teams don't get proportionally more done. To go from 5 to 7, you more than double the relationships that have to be built and kept healthy. In teams of 7-8 I've watched upwards of 90 minutes per person each day go into interacting with teammates, and as the group grows past that, people quietly withdraw from those interactions rather than lose their productive time, which is exactly the connective tissue a high-performing team needs.
91	
92	So when clients ask, I share the data and my experience: teams of 4-6 work well for most situations. They form faster and are as productive as larger ones, and a team of 5-6 can usually cross-skill enough to survive losing a member.
93	
94	What size has actually worked for your team? Too small, too big, or just right?
95	
96	#Scrum
97	
98	### Option B — bigger isn't faster
99	🧩 We all want to believe that going from 2 people to 4 doubles what a team gets done. We know intuitively it doesn't, and Amdahl's Law explains why: some work happens in parallel, but some has to happen one step at a time, and that serial part sets a ceiling no amount of extra people can lift. Even when 80% of the work parallelises, it takes 3 people to double one person's output, and 16 to quadruple it.
100	
101	Speed doesn't come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from building a high-performing team that's the right size for communication and quality. With teams of 9 or larger, I recommend splitting into two, because separate teams of 4 and 5 reliably get more done than the original large one.
102	
103	But the number of people was never the most important question. The real one is this: does the team have the capacity to get to truly Done, shippable, at the end of every Sprint? If it doesn't, that's your signal to re-examine the size and shape of the team, whatever the headcount happens to be.
104	
105	Is your team sized for looking busy, or for reaching Done every Sprint?
106	
107	#Scrum
108
