111	## 4. Newsletter — "Too Much Work in Progress" (2026-07-08)
112	**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
113	*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Both options come from the same issue.)*
114	
115	### Option A — Claude, the worst manager
116	🗃️ My friend Claude just told me a batch of experiments it designed for me had failed. That's odd, because they were never run. When Claude first suggested them they seemed interesting, but they were never the most important thing to do, most stayed hidden, and I simply forgot. Claude had assigned them target dates out of thin air, the dates passed, and now it was reporting failure.
117	
118	At moments like these Claude feels like the worst manager ever. No sense of priority. No understanding of Work In Progress or human capacity. It had no idea what else I had going on.
119	
120	Two problems, and neither is really about the tool. The experiments became commitments, and they were never visible. We constantly remind Scrum and Kanban teams to visualise the work and limit Work In Progress, and here I was caught in the same trap, with a GenAI assistant cheerfully making it worse.
121	
122	The fix is the boring one we already teach: put the experiments on a board where I can see what already exists and what else I've committed to, then limit how much is in flight at once.
123	
124	Where is an eager tool, or an eager stakeholder, quietly turning your maybes into commitments?
125	
126	#Agile
127	
128	### Option B — we preach it, then break it
129	📋 We constantly remind Scrum and Kanban teams to visualise the work and limit Work In Progress. Then we go and break our own advice. I certainly did.
130	
131	I let a GenAI assistant hand me a pile of experiments, each one plausible, none of them the most important thing to do. They never went on a board, so they were invisible, and invisible work has a way of becoming quiet commitments that follow you around. The experiments weren't the problem. Committing to all of them, and never making them visible, was.
132	
133	Before I build a board and plan even more experiments, there's a more basic question hiding underneath: what are people actually struggling with? What do they need help with? Piling up more work in progress felt like momentum, but the honest next step is smaller and slower, which is to talk to more people before running anything.
134	
135	That's the uncomfortable thing about limiting WIP. It isn't really about the board. It's about admitting that starting more things is not the same as finishing the things that matter.
136	
137	What's one thing you could stop starting this week?
138	
139	#Agile
140

143	## 5. Glossary — Technical Debt
144	**URL:** /glossary/technical-debt/
145	
146	### Option A — Cunningham's real point
147	💳 Technical Debt is one of the most misunderstood terms in our field. Ward Cunningham coined it back in 1992, and his original point was subtle: "Shipping first-time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with refactoring. The danger occurs when the debt is not repaid."
148	
149	Read that again, because most of us get it backwards. In Cunningham's definition, technical debt is okay when it's paid back promptly. It's a deliberate, short-term trade to move faster now, on the condition that you circle back and clean up.
150	
151	Somewhere along the way the term got hijacked to mean any mess left behind when a team rushes through the code because they feel pressure to get more done faster. That's not debt in Cunningham's sense, that's just an unpaid bill piling up interest.
152	
153	So the practical question isn't "do we have technical debt?" Every codebase does. It's "which debt did we take on deliberately, and are we actually paying it back?" A team that never refactors isn't avoiding debt, it's defaulting on it.
154	
155	When did your team last deliberately pay down a piece of technical debt, rather than just adding to it?
156	
157	#Scrum
158	
159	### Option B — the gym full of chairs
160	🏋️ Here's how I explain Technical Debt to non-technical people. Imagine your developers are in a large gym. Time how long it takes them to run across and back, and repeat until the number is stable. Now scatter a few chairs across the middle at random and ask them to run again. They're slower. Add more chairs. Eventually there are so many they can't walk around them, and they have to crawl to get across the room.
161	
162	The chairs are the technical debt. The extra time is the interest your team pays on it, every day, on every trip across the room. Nobody chose to make the gym unusable; the chairs just accumulated a few at a time until moving became painful.
163	
164	There's a new source of chairs worth naming. AI-generated code has become a major new source of technical debt. It's fast and it often runs, which is exactly what makes the chairs easy to add without noticing, until the day the team is crawling.
165	
166	The point isn't to keep the gym perfectly empty. It's to keep it clear enough that people can still run.
167	
168	How many chairs has your team quietly added this year, and when will you clear a few?
169	
170	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
171	
172	---

174	## 6. Glossary — Causal Loop Diagram
175	**URL:** /glossary/causal-loop-diagram/
176	
177	### Option A — draw it together
178	🔄 A Causal Loop Diagram is a simple visual that helps a group understand cause and effect: which things are increasing or decreasing, and how they push on each other. It sounds academic, but I reach for it whenever a team is stuck applying quick fix after quick fix to a problem that keeps coming back.
179	
180	The magic isn't the diagram, it's drawing it together. A CLD works best when people build it as a group, because the real value is the shared understanding that gets teased out while you argue about which arrow points where. One person's "obvious" cause turns out to be someone else's effect, and that conversation is the point.
181	
182	Once it's on the wall, it does something a bulleted list can't. It makes the loops visible: the reinforcing loops that quietly make a problem worse over time, and the balancing ones holding things in an uncomfortable equilibrium. That's how you move from treating symptoms to finding the leverage point that actually shifts the system.
183	
184	Next time your team solves the same problem for the third time, try drawing the loop together before you propose another fix.
185	
186	What recurring problem on your team might actually be a loop you haven't drawn yet?
187	
188	#Agile
189	
190	### Option B — spotting what you didn't intend
191	🔁 Before your team makes a big change, it's worth asking a question we usually skip: what might this set in motion that we didn't intend? A Causal Loop Diagram is a good tool for that. Because it maps how variables push on each other, it makes second- and third-order effects visible before you ship the change, not after.
192	
193	I also use CLDs to reason about dysfunction. When a team, an organization, or a system keeps misbehaving in the same way, drawing the loops often shows why. And they're especially useful for bottlenecks: instead of just noting that a bottleneck exists, you can ask why it keeps coming back, and trace the loop that keeps refilling it.
194	
195	That last one matters, because most bottlenecks aren't one-off events. They're the output of a loop. Clear the queue today and, if the loop is intact, it fills right back up next week. The diagram helps you find the leverage point that breaks the loop rather than the symptom that just relieves it for a Sprint.
196	
197	Where does your team keep clearing the same bottleneck, only to watch it return?
198	
199	#Agile
200	
201	---
202	
203	## 7. Glossary — Cross-Functional Teams
204	**URL:** /glossary/cross-functional-teams/
205	
206	### Option A — Done or Not Done
207	🤝 In the Agile world, a cross-functional team is one that has all the skills it needs to get the work finished, without relying on outside help. That's a mouthful, so here's what it looks like: a mix of development, analysis, testing, and design, held not by one specialist per skill but by people who already have several, or are willing to learn them. We call them T-shaped or M-shaped: deep in one or two areas, useful in several others.
208	
209	Why go to the trouble? Because when analysis, development, and quality assurance happen together inside one team, quality goes up. There are no handoffs between departments, feedback is rapid, and the work moves in small chunks instead of big batches that hide errors.
210	
211	Transparency is where it shows up most. A team that delivers complete features every Sprint can't play the game of declaring work 75% done and then blaming the next group downstream. With a cross-functional team, work is either Done or Not Done at the end of the Sprint. There is no 75%.
212	
213	Does your team own enough of the work to say Done and mean it, or does "done" still depend on a handoff?
214	
215	#Scrum
216	
217	### Option B — not departments
218	🚧 Cross-functional teams are not departments, and treating them as synonyms causes a lot of quiet pain. A department is organized by role or job title: the development group here, the QA group down the hall. A cross-functional team is organized around the work, from the moment a feature is considered until it's delivering value to a customer.
219	
220	The difference shows up as waiting. Whenever a team depends on an outside person or group, it spends time waiting for its high-priority work to reach the top of someone else's list. Inside a cross-functional team there's far less work that has to happen elsewhere, and even when a handoff remains, it happens in small chunks rather than big batches thrown over a wall.
221	
222	There's a culture shift too. When quality assurance is part of your team, and not another group down the hall, there's less griping about "their" work and more shared effort on improving it. The us-versus-them softens, because it's just us.
223	
224	Most teams don't start at the ideal, and that's fine. The point is the direction: fewer handoffs, less waiting, and a team that can see the customer at the end of the work.
225	
226	Where is your team still waiting on a group down the hall, and what would it take to pull that skill inside?
227	
228	#Scrum
229	
230	---
231	
232	## 8. Glossary — Story Mapping
233	**URL:** /glossary/story-mapping/
234	
235	### Option A — why Patton built it
236	🗺️ A Story Map is a way to visualize the flow, or the story, of a product. Across the top you place the major steps in the user's workflow, often the big features, in the order someone moves through them. Underneath each step sit the individual stories that build out that part of the product. In one picture you see both the whole journey and the detail.
237	
238	Jeff Patton invented story mapping out of frustration. He was tired of "flat" Product Backlogs, those long single-column lists that lose all track of the Product Vision. A flat backlog tells you what's next, but not how any of it fits together or why. A Story Map keeps the shape of the product visible while you work.
239	
240	That's why people use it as a stepping stone from Vision to User Stories. Instead of jumping straight from a big idea to a pile of tickets, you lay out the user's journey first, then slice stories against it, which makes it far easier to spot gaps and to choose a thin first slice that still tells a complete story.
241	
242	If your backlog is a flat list nobody can hold in their head, a Story Map might be the missing picture.
243	
244	What does your team lose when the backlog becomes one long column?
245	
246	#Scrum #ProductOwner
247	
248	### Option B — life raft for a huge backlog
249	🧭 Drowning in an oversized Product Backlog? A Story Map is a good life raft. When a backlog has grown into hundreds of items in one flat list, nobody can see the product anymore, only the pile. Story mapping gives that pile back its shape.
250	
251	The move is to stop reading the backlog top to bottom and instead lay it out as a journey. Across the top go the major steps in the user's workflow; underneath each step you arrange the stories that belong to it. Suddenly duplicates sit next to each other, whole regions of the map turn out to be features nobody will ever build, and the gaps you were missing become obvious.
252	
253	From there you can do the thing a flat list makes hard: draw a line and choose a thin first slice across the whole journey, enough to deliver a coherent product rather than a random handful of tickets. The rest stays on the map, visible but clearly below the line, instead of buried in a thousand-item list.
254	
255	Jeff Patton built this because flat backlogs lose the Product Vision. If yours has, the map is often the fastest way to find it again.
256	
257	When did you last delete a whole region of your backlog, rather than just adding to it?
258	
259	#Scrum #ProductOwner

🗂️ How many of these backlog refinement anti-patterns does your team have? Here's the one I see most: assigned work. During refinement, the team decides who will work on which item. But refinement is about understanding the work, not assigning it. In Scrum there is no assigned work, period.

It usually travels with a sibling: drifting into Sprint Planning. Instead of shaping the work and building shared understanding, the session turns into deciding who does what and committing to it. The conversation that was supposed to give everyone a common picture of the work has quietly become a scheduling exercise.

A couple more worth naming, because they're common and quiet. Refining too far ahead, detailing items six or more Sprints out that may never get built. Acceptance-criteria gold-plating, where the Product Owner writes 15 criteria covering every edge case and kills the conversation (I delay detailed acceptance criteria until after Sprint Planning). And "present but absent," where people attend while buried in laptops and Slack.

None of these is fatal on its own. Stacked together, they turn refinement into theatre.

Which one is your team's most stubborn? I'd like to hear about it.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

### Option A (ii) — the shared-understanding illusion
🗂️ Product Backlog Refinement has a quiet failure mode: everyone nods that they understand the item, and yet each person is holding a different picture in their head. It looks like agreement. It isn't. The gap only surfaces mid-Sprint, when the work turns out to mean three different things to three different people.

A couple of anti-patterns feed that. Jumping to the solution, where the team designs the "how" before anyone has agreed on the "why" and the "what." And forgetting the user and the why altogether, treating refinement as a queue of tickets to process rather than problems to solve for real people. The people and their needs should be front and centre.

When you're stuck and don't have agreement about a feature, write an example. In adult life, when two people get stuck in a conversation, we reach for an example to break the logjam, then somehow forget to do it as a team. It can be a pencil sketch of the interface, or a quick happy path showing how someone would actually use the feature. My rule is just enough detail to get everyone on the same page, and I delay the detailed acceptance criteria until after Sprint Planning.

The goal isn't a tidy backlog. It's a team that leaves the conversation holding the same picture.

Which item on your board does everyone "understand" in a slightly different way?

#Scrum #ProductOwner

## 3. Blog — Recommended Scrum Team Size (older)
**URL:** /blog/scrum-team-size/

### Option A — the relationships math
👥 What's the optimal Scrum team size? My honest answer is that there's no single right number, but there's a lot of signal in how relationships grow. On a team of 5 there are 10 relationships to form. A team of 7 has 21, and a team of 9 has 36. Each new person adds some individual productivity, but they also add an exponentially growing number of relationships to maintain.

That's why bigger teams don't get proportionally more done. To go from 5 to 7, you more than double the relationships that have to be built and kept healthy. In teams of 7-8 I've watched upwards of 90 minutes per person each day go into interacting with teammates, and as the group grows past that, people quietly withdraw from those interactions rather than lose their productive time, which is exactly the connective tissue a high-performing team needs.

So when clients ask, I share the data and my experience: teams of 4-6 work well for most situations. They form faster and are as productive as larger ones, and a team of 5-6 can usually cross-skill enough to survive losing a member.

What size has actually worked for your team? Too small, too big, or just right?

#Scrum

### Option B — bigger isn't faster
🧩 We all want to believe that going from 2 people to 4 doubles what a team gets done. We know intuitively it doesn't, and Amdahl's Law explains why: some work happens in parallel, but some has to happen one step at a time, and that serial part sets a ceiling no amount of extra people can lift. Even when 80% of the work parallelises, it takes 3 people to double one person's output, and 16 to quadruple it.

Speed doesn't come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from building a high-performing team that's the right size for communication and quality. With teams of 9 or larger, I recommend splitting into two, because separate teams of 4 and 5 reliably get more done than the original large one.

But the number of people was never the most important question. The real one is this: does the team have the capacity to get to truly Done, shippable, at the end of every Sprint? If it doesn't, that's your signal to re-examine the size and shape of the team, whatever the headcount happens to be.

Is your team sized for looking busy, or for reaching Done every Sprint?

#Scrum

## 5. Glossary — Technical Debt
**URL:** /glossary/technical-debt/

### Option A — Cunningham's real point
💳 Technical Debt is one of the most misunderstood terms in our field. Ward Cunningham coined it back in 1992, and his original point was subtle: "Shipping first-time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with refactoring. The danger occurs when the debt is not repaid."

Read that again, because most of us get it backwards. In Cunningham's definition, technical debt is okay when it's paid back promptly. It's a deliberate, short-term trade to move faster now, on the condition that you circle back and clean up.

Somewhere along the way the term got hijacked to mean any mess left behind when a team rushes through the code because they feel pressure to get more done faster. That's not debt in Cunningham's sense, that's just an unpaid bill piling up interest.

So the practical question isn't "do we have technical debt?" Every codebase does. It's "which debt did we take on deliberately, and are we actually paying it back?" A team that never refactors isn't avoiding debt, it's defaulting on it.

When did your team last deliberately pay down a piece of technical debt, rather than just adding to it?

#Scrum

### Option B — the gym full of chairs
🏋️ Here's how I explain Technical Debt to non-technical people. Imagine your developers are in a large gym. Time how long it takes them to run across and back, and repeat until the number is stable. Now scatter a few chairs across the middle at random and ask them to run again. They're slower. Add more chairs. Eventually there are so many they can't walk around them, and they have to crawl to get across the room.

The chairs are the technical debt. The extra time is the interest your team pays on it, every day, on every trip across the room. Nobody chose to make the gym unusable; the chairs just accumulated a few at a time until moving became painful.

There's a new source of chairs worth naming. AI-generated code has become a major new source of technical debt. It's fast and it often runs, which is exactly what makes the chairs easy to add without noticing, until the day the team is crawling.

The point isn't to keep the gym perfectly empty. It's to keep it clear enough that people can still run.

How many chairs has your team quietly added this year, and when will you clear a few?

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

## 6. Glossary — Causal Loop Diagram
**URL:** /glossary/causal-loop-diagram/

### Option A — draw it together
🔄 A Causal Loop Diagram is a simple visual that helps a group understand cause and effect: which things are increasing or decreasing, and how they push on each other. It sounds academic, but I reach for it whenever a team is stuck applying quick fix after quick fix to a problem that keeps coming back.

The magic isn't the diagram, it's drawing it together. A CLD works best when people build it as a group, because the real value is the shared understanding that gets teased out while you argue about which arrow points where. One person's "obvious" cause turns out to be someone else's effect, and that conversation is the point.

Once it's on the wall, it does something a bulleted list can't. It makes the loops visible: the reinforcing loops that quietly make a problem worse over time, and the balancing ones holding things in an uncomfortable equilibrium. That's how you move from treating symptoms to finding the leverage point that actually shifts the system.

Next time your team solves the same problem for the third time, try drawing the loop together before you propose another fix.

What recurring problem on your team might actually be a loop you haven't drawn yet?

#Agile

### Option B — spotting what you didn't intend
🔁 Before your team makes a big change, it's worth asking a question we usually skip: what might this set in motion that we didn't intend? A Causal Loop Diagram is a good tool for that. Because it maps how variables push on each other, it makes second- and third-order effects visible before you ship the change, not after.

I also use CLDs to reason about dysfunction. When a team, an organization, or a system keeps misbehaving in the same way, drawing the loops often shows why. And they're especially useful for bottlenecks: instead of just noting that a bottleneck exists, you can ask why it keeps coming back, and trace the loop that keeps refilling it.

That last one matters, because most bottlenecks aren't one-off events. They're the output of a loop. Clear the queue today and, if the loop is intact, it fills right back up next week. The diagram helps you find the leverage point that breaks the loop rather than the symptom that just relieves it for a Sprint.

Where does your team keep clearing the same bottleneck, only to watch it return?

#Agile

## 7. Glossary — Cross-Functional Teams
**URL:** /glossary/cross-functional-teams/

### Option A — Done or Not Done
🤝 In the Agile world, a cross-functional team is one that has all the skills it needs to get the work finished, without relying on outside help. That's a mouthful, so here's what it looks like: a mix of development, analysis, testing, and design, held not by one specialist per skill but by people who already have several, or are willing to learn them. We call them T-shaped or M-shaped: deep in one or two areas, useful in several others.

Why go to the trouble? Because when analysis, development, and quality assurance happen together inside one team, quality goes up. There are no handoffs between departments, feedback is rapid, and the work moves in small chunks instead of big batches that hide errors.

Transparency is where it shows up most. A team that delivers complete features every Sprint can't play the game of declaring work 75% done and then blaming the next group downstream. With a cross-functional team, work is either Done or Not Done at the end of the Sprint. There is no 75%.

Does your team own enough of the work to say Done and mean it, or does "done" still depend on a handoff?

#Scrum

### Option B — not departments
🚧 Cross-functional teams are not departments, and treating them as synonyms causes a lot of quiet pain. A department is organized by role or job title: the development group here, the QA group down the hall. A cross-functional team is organized around the work, from the moment a feature is considered until it's delivering value to a customer.

The difference shows up as waiting. Whenever a team depends on an outside person or group, it spends time waiting for its high-priority work to reach the top of someone else's list. Inside a cross-functional team there's far less work that has to happen elsewhere, and even when a handoff remains, it happens in small chunks rather than big batches thrown over a wall.

There's a culture shift too. When quality assurance is part of your team, and not another group down the hall, there's less griping about "their" work and more shared effort on improving it. The us-versus-them softens, because it's just us.

Most teams don't start at the ideal, and that's fine. The point is the direction: fewer handoffs, less waiting, and a team that can see the customer at the end of the work.

Where is your team still waiting on a group down the hall, and what would it take to pull that skill inside?

#Scrum

## 8. Glossary — Story Mapping
**URL:** /glossary/story-mapping/

### Option A — why Patton built it
🗺️ A Story Map is a way to visualize the flow, or the story, of a product. Across the top you place the major steps in the user's workflow, often the big features, in the order someone moves through them. Underneath each step sit the individual stories that build out that part of the product. In one picture you see both the whole journey and the detail.

Jeff Patton invented story mapping out of frustration. He was tired of "flat" Product Backlogs, those long single-column lists that lose all track of the Product Vision. A flat backlog tells you what's next, but not how any of it fits together or why. A Story Map keeps the shape of the product visible while you work.

That's why people use it as a stepping stone from Vision to User Stories. Instead of jumping straight from a big idea to a pile of tickets, you lay out the user's journey first, then slice stories against it, which makes it far easier to spot gaps and to choose a thin first slice that still tells a complete story.

If your backlog is a flat list nobody can hold in their head, a Story Map might be the missing picture.

What does your team lose when the backlog becomes one long column?

#Scrum #ProductOwner

### Option B — life raft for a huge backlog
🧭 Drowning in an oversized Product Backlog? A Story Map is a good life raft. When a backlog has grown into hundreds of items in one flat list, nobody can see the product anymore, only the pile. Story mapping gives that pile back its shape.

The move is to stop reading the backlog top to bottom and instead lay it out as a journey. Across the top go the major steps in the user's workflow; underneath each step you arrange the stories that belong to it. Suddenly duplicates sit next to each other, whole regions of the map turn out to be features nobody will ever build, and the gaps you were missing become obvious.

From there you can do the thing a flat list makes hard: draw a line and choose a thin first slice across the whole journey, enough to deliver a coherent product rather than a random handful of tickets. The rest stays on the map, visible but clearly below the line, instead of buried in a thousand-item list.

Jeff Patton built this because flat backlogs lose the Product Vision. If yours has, the map is often the fastest way to find it again.

When did you last delete a whole region of your backlog, rather than just adding to it?

#Scrum #ProductOwner

## Day 1

### Post 1 — Recent blog: GenAI Won't Speed Up Your Scrum Events
**URL:** /blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/
**Angle:** The pull toward speed skips the understanding the event exists to build.

Shortly after ChatGPT 4o came out, I saw people talking about doing Backlog Refinement in minutes with GenAI. Most people have realized that's just not a good idea.

Here's why speeding through the events doesn't help. At surface level it looks like we hold Sprint Planning to plan the outcome for the Sprint. That's true, but the real story is much deeper. Sprint Planning is really about the team having a deep conversation to understand the Sprint Goal, their capacity, and how they'll actually get there. The benefit isn't a Sprint Backlog that looks like a Tetris board. It's a team that has a good understanding of what they're working toward.

The pull with GenAI is always toward speed. But a faster event doesn't build that understanding, it skips it. So instead of asking how GenAI can make the event quicker, ask a different question: how can the tool help team members spot details that might get missed, look at deeper issues, and improve collaboration?

That reframe changes what's worth doing. GenAI is genuinely useful for stress-testing a Sprint plan, checking Product Backlog Items against the Definition of Done, or digging deeper on an impediment. It's a poor idea for writing your Sprint Goal or breaking work into tasks for you, because that's exactly where you shut down the critical thinking that good judgement needs.

If you can significantly speed up any of these events with GenAI, then you're probably not getting the value out of them in the first place. In my experience GenAI amplifies what you're already doing, both good and bad. So before you introduce it, make sure you're already facilitating events people actually want to participate in.

### Post 2 — Recent blog: Product Management with GenAI
**URL:** /blog/product-management-and-genai/
**Angle:** Building is cheap now; building the right thing is not. Discovery matters more, not less.

I'm seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They're full of features that don't fit well together, and some of them don't solve a real problem.

Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.

At Product Camp Ottawa I asked a room how many had shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code. About a third to a half put their hands up. Then I asked how many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written. Only three people, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI.

Here's the mechanism. Before GenAI, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance. With GenAI that problem doesn't change; we still have more features than we can possibly test. No one would suggest putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck, yet that's exactly what we're doing when we generate more code. (Classic Theory of Constraints.)

So what should Product Management do? Every feature is a hypothesis: if we build this, it will solve a specific problem for a group of users. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of Discovery, running experiments, building prototypes, analyzing user data. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning, not less.

### Post 3 — Older blog: Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster
**URL:** /blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/
**Angle:** The confidence gap — GenAI sounds most sure exactly when you should trust it least.

GenAI's superpower is speed, its ability to churn out text faster than any human. But there's a catch: it sounds too confident for what it actually "knows".

ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers keep asking me whether it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most of those questions come from a misunderstanding of how the current tools actually work. GenAI, properly called a Large Language Model, takes the text in your prompt and predicts the next word, then feeds the result back in and predicts the next, one word at a time. That is not how a human works. We consider what we want to express and then find the best way to say it.

The greatest danger sits right there. Research on the impact of GenAI on critical thinking found that the more confident the tool sounds, the more likely we are to believe it, even though there's no correlation between that confidence and whether the information is any good. It will find a signal in noise even when there's no signal. It starts its reply with "that's a great idea" whether or not it is.

None of that means don't use it. It means use it with guardrails. Before reaching for GenAI in your team, I ask a few questions: does this enhance collaboration? Is it addressing the team's actual bottleneck, or just shaving five minutes off a ten-minute task? Can we afford the errors it will make, and do we know the subject well enough to catch them?

GenAI is a valuable tool. It just isn't the only tool in a ScrumMaster's tool chest, and the real work of understanding a team and their situation can't be automated.

### Post 4 — Older blog: The Jenga Effect
**URL:** /blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/
**Angle:** Client-as-PO looks efficient and quietly topples the product.

I recently met a team where the client was the Product Owner. They kept saying their Product Backlog didn't make sense. They didn't understand the product they were trying to build, and they'd never seen a vision or a strategy. Despite all that, their PO wanted more features, faster, now, please.

Their product looked like a Jenga tower just before it topples. It hit quality and usability, and worse, the team was on the verge of burnout from the whiplash of the client's misunderstandings about how products actually get built.

It helps to be clear about what the role involves. The Product Owner owns the vision, the why behind the product. They own the strategy, the how of getting there. They own prioritization, the what we work on next and the reason for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, and build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together. Clients typically just want to know that it works.

People from the client side understand the business problem well, but not the product build. That's not a character flaw, it's a different trade. Most clients lack the background in product work to play the role effectively, aren't prepared to make it a full-time job, and in government often rotate out every 6 to 12 months, which is the opposite of what the role needs.

So don't make your client the Product Owner. Make them a stakeholder. A good Product Owner ensures the product solves the client's problem, but does it while holding the big picture, not just the next feature.

### Post 5 — Older blog: Don't Let Sprint Review be a Missed Opportunity
**URL:** /blog/dont-let-sprint-review-be-a-missed-opportunity/
**Angle:** Show and Tell puts everyone to sleep; Show and Play gets real feedback.

Too many Sprint Reviews are a Show and Tell. Someone demos every nook and cranny of a feature while the room nods along, says "good job", and offers nothing substantive. The goal of the event is to increase engagement with stakeholders and end users, not decrease it, and talking at people does the opposite.

I watched one go sideways recently. Every early feature drew vague praise and no real questions. The Director of Support spent the meeting on his phone. Then two features got torn apart late, once for a fraud risk that Marketing had apparently flagged weeks earlier, and the whole thing spiralled until the ScrumMaster called an early stop. By the end the developer doing the demo muttered that next time he's asked, the answer is no.

Two things would have changed that day. First, it starts long before the meeting: when the strategic work happens in Product Backlog Refinement, make sure key stakeholders like Marketing and Support are actually involved, so their concerns surface early instead of exploding in the Review. Second, replace Show and Tell with Show and Play. Have someone walk through the high-level features, then pair each developer with a stakeholder or end user and invite them to actually use the product, focused on the work completed this Sprint.

Show and Play generates a much deeper level of feedback, and there's nothing like watching someone else use your application to see exactly where they get confused. It's a trick borrowed from usability testing, and it beats a monologue every time.

A good Sprint Review gets features accepted and deployed. A great one engages the attendees and creates productive discussion about product direction.

### Post 6 — Glossary: Psychological Safety
**URL:** /glossary/psychological-safety/
**Angle:** Safety isn't trust, and it isn't the absence of conflict.

Psychological safety gets misunderstood a lot, usually in two directions.

The first: people treat it as trust. It isn't. We can trust each other and still not be safe. Amy Edmondson's definition is "the belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes." Trust is about the other person. Safety is knowing that if you take a chance or make a mistake, you'll be supported and not punished.

The second: people treat it as the avoidance of conflict, or agreement for the sake of agreement. Also wrong. Psychological safety is an environment where we can be honest about what we've seen and not be punished for it. If anything, higher safety tends to produce more open disagreement, not less.

Here's why it matters so much for a team. As safety increases, communication becomes more open. That openness leads to better awareness of what's really happening in the work. And as communication improves, mistakes get reported and fixed more rapidly. It's a virtuous circle, and it runs in reverse just as easily.

One warning worth repeating: safety isn't a licence to point out everyone else's mistakes. It's about being able to acknowledge your own, and what you learned, without repercussions.

If you want to see where your team actually sits, Edmondson has a short survey. A couple of the questions: "if you make a mistake on this team, is it held against you?" and "is it safe to take a risk on this team?" Run it, then let the team use the data to see how they might evolve.

### Post 7 — Glossary: Sprint Goal
**URL:** /glossary/sprint-goal/
**Angle:** "Finish 7 stories" is not a Sprint Goal.

Some teams set their Sprint Goal as "complete all the User Stories we committed to" or "finish seven stories". That misses almost the entire point of the tool.

A Sprint Goal is a single product objective, shared by the Scrum Team, that describes the purpose of the Sprint and keeps everyone moving in the same direction. A process-oriented goal like "finish the stories" tells you nothing about why the work matters. A good goal helps the team understand the business objective so their work rises above just finishing tasks.

It also isn't imposed on the team by the Product Owner. The PO explains the business objective they're trying to meet, then the team works with them to describe what's feasible. The Sprint Goal is created through negotiation, and because everyone helps set it, everyone feels more ownership and purpose during the Sprint.

Once you have one, it earns its keep. A simply-stated goal makes it easier to prioritize Product Backlog Items, to judge whether a piece of feedback is even relevant, and to summarize the work when a stakeholder asks. Some teams add "do we still believe in our Sprint Goal?" to the Daily Scrum, which is a good habit.

When a team really struggles to set one, it's often a hint that the underlying business strategy is unclear. That's a signal worth chasing, not a reason to give up on the goal. (Impact Mapping and Story Mapping help here.)

Sprint Goals are hard and not well understood, so many teams quietly skip them. That's a missed opportunity.

Does your team's Sprint Goal describe an outcome, or just count stories?

### Post 8 — Glossary: Impediments
**URL:** /glossary/impediments/
**Angle:** "No blockers" five days running usually means we don't agree on what an impediment is.

**Angle:** The pull toward speed skips the understanding the event exists to build.

Shortly after ChatGPT 4o came out, I saw people talking about doing Backlog Refinement in minutes with GenAI. Most people have realized that's just not a good idea.

**URL:** /blog/product-management-and-genai/
**Angle:** Building is cheap now; building the right thing is not. Discovery matters more, not less.

I'm seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They're full of features that don't fit well together, and some of them don't solve a real problem.

Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.

At Product Camp Ottawa I asked a room how many had shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code. About a third to a half put their hands up. Then I asked how many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written. Only three people, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI.

Here's the mechanism. Before GenAI, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance. With GenAI that problem doesn't change; we still have more features than we can possibly test. No one would suggest putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck, yet that's exactly what we're doing when we generate more code. (Classic Theory of Constraints.)

So what should Product Management do? Every feature is a hypothesis: if we build this, it will solve a specific problem for a group of users. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of Discovery, running experiments, building prototypes, analyzing user data. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning, not less.

The biggest risk is going through the motions: theatre, running the discovery process without learning anything. Ask one question this week: what did we learn that changed our plan? If nothing, it's theatre.

Building great products still comes down to the same things: talking to real users, running experiments, and listening to the feedback.

**URL:** /blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/
**Angle:** The confidence gap — GenAI sounds most sure exactly when you should trust it least.

GenAI's superpower is speed, its ability to churn out text faster than any human. But there's a catch: it sounds too confident for what it actually "knows".

ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers keep asking me whether it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most of those questions come from a misunderstanding of how the current tools actually work. GenAI, properly called a Large Language Model, takes the text in your prompt and predicts the next word, then feeds the result back in and predicts the next, one word at a time. That is not how a human works. We consider what we want to express and then find the best way to say it.

The greatest danger sits right there. Research on the impact of GenAI on critical thinking found that the more confident the tool sounds, the more likely we are to believe it, even though there's no correlation between that confidence and whether the information is any good. It will find a signal in noise even when there's no signal. It starts its reply with "that's a great idea" whether or not it is.

None of that means don't use it. It means use it with guardrails. Before reaching for GenAI in your team, I ask a few questions: does this enhance collaboration? Is it addressing the team's actual bottleneck, or just shaving five minutes off a ten-minute task? Can we afford the errors it will make, and do we know the subject well enough to catch them?

**URL:** /blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/
**Angle:** Client-as-PO looks efficient and quietly topples the product.

I recently met a team where the client was the Product Owner. They kept saying their Product Backlog didn't make sense. They didn't understand the product they were trying to build, and they'd never seen a vision or a strategy. Despite all that, their PO wanted more features, faster, now, please.

They own prioritization, the what we work on next and the reason for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, and build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together. Clients typically just want to know that it works.

**URL:** /blog/dont-let-sprint-review-be-a-missed-opportunity/

By the end the developer doing the demo muttered that next time he's asked, the answer is no.

### Post 6 — Glossary: Psychological Safety
**URL:** /glossary/psychological-safety/
**Angle:** Safety isn't trust, and it isn't the absence of conflict.

Psychological safety gets misunderstood a lot, usually in two directions.

The first: people treat it as trust. It isn't. We can trust each other and still not be safe. Amy Edmondson's definition is "the belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes." Trust is about the other person. Safety is knowing that if you take a chance or make a mistake, you'll be supported and not punished.

+ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers keep asking me whether it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most of those questions come from a misunderstanding of how the current tools actually work. -### Option A — the relationships math

-👥 What's the optimal Scrum team size? My honest answer is that there's no single right number, but there's a lot of signal in how relationships grow. On a team of 5 there are 10 relationships to form. A team of 7 has 21, and a team of 9 has 36. Each new person adds some individual productivity, but they also add an exponentially growing number of relationships to maintain.

+I recently met a team where the client was the Product Owner. They kept saying their Product Backlog didn't make sense. They didn't understand the product they were trying to build, and they'd never seen a vision or a strategy. Despite all that, their PO wanted more features, faster, now, please.

-That's why bigger teams don't get proportionally more done. To go from 5 to 7, you more than double the relationships that have to be built and kept healthy. In teams of 7-8 I've watched upwards of 90 minutes per person each day go into interacting with teammates, and as the group grows past that, people quietly withdraw from those interactions rather than lose their productive time, which is exactly the connective tissue a high-performing team needs.

+Their product looked like a Jenga tower just before it topples. It hit quality and usability, and worse, the team was on the verge of burnout from the whiplash of the client's misunderstandings about how products actually get built.

-So when clients ask, I share the data and my experience: teams of 4-6 work well for most situations. They form faster and are as productive as larger ones, and a team of 5-6 can usually cross-skill enough to survive losing a member.

+It helps to be clear about what the role involves. The Product Owner owns the vision, the why behind the product. They own the strategy, the how of getting there. They own prioritization, the what we work on next and the reason for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, and build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together. Clients typically just want to know that it works.
-What size has actually worked for your team? Too small, too big, or just right?

+People from the client side understand the business problem well, but not the product build. That's not a character flaw, it's a different trade. Most clients lack the background in product work to play the role effectively, aren't prepared to make it a full-time job, and in government often rotate out every 6 to 12 months, which is the opposite of what the role needs.
-#Scrum

+So don't make your client the Product Owner. Make them a stakeholder. A good Product Owner ensures the product solves the client's problem, but does it while holding the big picture, not just the next feature.
-### Option B — bigger isn't faster

-🧩 We all want to believe that going from 2 people to 4 doubles what a team gets done. We know intuitively it doesn't, and Amdahl's Law explains why: some work happens in parallel, but some has to happen one step at a time, and that serial part sets a ceiling no amount of extra people can lift. Even when 80% of the work parallelises, it takes 3 people to double one person's output, and 16 to quadruple it.
+Have you watched the Jenga tower wobble on a team you've worked with?

-Speed doesn't come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from building a high-performing team that's the right size for communication and quality. -But the number of people was never the most important question. The real one is this: does the team have the capacity to get to truly Done, shippable, at the end of every Sprint? If it doesn't, that's your signal to re-examine the size and shape of the team, whatever the headcount happens to be.
-Is your team sized for looking busy, or for reaching Done every Sprint?
-#Scrum

+### Post 6 — Glossary: Psychological Safety
+**URL:** /glossary/psychological-safety/
+**Angle:** Safety isn't trust, and it isn't the absence of conflict.
-### Option A — Cunningham's real point

-💳 Technical Debt is one of the most misunderstood terms in our field. Ward Cunningham coined it back in 1992, and his original point was subtle: "Shipping first-time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with refactoring. The danger occurs when the debt is not repaid."
+Psychological safety gets misunderstood a lot, usually in two directions.

-Read that again, because most of us get it backwards. In Cunningham's definition, technical debt is okay when it's paid back promptly. It's a deliberate, short-term trade to move faster now, on the condition that you circle back and clean up.

+The first: people treat it as trust. It isn't. We can trust each other and still not be safe. Amy Edmondson's definition is "the belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes." Trust is about the other person. Safety is knowing that if you take a chance or make a mistake, you'll be supported and not punished.

-Somewhere along the way the term got hijacked to mean any mess left behind when a team rushes through the code because they feel pressure to get more done faster. That's not debt in Cunningham's sense, that's just an unpaid bill piling up interest.

+The second: people treat it as the avoidance of conflict, or agreement for the sake of agreement. Also wrong. Psychological safety is an environment where we can be honest about what we've seen and not be punished for it. If anything, higher safety tends to produce more open disagreement, not less.

-So the practical question isn't "do we have technical debt?" Every codebase does. It's "which debt did we take on deliberately, and are we actually paying it back?" A team that never refactors isn't avoiding debt, it's defaulting on it.

+Here's why it matters so much for a team. As safety increases, communication becomes more open. That openness leads to better awareness of what's really happening in the work. And as communication improves, mistakes get reported and fixed more rapidly. It's a virtuous circle, and it runs in reverse just as easily.
-When did your team last deliberately pay down a piece of technical debt, rather than just adding to it?
+One warning worth repeating: safety isn't a licence to point out everyone else's mistakes. It's about being able to acknowledge your own, and what you learned, without repercussions.
-#Scrum

+If you want to see where your team actually sits, Edmondson has a short survey. A couple of the questions: "if you make a mistake on this team, is it held against you?" and "is it safe to take a risk on this team?" Run it, then let the team use the data to see how they might evolve.
-### Option B — the gym full of chairs

-🏋️ Here's how I explain Technical Debt to non-technical people. Imagine your developers are in a large gym. Time how long it takes them to run across and back, and repeat until the number is stable. Now scatter a few chairs across the middle at random and ask them to run again. They're slower. Add more chairs. Eventually there are so many they can't walk around them, and they have to crawl to get across the room.
+Which of those two misreadings do you run into more often?

-The chairs are the technical debt. The extra time is the interest your team pays on it, every day, on every trip across the room. Nobody chose to make the gym unusable; the chairs just accumulated a few at a time until moving became painful.

-There's a new source of chairs worth naming. AI-generated code has become a major new source of technical debt. It's fast and it often runs, which is exactly what makes the chairs easy to add without noticing, until the day the team is crawling.
-The point isn't to keep the gym perfectly empty. It's to keep it clear enough that people can still run.
-How many chairs has your team quietly added this year, and when will you clear a few?
-#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

+### Post 7 — Glossary: Sprint Goal
+**URL:** /glossary/sprint-goal/

-The magic isn't the diagram, it's drawing it together. +Some teams set their Sprint Goal as "complete all the User Stories we committed to" or "finish seven stories". That misses almost the entire point of the tool.

-Once it's on the wall, it does something a bulleted list can't. +A Sprint Goal is a single product objective, shared by the Scrum Team, that describes the purpose of the Sprint and keeps everyone moving in the same direction. -Next time your team solves the same problem for the third time, try drawing the loop together before you propose another fix.

+It also isn't imposed on the team by the Product Owner. The PO explains the business objective they're trying to meet, then the team works with them to describe what's feasible. -What recurring problem on your team might actually be a loop you haven't drawn yet?

-🔁 Before your team makes a big change, it's worth asking a question we usually skip: what might this set in motion that we didn't intend? A Causal Loop Diagram is a good tool for that. +### Post 8 — Glossary: Impediments
+**URL:** /glossary/impediments/
+**Angle:** "No blockers" five days running usually means we don't agree on what an impediment is.
-### Option A — Done or Not Done

-🤝 In the Agile world, a cross-functional team is one that has all the skills it needs to get the work finished, without relying on outside help. That's a mouthful, so here's what it looks like: a mix of development, analysis, testing, and design, held not by one specialist per skill but by people who already have several, or are willing to learn them. We call them T-shaped or M-shaped: deep in one or two areas, useful in several others.

+All too often I hear a Developer in the Daily Scrum mention the same chunk of work four or five days running and still say "no blockers." Why? There are lots of factors, but the biggest is that the team doesn't share a common understanding of what an impediment actually is.

-Why go to the trouble? Because when analysis, development, and quality assurance happen together inside one team, quality goes up. There are no handoffs between departments, feedback is rapid, and the work moves in small chunks instead of big batches that hide errors.

+Here's the working definition: anything that slows the team's progress towards the Sprint Goal is an impediment. Not just the dramatic stuff. A low-bandwidth connection at home, email and Slack interruptions, waiting on another team or a vendor, a poorly understood Product Backlog Item, frequent broken builds, slow decision-making, a changing requirement mid-Sprint. All impediments.

-Transparency is where it shows up most. A team that delivers complete features every Sprint can't play the game of declaring work 75% done and then blaming the next group downstream. With a cross-functional team, work is either Done or Not Done at the end of the Sprint. There is no 75%.

+One small trick helps enormously: swap the word "impediment" for "slowdown". It's a lot easier to admit you were slowed by something than to say you were impeded, which sounds like you were stopped cold. Then go looking at the Sprint Backlog or Kanban board for items that have sat in the same state for several days. Those are almost certainly impeded by something.
-Does your team own enough of the work to say Done and mean it, or does "done" still depend on a handoff?

+There's a second misunderstanding worth clearing up, about whose job removal is. Too many teams think the ScrumMaster's job is to directly remove every impediment. "ScrumMaster, I'm out of sticky notes, can you get me more?" If the ScrumMaster removes everything, the team only learns that someone else solves their problems, and the ScrumMaster turns into a babysitter. A good ScrumMaster helps the team learn to remove their own impediments, and steps in directly only when it's genuinely beyond them.
-#Scrum
+And when the same impediment keeps coming back, resist 5 Whys. It tends to surface the recent and the shallow. Use Systems Thinking to find the underlying issue, and fix that.
-### Option B — not departments

-🚧 Cross-functional teams are not departments, and treating them as synonyms causes a lot of quiet pain. A department is organized by role or job title: the development group here, the QA group down the hall. A cross-functional team is organized around the work, from the moment a feature is considered until it's delivering value to a customer.
+What's an impediment your team stopped noticing because it's just "how things are"?

-The difference shows up as waiting. Whenever a team depends on an outside person or group, it spends time waiting for its high-priority work to reach the top of someone else's list. Inside a cross-functional team there's far less work that has to happen elsewhere, and even when a handoff remains, it happens in small chunks rather than big batches thrown over a wall.

-There's a culture shift too. When quality assurance is part of your team, and not another group down the hall, there's less griping about "their" work and more shared effort on improving it. The us-versus-them softens, because it's just us.

-## 8. Glossary — Story Mapping

+This isn't really an AI problem, it's an old measurement problem wearing new clothes. -### Option A — why Patton built it

-🗺️ A Story Map is a way to visualize the flow, or the story, of a product. -Jeff Patton invented story mapping out of frustration. He was tired of "flat" Product Backlogs, those long single-column lists that lose all track of the Product Vision. -That's why people use it as a stepping stone from Vision to User Stories. -### Option B — life raft for a huge backlog

-🧭 Drowning in an oversized Product Backlog? A Story Map is a good life raft. When a backlog has grown into hundreds of items in one flat list, nobody can see the product anymore, only the pile. Story mapping gives that pile back its shape.

+Here's the part worth keeping. There's a popular idea in booster circles that you can use agents to offset the mistakes of other agents. I don't buy it. Assume each agent is imperfect at its task. You can't reliably mask the imperfections of one agent with another one that's also imperfect. If anything, I'd expect the imperfections to multiply, not cancel out.

-The move is to stop reading the backlog top to bottom and instead lay it out as a journey. Across the top go the major steps in the user's workflow; underneath each step you arrange the stories that belong to it. Suddenly duplicates sit next to each other, whole regions of the map turn out to be features nobody will ever build, and the gaps you were missing become obvious.

+More compute and more agents is progress by throwing more of everything at the problem. Sometimes that helps. But it's not the same as the tool getting genuinely smarter, and it's easy to mistake the size of the machinery for the quality of the answer.

-From there you can do the thing a flat list makes hard: draw a line and choose a thin first slice across the whole journey, enough to deliver a coherent product rather than a random handful of tickets. The rest stays on the map, visible but clearly below the line, instead of buried in a thousand-item list.

+By the way, one of those two insights was a good one: the single most effective way to grow a newsletter is a direct recommendation from an existing reader. So if a friend would get something from mine, send it their way.
-Jeff Patton built this because flat backlogs lose the Product Vision. If yours has, the map is often the fastest way to find it again.
-When did you last delete a whole region of your backlog, rather than just adding to it?
-#Scrum #ProductOwner
+If you've tried multi-agent setups, did stacking agents actually improve the output, or just the bill?

1	---
2	title: "Agile Bonuses - The Damage They Do"
3	date: "2022-12-07"
4	lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
5	categories:
6	  - "anti-patterns"
7	coverImage: "@/content/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/images/Bonuses-anti-pattern-CLD.png"
8	excerpt: 'Bonuses might get more features now, but at the cost of quality, collaboration, and a sustainable system'
9	---
10	
11	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
12	import BonusesAntiPatternCLD1 from '@/content/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/images/Bonuses-anti-pattern-CLD-1.png';
13	import BonusesAntiPatternCLD2 from '@/content/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/images/Bonuses-anti-pattern-CLD-2.png';
14	import BonusesAntiPatternCLD from '@/content/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/images/Bonuses-anti-pattern-CLD.png';
15	
16	_A design pattern is a description of a solution to a recurring problem. It outlines the elements that are necessary to solve the challenge without prompting the reader to address the issue in a specific way._ _Unfortunately, we also regularly see recurring patterns of ineffective behaviour. These are called Anti-Patterns. The following explores the common anti-pattern of a performance bonus. Micromanagement._
17	
18	A few months ago a friend asked me about setting up a bonus scheme at his work. From working with Scrum and Kanban teams, I know that bonuses are counter-productive anywhere team members are doing knowledge work and their work is interdependent. The same might apply in other areas too, but I know this to be true in the context of software development in particular, because of my experience and study.
19	
20	What kind of bonuses are we talking about here? Not Christmas bonuses, profit sharing, employee stock ownership plans or stock options (although, if not used carefully, even those have risks). We will focus on only performance bonuses for this article, which is what my friend was discussing.
21	
22	"A performance-based bonus is an extra compensation granted to an employee as a reward for reaching pre-established goals and benchmarks."[^1]
23	
24	In software development, individual performance bonuses are often geared to something like personal velocity if you're a developer, or number of defects found if you're a tester. For team bonus, maybe the target would be set as "greater than 75% of committed stories are completed in most Sprints". We'll use the developer example in our illustrations, but others would have similar effects.
25	
26	After a short conversation with my friend, we managed to identify a number of ways that bonuses would be a bad idea and I offered to assemble research for him as ammunition to convince his boss. And what I found in the research was curious. It showed that researchers have a very narrow focus when studying bonuses. With a couple of exceptions, they assumed that the people designing the incentive had chosen a good target.
27	
28	Of course, from our experience in the agile world, we know that most targets are either outright dangerous (e.g. velocity as a measure of throughput) or far enough from the truth that focusing on them may cause harm (e.g. defects as a proxy for quality). Researchers don't tend to look very far forward when they assume that bonuses will have a positive effect and they end up measuring the wrong things. If they instead ignore any assumed target, and follow cause and effect to the unbiased end results, they would see that.
29	
30	Other challenges with common research:
31	
32	- Many of the tasks being measured are too simple. For example, in online game play, the task is designed to measure collaboration and competition. Unfortunately, the limited complexity of game play doesn't simulate product development work well.
33	- Many studies are run over a short period of time - hours or days - so would not show the long-term effects of most bonus schemes.
34	- Since the research is typically based on short time periods, it rarely examines the effects of bonuses on morale or intrinsic motivation. Adding more effective motivation tools to this article might double its length.
35	
36	To see what goes wrong with bonuses, we're going to draw on a few tools.
37	
38	- Goodhart's Law - "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"
39	- Motivational Models - specifically ARC
40	- Systems Thinking - many of the problems created by bonuses come from a lack of consideration to knock effects. I.E. If we do X, what other effects will that have downstream? What effects will it have in a few months?
41	
42	And to visually illustrate cause and effect, we'll use Causal Loop diagrams to show positive and negative links. Remember, "positive" and "negative" shouldn't be read as good or bad, but simply as increasing or decreasing.
43	
44	### Individual Bonuses
45	
46	Here's a hint right out of the gate if you're new to Agile: you never want to measure anything for one person.
47	
48	**Individual Bonus (-ve)-> Autonomy** - Chasing a bonus lessens the opportunities we have to make decisions to better the team because meeting the bonus requirements becomes the higher priority. This reduces (i.e. negative link) a team member's _Autonomy_ (see ARC and SCARF models).
49	
50	**Autonomy (delayed ->) Engagement** - When we have Autonomy —control over our own choices— we have a greater sense of Engagement. But the bonus has reduced Autonomy, causing an opposite effect. It turns out, Autonomy is a core driver for _Engagement_ at work.
51	
52	**Individual Bonus -> Competition** - An individual bonus also increases (i.e. positive link) _Competition_ between team members. It automatically means you should put your own needs ahead of the team's needs, to maximize your bonus payout. Since others are doing the same thing, your cooperative Scrum team starts to have competition between members.
53	
54	<Figure
55	  src={BonusesAntiPatternCLD1}
56	  alt="Causal loop diagram showing how individual bonuses increase competition and reduce peer-to-peer help, quality, and relatedness"
57	  caption=""
58	/>
59	
60	
61	Competition is a fun one because it sparks a lot of effects of its own…
62	
63	**Competition (-ve)-> Peer to Peer Help** - You will still help others, but only after your own work is done and mostly on a quid-pro-quo basis. This isn't healthy collaboration and reduces the amount of _Peer to Peer Help_ that happens.
64	
65	**Competition (Delayed -ve)-> Quality** - As Competition increases and communication declines, more errors creep in. There is reduced cooperation between individual developers and, much worse, reduced cooperation between developers and testers. Have you ever been in a bug triage meeting where one party claims they've found a bug and another person claims it works as designed? This happens enough even without incentives getting in the way, and bonuses just make this much worse. Reduced _Quality_ is a delayed effect; it will take a lot longer to show up.
66	
67	**Competition (Delayed -ve)-> Relatedness** - We have a need to care about, and feel cared for by, others. As the feeling of Competition increases even a little bit, that harms our ability to _Relate_ to others.
68	
69	**Relatedness -> Peer to Peer Help** - As we get to know our teammates better and learn to care about them, our willingness to provide support increases. Unfortunately, Competition harms Relatedness and, therefore, further undermines the _Peer to Peer collaboration_ required for Agile to be effective.
70	
71	**Relatedness (Delayed)-> Engagement** - When we feel we're part of something bigger than ourselves, our _Engagement_ goes up and then we become more productive. The competitive environment which harms Relatedness, also creates dis-engagement.[^2]
72	
73	**Autonomy -> Peer to Peer Help** - When we have freedom to make choices, it is easier to collaborate because you don't feel as much pressure inside yourself to get your own work done first. Instead, you can help a peer and expect the help will be repaid.
74	
75	<Figure
76	  src={BonusesAntiPatternCLD2}
77	  alt="Extended causal loop diagram showing how bonuses reduce autonomy and engagement, further undermining collaboration"
78	  caption=""
79	/>
80	
81	
82	**Individual Bonus (-ve)-> Experimentation** - Experimentation allows a team to learn and improve through learning what succeeds and what fails. As people focus on meeting their bonus, and avoiding failure, Experiments are reduced and so is team learning and improvement.
83	
84	**Individual Bonus -> # of Features** – Yay, a net good; we got more _Features_! But at what cost? ;-)
85	
86	**\# of Features (-ve) -> Done** - As the number of Features being worked on at any one time increases, there will be pressure to call them 'Done' sooner, even though they're likely not done. The best part is, with a good bonus, this pressure doesn't need to come from outside - the individual can create it for themselves.
87	
88	**\# of Features (-ve) -> Quality** – The more Features being worked on at the same time, puts increased pressure on the people doing the testing. This will have two effects: items will wait in a queue longer making their defects harder to fix, and more defects will slip through unnoticed. Reduced _Quality_ will be the result.
89	
90	**\# of Features (-ve) -> Peer to Peer Help** - As the number of Features being worked on at any one time increases, there are fewer people who have capacity to help their peers.
91	
92	**Peer to Peer Help -> Throughput at the Bottleneck** - We know from the Theory of Constraints that all systems have bottlenecks that limit its throughput. Bottlenecks are inevitable in a normal Agile environment, but when a bottleneck happens, we would expect another team member to help out until it is no longer the constraint for Throughput. If a bonus makes Peer to Peer Help less likely, _Throughput at the Bottleneck_ will not improve.
93	
94	**Throughput at the Bottleneck -> Number of Features** - If we improve the bottleneck, the number of features delivered will increase. Unfortunately, the use of bonuses means that there's no incentive to help clear the constraint, so the bottleneck is likely to persist.
95	
96	**Peer to Peer Help -> Quality** - Collaboration increases Quality through Pair Programming, Code Reviews, and even just having someone to bounce ideas off of. All this requires team members who feel that they have enough slack in their own work that they can help you. Bonuses ratchet up the pressure to meet a target and therefore reduce the amount of time anyone feels they have to provide help to others.
97	
98	**Done -> Quality** - Scrum includes a Definition of Done as a quality leveler. Scrum challenges the team to ensure that level of quality is met whenever a Product Backlog Item is complete. As a team grows in skill, it normally strengthens its 'Done' criteria, therefore improving Quality. Unfortunately, in the land of bonuses and focusing on the # of Features, team members will feel pressure to skip parts of Done, as they feel it slows them down. _Hint: over the long haul you never speed up by reducing quality standards._
99	
100	**Quality (Delayed) -> # of Features** - When a team makes the effort to do quality work, through the Agile Engineering Practices, they increase the code quality. It is easier and faster to add new features in a code base where team members tidy up small messes and automate many of their acceptance tests. Unfortunately, in an environment where # of Features is consider a measure of success, corners get cut and quality degrades slowly.
101	
102	<Figure
103	  src={BonusesAntiPatternCLD}
104	  alt="Bonuses anti pattern CLD"
105	  caption="Bonuses anti pattern CLD"
106	/>
107	
108	
109	Reviewing these results, we can see that bonuses might result in an increased number of features, but to stop analysis there is short-sighted and foolish. An increase in features doesn't automatically lead to greater customer happiness. We should be focusing on Outcomes (features with good quality, that solved the customer problem) over Output (# of Features delivered). We may have got more of the target, but if the target was poorly chosen in the first place, the focus on it didn't give us more of what we wanted.
110	
111	Individual Bonuses can work in situations where we want competition. On a sports team, for example, a bonus for home runs might be helpful. Even here we have to be careful, because home runs alone don't win baseball games. Bonuses may also help if there is a certain class of work that no one wants to do, for example update and maintain the build system. Again, this isn't without consequences because, having provided a bonus for a mildly unpleasant task, all of sudden people will want bonuses for any task that is out of the ordinary.
112	
113	In the context of Scrum and Agile teams we know competition is actively harmful and we want people to volunteer for the unpleasant tasks, so staying away from bonuses continues to be a good idea.
114	
115	### Team Bonuses
116	
117	When we move bonuses to the Team level from the individual level, we reduce the competition within the team (Yay?), but now create competition between teams. The causal loop diagram won't change very much.
