---
title: "Agile Bonuses - The Damage They Do"
date: "2022-12-07"
lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
categories:
  - "anti-patterns"
coverImage: "@/content/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/images/Bonuses-anti-pattern-CLD.png"
excerpt: 'Bonuses might get more features now, but at the cost of quality, collaboration, and a sustainable system'
---

import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import BonusesAntiPatternCLD1 from '@/content/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/images/Bonuses-anti-pattern-CLD-1.png';
import BonusesAntiPatternCLD2 from '@/content/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/images/Bonuses-anti-pattern-CLD-2.png';
import BonusesAntiPatternCLD from '@/content/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/images/Bonuses-anti-pattern-CLD.png';

_A design pattern is a description of a solution to a recurring problem. It outlines the elements that are necessary to solve the challenge without prompting the reader to address the issue in a specific way._ _Unfortunately, we also regularly see recurring patterns of ineffective behaviour. These are called Anti-Patterns. The following explores the common anti-pattern of a performance bonus. Micromanagement._

A few months ago a friend asked me about setting up a bonus scheme at his work. From working with Scrum and Kanban teams, I know that bonuses are counter-productive anywhere team members are doing knowledge work and their work is interdependent. The same might apply in other areas too, but I know this to be true in the context of software development in particular, because of my experience and study.

What kind of bonuses are we talking about here? Not Christmas bonuses, profit sharing, employee stock ownership plans or stock options (although, if not used carefully, even those have risks). We will focus on only performance bonuses for this article, which is what my friend was discussing.

"A performance-based bonus is an extra compensation granted to an employee as a reward for reaching pre-established goals and benchmarks."[^1]

In software development, individual performance bonuses are often geared to something like personal velocity if you're a developer, or number of defects found if you're a tester. For team bonus, maybe the target would be set as "greater than 75% of committed stories are completed in most Sprints". We'll use the developer example in our illustrations, but others would have similar effects.

After a short conversation with my friend, we managed to identify a number of ways that bonuses would be a bad idea and I offered to assemble research for him as ammunition to convince his boss. And what I found in the research was curious. It showed that researchers have a very narrow focus when studying bonuses. With a couple of exceptions, they assumed that the people designing the incentive had chosen a good target.

Of course, from our experience in the agile world, we know that most targets are either outright dangerous (e.g. velocity as a measure of throughput) or far enough from the truth that focusing on them may cause harm (e.g. defects as a proxy for quality). Researchers don't tend to look very far forward when they assume that bonuses will have a positive effect and they end up measuring the wrong things. If they instead ignore any assumed target, and follow cause and effect to the unbiased end results, they would see that.

Other challenges with common research:

- Many of the tasks being measured are too simple. For example, in online game play, the task is designed to measure collaboration and competition. Unfortunately, the limited complexity of game play doesn't simulate product development work well.
- Many studies are run over a short period of time - hours or days - so would not show the long-term effects of most bonus schemes.
- Since the research is typically based on short time periods, it rarely examines the effects of bonuses on morale or intrinsic motivation. Adding more effective motivation tools to this article might double its length.

To see what goes wrong with bonuses, we're going to draw on a few tools.

- Goodhart's Law - "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"
- Motivational Models - specifically ARC
- Systems Thinking - many of the problems created by bonuses come from a lack of consideration to knock effects. I.E. If we do X, what other effects will that have downstream? What effects will it have in a few months?

And to visually illustrate cause and effect, we'll use Causal Loop diagrams to show positive and negative links. Remember, "positive" and "negative" shouldn't be read as good or bad, but simply as increasing or decreasing.

### Individual Bonuses

Here's a hint right out of the gate if you're new to Agile: you never want to measure anything for one person.

**Individual Bonus (-ve)-> Autonomy** - Chasing a bonus lessens the opportunities we have to make decisions to better the team because meeting the bonus requirements becomes the higher priority. This reduces (i.e. negative link) a team member's _Autonomy_ (see ARC and SCARF models).

**Autonomy (delayed ->) Engagement** - When we have Autonomy —control over our own choices— we have a greater sense of Engagement. But the bonus has reduced Autonomy, causing an opposite effect. It turns out, Autonomy is a core driver for _Engagement_ at work.

**Individual Bonus -> Competition** - An individual bonus also increases (i.e. positive link) _Competition_ between team members. It automatically means you should put your own needs ahead of the team's needs, to maximize your bonus payout. Since others are doing the same thing, your cooperative Scrum team starts to have competition between members.

<Figure
  src={BonusesAntiPatternCLD1}
  alt="Causal loop diagram showing how individual bonuses increase competition and reduce peer-to-peer help, quality, and relatedness"
  caption=""
/>


Competition is a fun one because it sparks a lot of effects of its own…

**Competition (-ve)-> Peer to Peer Help** - You will still help others, but only after your own work is done and mostly on a quid-pro-quo basis. This isn't healthy collaboration and reduces the amount of _Peer to Peer Help_ that happens.

**Competition (Delayed -ve)-> Quality** - As Competition increases and communication declines, more errors creep in. There is reduced cooperation between individual developers and, much worse, reduced cooperation between developers and testers. Have you ever been in a bug triage meeting where one party claims they've found a bug and another person claims it works as designed? This happens enough even without incentives getting in the way, and bonuses just make this much worse. Reduced _Quality_ is a delayed effect; it will take a lot longer to show up.

**Competition (Delayed -ve)-> Relatedness** - We have a need to care about, and feel cared for by, others. As the feeling of Competition increases even a little bit, that harms our ability to _Relate_ to others.

**Relatedness -> Peer to Peer Help** - As we get to know our teammates better and learn to care about them, our willingness to provide support increases. Unfortunately, Competition harms Relatedness and, therefore, further undermines the _Peer to Peer collaboration_ required for Agile to be effective.

**Relatedness (Delayed)-> Engagement** - When we feel we're part of something bigger than ourselves, our _Engagement_ goes up and then we become more productive. The competitive environment which harms Relatedness, also creates dis-engagement.[^2]

**Autonomy -> Peer to Peer Help** - When we have freedom to make choices, it is easier to collaborate because you don't feel as much pressure inside yourself to get your own work done first. Instead, you can help a peer and expect the help will be repaid.

<Figure
  src={BonusesAntiPatternCLD2}
  alt="Extended causal loop diagram showing how bonuses reduce autonomy and engagement, further undermining collaboration"
  caption=""
/>


**Individual Bonus (-ve)-> Experimentation** - Experimentation allows a team to learn and improve through learning what succeeds and what fails. As people focus on meeting their bonus, and avoiding failure, Experiments are reduced and so is team learning and improvement.

**Individual Bonus -> # of Features** – Yay, a net good; we got more _Features_! But at what cost? ;-)

**\# of Features (-ve) -> Done** - As the number of Features being worked on at any one time increases, there will be pressure to call them 'Done' sooner, even though they're likely not done. The best part is, with a good bonus, this pressure doesn't need to come from outside - the individual can create it for themselves.

**\# of Features (-ve) -> Quality** – The more Features being worked on at the same time, puts increased pressure on the people doing the testing. This will have two effects: items will wait in a queue longer making their defects harder to fix, and more defects will slip through unnoticed. Reduced _Quality_ will be the result.

**\# of Features (-ve) -> Peer to Peer Help** - As the number of Features being worked on at any one time increases, there are fewer people who have capacity to help their peers.

**Peer to Peer Help -> Throughput at the Bottleneck** - We know from the Theory of Constraints that all systems have bottlenecks that limit its throughput. Bottlenecks are inevitable in a normal Agile environment, but when a bottleneck happens, we would expect another team member to help out until it is no longer the constraint for Throughput. If a bonus makes Peer to Peer Help less likely, _Throughput at the Bottleneck_ will not improve.

**Throughput at the Bottleneck -> Number of Features** - If we improve the bottleneck, the number of features delivered will increase. Unfortunately, the use of bonuses means that there's no incentive to help clear the constraint, so the bottleneck is likely to persist.

**Peer to Peer Help -> Quality** - Collaboration increases Quality through Pair Programming, Code Reviews, and even just having someone to bounce ideas off of. All this requires team members who feel that they have enough slack in their own work that they can help you. Bonuses ratchet up the pressure to meet a target and therefore reduce the amount of time anyone feels they have to provide help to others.

**Done -> Quality** - Scrum includes a Definition of Done as a quality leveler. Scrum challenges the team to ensure that level of quality is met whenever a Product Backlog Item is complete. As a team grows in skill, it normally strengthens its 'Done' criteria, therefore improving Quality. Unfortunately, in the land of bonuses and focusing on the # of Features, team members will feel pressure to skip parts of Done, as they feel it slows them down. _Hint: over the long haul you never speed up by reducing quality standards._

**Quality (Delayed) -> # of Features** - When a team makes the effort to do quality work, through the Agile Engineering Practices, they increase the code quality. It is easier and faster to add new features in a code base where team members tidy up small messes and automate many of their acceptance tests. Unfortunately, in an environment where # of Features is consider a measure of success, corners get cut and quality degrades slowly.

<Figure
  src={BonusesAntiPatternCLD}
  alt="Bonuses anti pattern CLD"
  caption="Bonuses anti pattern CLD"
/>


Reviewing these results, we can see that bonuses might result in an increased number of features, but to stop analysis there is short-sighted and foolish. An increase in features doesn't automatically lead to greater customer happiness. We should be focusing on Outcomes (features with good quality, that solved the customer problem) over Output (# of Features delivered). We may have got more of the target, but if the target was poorly chosen in the first place, the focus on it didn't give us more of what we wanted.

Individual Bonuses can work in situations where we want competition. On a sports team, for example, a bonus for home runs might be helpful. Even here we have to be careful, because home runs alone don't win baseball games. Bonuses may also help if there is a certain class of work that no one wants to do, for example update and maintain the build system. Again, this isn't without consequences because, having provided a bonus for a mildly unpleasant task, all of sudden people will want bonuses for any task that is out of the ordinary.

In the context of Scrum and Agile teams we know competition is actively harmful and we want people to volunteer for the unpleasant tasks, so staying away from bonuses continues to be a good idea.

### Team Bonuses

When we move bonuses to the Team level from the individual level, we reduce the competition within the team (Yay?), but now create competition between teams. The causal loop diagram won't change very much. The effect of competition on things like cross-skilling will be reduced, but new elements will appear that affect cross-team dependencies and improvements.[^3]

### Thank You or Spot Bonuses

These are impromptu bonuses awarded to thank a team member for a particular success, such as delighting a challenging client or solving a really deep problem. These at least avoid the damage of encouraging changed behaviour to achieve the bonus, and they can have a positive impact on the team. But they still come with their own challenges.

- How to decide the recipient(s)? There is a risk that the award will acknowledge an obvious team member but overlook the contribution of someone else who provided invaluable ideas and advice but not hands-on work.
- Don't reward overtime - this always backfires. Not everyone is able to do overtime (e.g. single parent or a team member going to school part time) so it creates unfair advantage. Overtime also leads to a variety of negative effects in the long run, both for the individual and the organization, so rewarding it sustains the harm.[^4]

### Fairness

Our causal loop diagram was already way too crowded, but fairness is another challenge. For many people, fairness is an important factor in motivation. (In the language of the SCARF Model[^5] this is a threat and reward). If members of the team feel that a bonus is unfairly awarded to one person for doing something (perhaps maintaining the build system) and the contributions of others are missed, they will feel unfairly treated. This will become a demotivator. I can't readily imagine a case where the use of bonuses was a fairness motivator.

### Conclusion

Bonuses are a bit like telling someone, "We value you enough to pay you X, however we will only pay you the last 10% of X if you jump through the following hoops." Or, to use a different analogy, like large quantities of sugar where they taste great when we eat it, but the long-term effects are harmful. Bonuses attempt to improve performance by supplementing a person's internal motivation with the allure of a sweet reward.

Instead of fighting against people's internal motivation, find a way to align a team member's own motivations with the needs of the team. When our team is working in an Agile way, this happens organically as part of the way we structure work.

The worst thing about bonuses is they seem so compelling in the short term but, when we add up all the delayed effects, it becomes clear just how insanely expensive bonuses are. So don't waste money on a bonus scheme. They don't improve performance. They destroy intrinsic motivation. Pay your people well and then give them the tools to find their own sense of motivation, and the performance results will follow.

Not yet convinced? You will be after you read this research that wasn't conducted with an assumed target.

#### Research That Doesn't Suck

**[_Why Motivating People Doesn't Work and What Does_](https://www.amazon.ca/Motivating-People-Doesnt-Work-What/dp/1626569452/&tag=notesfromatoo-20)** – Susan Fowler Intrinsic motivation—motivation that comes from inside us— is more sustainable than extrinsic or external motivation. The famous carrot or stick.

[**Self-Determination Theory in Work Organizations: The State of a Science**](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/312960448_Self-Determination_Theory_in_Work_Organizations_The_State_of_a_Science) – Deci, Olafsen, Ryan When our work environment has bonuses, the bonuses reduce the effect of the intrinsic motivation.

The first important finding in the meta-analysis by Cerasoli et al. (2014) showed that intrinsic motivation had a moderate to strong relation to performance across all studies and all types of performance, whether or not incentives were also being used. Accordingly, this indicates that intrinsic motivation is extremely important for the workplace. Furthermore, in line with the undermining effect of rewards on intrinsic motivation, Cerasoli et al. found that intrinsic motivation had a weaker effect on performance when incentives were directly salient, and a stronger relation to performance when the incentives were not directly salient.

The same paper shows that rewards help when the work is simple, but when the work is more complex (e.g. knowledge work) they don't help at all and just interfere with intrinsic motivation.

In more nuanced analyses, Cerasoli et al. (2014) found that intrinsic motivation was a stronger predictor of performance quality, whereas extrinsic incentives were a stronger predictor of performance quantity. In a similar vein, Weibel et al. (2010) in their meta-analysis found that extrinsic incentives led to better performance on simple tasks but to poorer performance on more complex tasks. In short, PFP appears to be effective for motivating performance as quantity of simple, algorithmic tasks, but not performance as quality of complex heuristic tasks. Furthermore, PFP seems to interfere with the relation of intrinsic motivation to high-quality performance.

[**Do incentive systems spur work motivations of inventors in high-tech firms**](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Alain-Raybaut/publication/281356235_Do_incentive_systems_spur_work_motivations_of_inventors_in_high-tech_firms/links/5631365f08ae506cea677a7d/Do-incentive-systems-spur-work-motivations-of-inventors-in-high-tech-firms.pdf?origin=publication_detail)  – Lazaric and Raybaut

Instead of spurring work motivation, it may produce crowding out effects with a decline in motivations of some groups."

content.thinking:
I'm seeing two strong angles for "Agile Bonuses" here. The first is that while bonuses might drive more features initially, the downstream costs are brutal—competition erodes peer collaboration, intrinsic motivation tanks, and quality suffers, making the whole approach economically wasteful. The second angle is Goodhart's Law: once you measure something like velocity or defects and turn it into a target, it stops being a useful measure, yet teams often assume their chosen metrics are actually good proxies for what matters.

Now I'm moving through all ten items with sources and need to write out the full A/B treatment for each. I already have A-side drafts for items 1-8 from earlier posts, so I'm working on the B sides for those, plus both angles for items 9 and 10. For the Bonuses B-side, I'm exploring how polished AI-generated user stories create a false sense of shared understanding in refinement sessions—the team nods along thinking they all get it, but they don't, and that false consensus isn't new to GenAI, just amplified by it. If a story looks polished before the team has actually discussed it, that's a red flag—polish tends to mask disagreement rather than reveal it. I'm thinking about how GenAI creates a similar problem in product management: a prototype that looks finished and polished gets mistaken for certainty, and people start critiquing the visual details instead of testing whether it actually solves the problem. The grayscale trick from usability work solves this—strip away color and polish, and suddenly people focus on what matters: does this actually work? There's a bigger version of this trap lurking too, where it's tempting to over-invest in making something look complete.

The same logic applies to how we use GenAI for analysis. It's easy to feed all your interview data and survey results to the tool and ask it to find the insights, but that's outsourcing your thinking to something that can hallucinate and carry its own biases. Better to do the analysis yourself first, then use GenAI as a sanity check on what you found. And definitely don't simulate users with AI agents—talk to actual people, even just three of them. The real question to ask every week is whether you learned something that actually changed your plan. If nothing changed, you're just going through the motions, and GenAI just makes those empty motions faster. The speed is useful only if we're spending that saved time actually thinking and learning.

I'm noticing a pattern with tools that claim to automate the human parts of Scrum. They borrow Scrum's language but miss what Scrum is actually for. One vendor wants to replace the Daily Scrum with asynchronous messages and automated reports, but the whole point of the Daily Scrum is the synchronous moment where the team hears what everyone's working on, learns about blockers, and finds ways to help each other. That doesn't happen in a report. The same vendor pitches replacing Retrospectives with surveys, which strips away the conversation that actually generates insights.

I'm not against using AI to help with data collection or meeting notes, but there's a difference between supporting a conversation and replacing it. When you hand the grouping of problems or the generation of action items to an AI, you're removing the human insight that was the whole reason for the meeting. Before adopting any of these tools, I should ask whether they actually solve a real bottleneck for the team or just automate away something that matters.

I've seen plenty of "AI for Scrum" tools that completely miss the point. The Product Owner role is a craft that people constantly underestimate—many discover the actual scope of the work and leave within months. It's not just about wanting features; it's about owning the vision, the strategy, the prioritization, understanding the regulatory and accessibility landscape, talking to users, running experiments, and building trust with the team.

This is why clients rarely make good Product Owners. They understand the business problem but not the product build, and they can't commit full-time. A client makes an excellent stakeholder, but the Product Owner needs to hold the bigger picture while ensuring the product actually solves the client's problem.

If your PO is juggling this role alongside other responsibilities, that's not a shortcut—it's a house of cards waiting to collapse. The real question is whether your Product Owner is actually resourced to do this work, or just squeezing it in between other things.

Now I'm thinking about Sprint Reviews and how surprises there usually mean someone critical wasn't involved in refinement. The worst reviews aren't the boring ones—they're the ambushes, where a feature gets demoed and suddenly Marketing or Support says "we can't ship that." That's when you get the frustration on both sides: the team wondering why they wasted effort, and the stakeholder who tried to raise concerns weeks ago but nobody listened.

I've seen this play out badly. Features get torn apart in the Review over risks nobody caught earlier, and the team's morale takes a hit. The fix isn't to have better reviews—it's to pull the right people into refinement sessions before the work starts. When Marketing, Support, and other key stakeholders are actually in the room during backlog refinement, they can flag concerns while it's still cheap to pivot. The ScrumMaster and Product Owner should carve out time each month to review strategy together and hunt for these blind spots before they become problems.

Now I'm thinking about psychological safety and how it creates a virtuous cycle—as safety increases, communication opens up, which surfaces problems faster, which gets them fixed more quickly.

The flip side is just as powerful: low safety creates a downward spiral where people stay silent, issues hide, and small problems compound into bigger ones. The useful part is that you can actually measure where your team sits using Edmondson's survey approach, asking people to rate statements about mistakes being held against them, whether they can bring up tough issues, and if it's safe to take risks. Timothy Clark's framework adds another layer, breaking psychological safety into four progressive levels: feeling included, safe to learn, safe to contribute, and safe to challenge.

Most teams plateau somewhere in the middle, never reaching that final level where real change happens. If you haven't measured this yet, running that survey is a straightforward, low-pressure way to start.

Now, moving to Sprint Goals—a lot of teams skip them because they're genuinely difficult to nail. The key misconception is that the Product Owner dictates the goal, but that's backwards. The PO brings the business objective, and then the team collaborates with them to shape what the goal actually is.

Since everyone has a hand in creating it, there's genuine ownership and purpose baked in from the start. For teams that resist, there's a surprisingly effective tactic: friendly brinksmanship. Tell them if they won't set a real, product-focused goal, you'll set a mediocre one for them—and follow through a couple times. They'll start engaging without needing to be pushed.

The trap to avoid is calling "finish all seven stories" a Sprint Goal. That's just process wrapped in different language, and it completely misses the point. A real goal connects the team to the business outcome, so their work becomes about something bigger than just checking boxes.

Once you have one, it pays dividends: it clarifies which Product Backlog Items matter most, it filters out irrelevant feedback, and some teams use it as a reality check in the Daily Scrum by asking whether they still believe in it.

That's a trap. If the ScrumMaster removes every obstacle, the team learns to wait for rescue instead of solving problems themselves. The real move is pushing the team toward self-organization: when something blocks them, I ask what they've already tried and whether they've looped in their teammates first.

When the same problem keeps surfacing, I skip the quick Root Cause Analysis—those tend to find surface-level answers that lead to band-aid fixes. Instead, I look at the system underneath to find what's actually broken, so it doesn't haunt us next Sprint. ## Day 1

### 1. Blog — GenAI Won't Speed Up Your Scrum Events (recent)
**URL:** /blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/

#### Option A — speed skips the understanding
Shortly after ChatGPT 4o came out, I saw people talking about doing Backlog Refinement in minutes with GenAI. Most people have realized that's just not a good idea.

Here's why speeding through the events doesn't help. At surface level it looks like we hold Sprint Planning to plan the outcome for the Sprint. That's true, but the real story is much deeper. Sprint Planning is really about the team having a deep conversation to understand the Sprint Goal, their capacity, and how they'll actually get there. The benefit isn't a Sprint Backlog that looks like a Tetris board. It's a team that has a good understanding of what they're working toward.

The pull with GenAI is always toward speed. But a faster event doesn't build that understanding, it skips it. So instead of asking how GenAI can make the event quicker, ask a different question: how can the tool help team members spot details that might get missed, look at deeper issues, and improve collaboration?

That reframe changes what's worth doing. GenAI is genuinely useful for stress-testing a Sprint plan, checking Product Backlog Items against the Definition of Done, or digging deeper on an impediment. It's a poor idea for writing your Sprint Goal or breaking work into tasks for you, because that's exactly where you shut down the critical thinking that good judgement needs.

If you can significantly speed up any of these events with GenAI, then you're probably not getting the value out of them in the first place. In my experience GenAI amplifies what you're already doing, both good and bad. So before you introduce it, make sure you're already facilitating events people actually want to participate in.

Where has GenAI helped or hurt your Scrum events?

#### Option B — polished user stories, false consensus
Here's the quiet damage GenAI does in Backlog Refinement. You hand the team a list of finished-looking user stories. They read them, they nod, they say "I understand." And because there was no real conversation, each of them understands something different.

That false agreement isn't new. Product Owners were bashing out lists of polished user stories and getting false consensus long before GenAI showed up. GenAI has simply made the existing problem worse, because it can now generate that finished-looking list in seconds.

The thing is, all of these artifacts, epics, user stories, acceptance criteria, exist for one reason: to help humans reach a common understanding of what's going to be built. The team should be asking who is this for? What problem does it solve? Why is it valuable? Those questions are the point of refinement. GenAI doesn't replace that human understanding, and no matter how much information you feed it, it's still just generating the next most plausible token in response to your prompt.

None of this means the tool is useless in refinement. It's genuinely helpful for questioning a story: does it meet INVEST? Is the why clear? Where's the ambiguity? Struggling to split a story, ask it to apply the well-known splitting patterns. Get it to challenge a prioritization decision. What it shouldn't do is generate the stories for you, because then the team reads, nods, and quietly disagrees.

If a story looks polished before the team has talked about it, be suspicious. Polish is what hides the disagreement.

What's a "finished" story your team turned out to understand three different ways?

---

### 2. Blog — Product Management with GenAI (recent)
**URL:** /blog/product-management-and-genai/

#### Option A — building is cheap, building the right thing isn't
I'm seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They're full of features that don't fit well together, and some of them don't solve a real problem.

Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.

At Product Camp Ottawa I asked a room how many had shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code. About a third to a half put their hands up. Then I asked how many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written. Only three people, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI.

Here's the mechanism. Before GenAI, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance. With GenAI that problem doesn't change; we still have more features than we can possibly test. No one would suggest putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck, yet that's exactly what we're doing when we generate more code. (Classic Theory of Constraints.)

So what should Product Management do? Every feature is a hypothesis: if we build this, it will solve a specific problem for a group of users. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of Discovery, running experiments, building prototypes, analyzing user data. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning, not less.

The biggest risk is going through the motions: theatre, running the discovery process without learning anything. Ask one question this week: what did we learn that changed our plan? If nothing, it's theatre.

Building great products still comes down to the same things: talking to real users, running experiments, and listening to the feedback.

#### Option B — a polished prototype gets mistaken for certainty
GenAI makes prototypes easy to build, and that's exactly where a subtle trap opens up. A prototype that looks polished and complete gets mistaken for certainty. People see something that looks like the real product and start reacting to the font and the colour, instead of telling you whether it actually solves their problem.

I learned the fix more than 30 years ago doing usability work: grayscale. Build the prototype without colour. No one can mistake it for the finished thing, and because it's deliberately simple, you get far more information about the usability and far less about the shade of blue.

There's a bigger version of the same trap. It's tempting to outsource all of your analysis to GenAI, feeding it the interviews and the survey data and asking for the insights. The risk is that you miss the important insights and inherit the tool's biases and hallucinations. So do your own analysis first, then use the tool as a cross-check on what you found, not as a replacement for doing it.

And please, don't use AI agents to simulate real users. Talk to real users, even if only three of them, instead.

Underneath all of it is one honest question worth asking every week: what did we learn this week that changed our plan? If the answer is nothing, the discovery process has become theatre. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of that process, which is great, but speeding up the mechanics just means we need to spend more time thinking and learning.

Where has a polished prototype fooled your team into thinking a question was answered?

## Day 2

### 3. Blog — Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster (older)
**URL:** /blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/

#### Option A — the confidence gap
GenAI's superpower is speed, its ability to churn out text faster than any human. But there's a catch: it sounds too confident for what it actually "knows".

ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers keep asking me whether it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most of those questions come from a misunderstanding of how the current tools actually work. GenAI, properly called a Large Language Model, takes the text in your prompt and predicts the next word, then feeds the result back in and predicts the next, one word at a time. That is not how a human works. We consider what we want to express and then find the best way to say it.

The greatest danger sits right there. Research on the impact of GenAI on critical thinking found that the more confident the tool sounds, the more likely we are to believe it, even though there's no correlation between that confidence and whether the information is any good. It will find a signal in noise even when there's no signal. It starts its reply with "that's a great idea" whether or not it is.

None of that means don't use it. It means use it with guardrails. Before reaching for GenAI in your team, I ask a few questions: does this enhance collaboration? Is it addressing the team's actual bottleneck, or just shaving five minutes off a ten-minute task? Can we afford the errors it will make, and do we know the subject well enough to catch them?

GenAI is a valuable tool. It just isn't the only tool in a ScrumMaster's tool chest, and the real work of understanding a team and their situation can't be automated.

Where have you found GenAI helping or harming your team?

#### Option B — the tools that stole Scrum's language
I keep seeing tools that promise to automate the parts of Scrum that are entirely about human connection, and it's worth naming why they miss.

One vendor promises to replace the Daily Scrum with text, voice and video messages, then run reports on a schedule and share them with multiple admins. But the Daily Scrum exists to give the team time to understand what their peers are working on, hear about impediments others face, and spark collaboration for the day. None of that is served by an automated tool. This tool has nothing to do with Scrum, except that it stole the language.

The same vendor pitched running Retrospectives on autopilot by gathering individual survey submissions: "replace retrospective meetings with scheduled team surveys." Is replacing human interaction with writing to an AI really the way to build effective teams? Is keeping to a schedule the most important thing about a Retrospective?

I'm not against using GenAI here. Automated data collection can make it more likely that valuable data actually reaches the Retrospective. Meeting notes and action items can save a little time, as long as participants review them right after. But grouping exercises in a Retrospective exist to start a conversation among people about how their problems connect, so handing that to AI grouping, or worse, AI-generated action items, replaces the human insight that was the whole point.

Before you adopt any of these, ask where your team is actually bottlenecked, and whether the tool helps there or just automates away a conversation.

Which "AI for Scrum" tool have you seen that clearly missed the point of the event?

---

### 4. Blog — The Jenga Effect (older)
**URL:** /blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/

#### Option A — the tower about to topple
I recently met a team where the client was the Product Owner. They kept saying their Product Backlog didn't make sense. They didn't understand the product they were trying to build, and they'd never seen a vision or a strategy. Despite all that, their PO wanted more features, faster, now, please.

Their product looked like a Jenga tower just before it topples. It hit quality and usability, and worse, the team was on the verge of burnout from the whiplash of the client's misunderstandings about how products actually get built.

It helps to be clear about what the role involves. The Product Owner owns the vision, the why behind the product. They own the strategy, the how of getting there. They own prioritization, the what we work on next and the reason for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, and build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together. Clients typically just want to know that it works.

People from the client side understand the business problem well, but not the product build. That's not a character flaw, it's a different trade. Most clients lack the background in product work to play the role effectively, aren't prepared to make it a full-time job, and in government often rotate out every 6 to 12 months, which is the opposite of what the role needs.

So don't make your client the Product Owner. Make them a stakeholder. A good Product Owner ensures the product solves the client's problem, but does it while holding the big picture, not just the next feature.

Have you watched the Jenga tower wobble on a team you've worked with?

#### Option B — being a PO is a trade craft
People underestimate the Product Owner role constantly, and the clearest tell is how many run away from it. Many people, once they discover the actual work involved in being a PO, leave after a few months.

Look at what the role really asks. A Product Owner owns the vision, the why. They own the strategy, the how. They own prioritization, the what next and the justification for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, digest what they hear, and design and run experiments. And they have to build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together: how much detail does this team need, which decisions can they handle on their own.

That's a trade craft. Effective Product Owners have a background in product management, and where they're weak, they take the time to learn, because it's their craft. It isn't something you pick up on the side while rotating out every 6 to 12 months, which is exactly what happens in a lot of organizations, government especially.

This is why handing the role to a client rarely works. They understand the business problem well, but not the product build, and they're not set up to make it a full-time role. Your client makes an excellent stakeholder. The Product Owner makes sure the product solves the client's problem, while holding the big picture, not just the next feature.

If your PO is doing the job off the corner of a desk, that's not a shortcut. It's the Jenga tower waiting to fall.

Is your Product Owner actually resourced to do the craft, or fitting it around another full-time job?

## Day 3

### 5. Blog — Don't Let Sprint Review be a Missed Opportunity (older)
**URL:** /blog/dont-let-sprint-review-be-a-missed-opportunity/

#### Option A — Show and Tell vs Show and Play
Too many Sprint Reviews are a Show and Tell. Someone demos every nook and cranny of a feature while the room nods along, says "good job", and offers nothing substantive. The goal of the event is to increase engagement with stakeholders and end users, not decrease it, and talking at people does the opposite.

I watched one go sideways recently. Every early feature drew vague praise and no real questions. The Director of Support spent the meeting on his phone. Then two features got torn apart late, once for a fraud risk that Marketing had apparently flagged weeks earlier, and the whole thing spiralled until the ScrumMaster called an early stop. By the end the developer doing the demo muttered that next time he's asked, the answer is no.

Two things would have changed that day. First, it starts long before the meeting: when the strategic work happens in Product Backlog Refinement, make sure key stakeholders like Marketing and Support are actually involved, so their concerns surface early instead of exploding in the Review. Second, replace Show and Tell with Show and Play. Have someone walk through the high-level features, then pair each developer with a stakeholder or end user and invite them to actually use the product, focused on the work completed this Sprint.

Show and Play generates a much deeper level of feedback, and there's nothing like watching someone else use your application to see exactly where they get confused. It's a trick borrowed from usability testing, and it beats a monologue every time.

A good Sprint Review gets features accepted and deployed. A great one engages the attendees and creates productive discussion about product direction.

What's the last Sprint Review you were in that people actually enjoyed?

#### Option B — the ambush traces back to Refinement
The worst Sprint Reviews aren't boring, they're ambushes. A feature gets demoed, and only then does someone from Marketing or Support say "we can't ship that." Cue the frustrated "why didn't you tell us this before we wasted the team's effort?" and the equally frustrated "I tried to warn you weeks ago, but you didn't listen."

I watched exactly that happen. Two finished features got torn apart late in a Review over fraud risks that Marketing believed they'd flagged earlier. The team had built the wrong thing, nobody caught it until the demo, and morale took the hit.

Here's the thing: a Sprint Review is the wrong place to discover that. The fix starts long before the meeting. When the strategic work happens in Product Backlog Refinement, make sure the key stakeholders, the Marketing director, the Support lead, are actually involved. When an item carries real risk or challenge, invite those stakeholders into the Refinement session so they can give input and clarity while it's still cheap to change course.

It helps for the ScrumMaster and Product Owner to commit to a couple of hours a month reviewing the strategy together, specifically hunting for the things that could turn into surprises. Those two habits go a long way toward keeping the Review free of ambushes.

A Sprint Review should be where you confirm you built the right thing, not where you find out you didn't.

When did a Sprint Review surface a problem that should have come up in Refinement?

---

### 6. Glossary — Psychological Safety
**URL:** /glossary/psychological-safety/

#### Option A — it isn't trust, and it isn't the absence of conflict
Psychological safety gets misunderstood a lot, usually in two directions.

The first: people treat it as trust. It isn't. We can trust each other and still not be safe. Amy Edmondson's definition is "the belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes." Trust is about the other person. Safety is knowing that if you take a chance or make a mistake, you'll be supported and not punished.

The second: people treat it as the avoidance of conflict, or agreement for the sake of agreement. Also wrong. Psychological safety is an environment where we can be honest about what we've seen and not be punished for it. If anything, higher safety tends to produce more open disagreement, not less.

Here's why it matters so much for a team. As safety increases, communication becomes more open. That openness leads to better awareness of what's really happening in the work. And as communication improves, mistakes get reported and fixed more rapidly. It's a virtuous circle, and it runs in reverse just as easily.

One warning worth repeating: safety isn't a licence to point out everyone else's mistakes. It's about being able to acknowledge your own, and what you learned, without repercussions.

If you want to see where your team actually sits, Edmondson has a short survey. A couple of the questions: "if you make a mistake on this team, is it held against you?" and "is it safe to take a risk on this team?" Run it, then let the team use the data to see how they might evolve.

Which of those two misreadings do you run into more often?

#### Option B — the virtuous circle, and how to measure it
Psychological safety isn't a vibe, it's a loop you can watch turn.

As safety increases, communication inside the team becomes more open. That openness leads to better awareness of what's really happening in the work. And as communication improves, mistakes get reported and fixed more rapidly. It's a virtuous circle, and each turn makes the next one easier. The uncomfortable part: it runs just as smoothly in reverse. Low safety means people go quiet, problems stay hidden, and small mistakes grow into expensive ones.

The good news is you don't have to guess where your team sits. Amy Edmondson, who wrote the book on this, uses a short survey. A few of the statements people rate from strongly agree to strongly disagree: "if you make a mistake on this team, it is often held against you," "members of this team are able to bring up problems and tough issues," "it is safe to take a risk on this team," and "it is difficult to ask other members of this team for help." Run it, and let the team use the results to see how they might evolve.

Timothy Clark extends the idea into four levels worth knowing: feeling included, safe to learn, safe to contribute, and finally safe to challenge the status quo. Most teams get stuck well before that last one, which is the level where real improvement lives.

If you've never measured your team's safety, that survey is a quiet, low-drama place to start.

Would your team rate "it is safe to take a risk here" as agree, or disagree?

## Day 4

### 7. Glossary — Sprint Goal
**URL:** /glossary/sprint-goal/

#### Option A — "finish 7 stories" is not a Sprint Goal
Some teams set their Sprint Goal as "complete all the User Stories we committed to" or "finish seven stories". That misses almost the entire point of the tool.

A Sprint Goal is a single product objective, shared by the Scrum Team, that describes the purpose of the Sprint and keeps everyone moving in the same direction. A process-oriented goal like "finish the stories" tells you nothing about why the work matters. A good goal helps the team understand the business objective so their work rises above just finishing tasks.

It also isn't imposed on the team by the Product Owner. The PO explains the business objective they're trying to meet, then the team works with them to describe what's feasible. The Sprint Goal is created through negotiation, and because everyone helps set it, everyone feels more ownership and purpose during the Sprint.

Once you have one, it earns its keep. A simply-stated goal makes it easier to prioritize Product Backlog Items, to judge whether a piece of feedback is even relevant, and to summarize the work when a stakeholder asks. Some teams add "do we still believe in our Sprint Goal?" to the Daily Scrum, which is a good habit.

When a team really struggles to set one, it's often a hint that the underlying business strategy is unclear. That's a signal worth chasing, not a reason to give up on the goal. (Impact Mapping and Story Mapping help here.)

Sprint Goals are hard and not well understood, so many teams quietly skip them. That's a missed opportunity.

Does your team's Sprint Goal describe an outcome, or just count stories?

#### Option B — how to get a reluctant team to set one
A lot of teams avoid Sprint Goals because they're genuinely hard, so let me share how I get reluctant teams over the hump.

First, kill the misconception that the Product Owner hands down the goal. That's not how it works. The PO explains the business objective they're trying to meet, and then the team works with them to describe what's actually feasible. The Sprint Goal is created through negotiation. Because everyone helps set it, everyone leaves with a real sense of ownership and purpose for the Sprint, which is most of the value.

For teams that just won't engage, there's a trick that works more often than it should: a bit of friendly brinksmanship. "If you don't set a real, product-oriented Sprint Goal, I'll set a bad one for you." After you follow through a couple of times, team members start participating in goal-setting without being prodded.

Watch out for the counterfeit version, where the goal becomes "finish all seven committed stories." That's process dressed up as purpose, and it misses the point. A good Sprint Goal helps the team understand the business objective so their work rises above just ticking off tasks. And once you've got one, it earns its keep: it makes prioritizing Product Backlog Items easier, it tells you whether a piece of feedback is even relevant, and some teams keep it honest by asking "do we still believe in our Sprint Goal?" in the Daily Scrum.

If your team resists Sprint Goals, don't drop them. Negotiate one, and if you must, threaten a bad one.

What's stopped your team from setting real Sprint Goals?

### 8. Glossary — Impediments
**URL:** /glossary/impediments/

#### Option A — "no blockers" for five days running
All too often I hear a Developer in the Daily Scrum mention the same chunk of work four or five days running and still say "no blockers." Why? There are lots of factors, but the biggest is that the team doesn't share a common understanding of what an impediment actually is.

Here's the working definition: anything that slows the team's progress towards the Sprint Goal is an impediment. Not just the dramatic stuff. A low-bandwidth connection at home, email and Slack interruptions, waiting on another team or a vendor, a poorly understood Product Backlog Item, frequent broken builds, slow decision-making, a changing requirement mid-Sprint. All impediments.

One small trick helps enormously: swap the word "impediment" for "slowdown". It's a lot easier to admit you were slowed by something than to say you were impeded, which sounds like you were stopped cold. Then go looking at the Sprint Backlog or Kanban board for items that have sat in the same state for several days. Those are almost certainly impeded by something.

Is work piling up somewhere? Sometimes bottlenecks or missing skills are the impediment, and too many teams don't even notice they have one. Those spots are great indicators of where a bit of cross-skilling would make the whole team faster.

The point isn't to file more complaints. It's that an impediment you can't name is one nobody can remove.

What's an impediment your team stopped noticing because it's just "how things are"?

#### Option B — removing them isn't the ScrumMaster's solo job
There's a well-meaning misunderstanding that quietly turns good ScrumMasters into babysitters: the belief that it's their job to personally remove every impediment.

The Scrum Guide says the ScrumMaster causes the removal of impediments to the team's progress. Simple enough on the surface, and yet it gets read as "the ScrumMaster fetches the coffee and the sticky notes." That's ridiculous, and it's also a trap. If the ScrumMaster removes everything, the team only learns one thing: that when they hit a problem, someone else will solve it. The ScrumMaster becomes a babysitter, and the team never builds the muscle.

So what actually works is promoting self-organization. When a problem shows up, I encourage ScrumMasters to ask the team member a few questions first: what have you already tried? Have you asked the rest of the team for help? Have we hit something like this before, and what worked then? A good ScrumMaster helps the team learn to remove their own impediments, and steps in directly only when the problem is genuinely beyond the team's capacity.

And when the same impediment keeps returning, resist the urge to run a quick 5 Whys or Root Cause Analysis. Those tend to surface the recent and the shallow, which is why the last fix was a band-aid. Use Systems Thinking to find the underlying issue, and address that so it doesn't come back next Sprint.

Removing impediments is real work. Doing it for the team, forever, isn't help, it's dependency.

Where are you solving something your team could learn to solve themselves?

## Day 5

### 9. Blog — Agile Bonuses: The Damage They Do (older)
**URL:** /blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/

#### Option A — more features now, everything else later
A friend recently asked me about setting up a performance bonus scheme at his work. My honest answer, from years with Scrum and Kanban teams: bonuses are counter-productive anywhere people are doing knowledge work and their work is interdependent.

Here's the trap. An individual bonus does get you one thing: more features. Yay. But follow the delayed effects and the bill arrives. Chasing a bonus lessens the decisions a person makes to better the team, because hitting the target becomes the higher priority, and that reduces their autonomy, which is a core driver of engagement. It increases competition between teammates, because now you put your own numbers ahead of the team's. Competition then chips away at peer-to-peer help, at quality, and at how much people relate to each other, and all of those are the connective tissue Agile depends on.

None of that shows up on payday. Reduced quality is a delayed effect, it takes a while to surface, and by then no one connects it back to the incentive.

The worst thing about bonuses is that they seem so compelling in the short term, but when you add up all the delayed effects, it becomes clear how insanely expensive they are. They're a bit like large quantities of sugar: great going down, harmful over time.

So instead of fighting people's internal motivation with a sweeter carrot, align their own motivations with what the team needs. In an Agile way of working, that alignment tends to happen organically. Pay your people well, give them the tools to find their own motivation, and the performance follows.

Where has a well-meant incentive on your team quietly bought output at the cost of the team?

#### Option B — the problem is the target, not the money
Most arguments about bonuses skip the real problem, which isn't the money, it's the target.

Goodhart's Law puts it cleanly: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. In software we see this constantly. Tie a developer's bonus to personal velocity and velocity stops telling you anything about throughput. Tie a tester's to defects found and "quality" quietly detaches from the number. The moment people are paid to move a metric, they move the metric, not the thing you actually cared about.

What surprised me when I dug into the research was how narrow it is. With a couple of exceptions, researchers studying bonuses assumed the people designing the incentive had chosen a good target. But from the Agile world we know most targets are either outright dangerous, like velocity as a measure of throughput, or far enough from the truth that focusing on them causes harm, like defects as a proxy for quality. Follow cause and effect to the unbiased end, ignoring the assumed target, and the picture changes.

The deeper fix is to stop confusing output with outcome. More features delivered is output. Features with good quality that actually solved the customer's problem is outcome. A bonus might get you more of the target, but if the target was poorly chosen, more of it doesn't give you more of what you wanted.

Before you attach a reward to a number, ask the harder question: if people optimise this number and nothing else, do we still get what we want?

What's a metric your organization rewards that stopped measuring the thing it was meant to?

**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/

#### Option A — adoption is not productivity
Canada's draft AI strategy has some genuine good in it: real emphasis on safety and education. But there's a measurement problem buried in the key pillar, "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity." Dig into it and you find they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for productivity.

That's the part that made me laugh, and then wince. We've all seen "AI adoption" up close: someone takes a few bullet points and asks ChatGPT to turn them into a presentation. Faster than doing it by hand? Sure. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who made it learn anything about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.

The strategy picks five areas to push on, including healthcare, which is the one I know a little about. The same trap shows up. Instead of doing the hard work of systemic improvement to a healthcare system, the plan is betting on a magic wand. Adoption goes up, a number on a dashboard climbs, and the underlying flow doesn't get any better.

This isn't really an AI problem, it's an old measurement problem wearing new clothes. When you measure the adoption of a tool instead of the outcome you actually care about, you get more of the tool and none of the outcome. Teams do this too, counting story points or features shipped and calling it value.

One more prediction while I'm here: expect a lot of "AI washing" over the next few years, where plain old machine learning quietly gets rebranded as AI.

If you're being asked to measure GenAI adoption on your team, what outcome could you measure instead?

*(Companion blog if you'd rather link to an article: /blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/)*

#### Option B — 150 agents, 2 insights
I accidentally ran an experiment on whether "more agents" makes GenAI better. The short answer: no.

I asked Claude Opus to do some research on newsletter lead magnets, and I made the mistake of asking for "deep research." Don't do that unless you enjoy watching tokens evaporate. It decided to spin up a swarm of agents, each taking a small task and reporting back to a central agent that would combine the results. It even invented a three-vote rule: for each idea, three agents analyzed a different source and then voted on the claim. Fifty claims, evaluated by 150 agents. It took thirty minutes, burned through my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait until that evening to get the finish.

For that much compute I was expecting a long report with real depth. What I got was three pages with two good insights.

Here's the part worth keeping. There's a popular idea in booster circles that you can use agents to offset the mistakes of other agents. I don't buy it. Assume each agent is imperfect at its task. You can't reliably mask the imperfections of one agent with another one that's also imperfect. If anything, I'd expect the imperfections to multiply, not cancel out.

More compute and more agents is progress by throwing more of everything at the problem. Sometimes that helps. But it's not the same as the tool getting genuinely smarter, and it's easy to mistake the size of the machinery for the quality of the answer.

By the way, one of those two insights was a good one: the single most effective way to grow a newsletter is a direct recommendation from an existing reader. So if a friend would get something from mine, send it their way.

If you've tried multi-agent setups, did stacking agents actually improve the output, or just the bill?

## Day 1

### 1. Blog — GenAI Won't Speed Up Your Scrum Events (recent)
**URL:** /blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/

#### Option A — speed skips the understanding
Shortly after ChatGPT 4o came out, I saw people talking about doing Backlog Refinement in minutes with GenAI. Most people have realized that's just not a good idea.

Here's why speeding through the events doesn't help. At surface level it looks like we hold Sprint Planning to plan the outcome for the Sprint. That's true, but the real story is much deeper. Sprint Planning is really about the team having a deep conversation to understand the Sprint Goal, their capacity, and how they'll actually get there. The benefit isn't a Sprint Backlog that looks like a Tetris board. It's a team that has a good understanding of what they're working toward.

The pull with GenAI is always toward speed. But a faster event doesn't build that understanding, it skips it. So instead of asking how GenAI can make the event quicker, ask a different question: how can the tool help team members spot details that might get missed, look at deeper issues, and improve collaboration?

That reframe changes what's worth doing. GenAI is genuinely useful for stress-testing a Sprint plan, checking Product Backlog Items against the Definition of Done, or digging deeper on an impediment. It's a poor idea for writing your Sprint Goal or breaking work into tasks for you, because that's exactly where you shut down the critical thinking that good judgement needs.

If you can significantly speed up any of these events with GenAI, then you're probably not getting the value out of them in the first place. In my experience GenAI amplifies what you're already doing, both good and bad. So before you introduce it, make sure you're already facilitating events people actually want to participate in.

Where has GenAI helped or hurt your Scrum events?

#### Option B — polished user stories, false consensus
Here's the quiet damage GenAI does in Backlog Refinement. You hand the team a list of finished-looking user stories. They read them, they nod, they say "I understand." And because there was no real conversation, each of them understands something different.

That false agreement isn't new. Product Owners were bashing out lists of polished user stories and getting false consensus long before GenAI showed up. GenAI has simply made the existing problem worse, because it can now generate that finished-looking list in seconds.

The thing is, all of these artifacts, epics, user stories, acceptance criteria, exist for one reason: to help humans reach a common understanding of what's going to be built. The team should be asking who is this for? What problem does it solve? Why is it valuable? Those questions are the point of refinement. GenAI doesn't replace that human understanding, and no matter how much information you feed it, it's still just generating the next most plausible token in response to your prompt.

None of this means the tool is useless in refinement. It's genuinely helpful for questioning a story: does it meet INVEST? Is the why clear? Where's the ambiguity? Struggling to split a story, ask it to apply the well-known splitting patterns. Get it to challenge a prioritization decision. What it shouldn't do is generate the stories for you, because then the team reads, nods, and quietly disagrees.

If a story looks polished before the team has talked about it, be suspicious. Polish is what hides the disagreement.

What's a "finished" story your team turned out to understand three different ways?

### 2. Blog — Product Management with GenAI (recent)
**URL:** /blog/product-management-and-genai/

#### Option A — building is cheap, building the right thing isn't
I'm seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They're full of features that don't fit well together, and some of them don't solve a real problem.

Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.

At Product Camp Ottawa I asked a room how many had shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code. About a third to a half put their hands up. Then I asked how many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written. Only three people, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI.

Here's the mechanism. Before GenAI, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance. With GenAI that problem doesn't change; we still have more features than we can possibly test. No one would suggest putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck, yet that's exactly what we're doing when we generate more code. (Classic Theory of Constraints.)

So what should Product Management do? Every feature is a hypothesis: if we build this, it will solve a specific problem for a group of users. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of Discovery, running experiments, building prototypes, analyzing user data. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning, not less.

The biggest risk is going through the motions: theatre, running the discovery process without learning anything. Ask one question this week: what did we learn that changed our plan? If nothing, it's theatre.

Building great products still comes down to the same things: talking to real users, running experiments, and listening to the feedback.

#### Option B — a polished prototype gets mistaken for certainty
GenAI makes prototypes easy to build, and that's exactly where a subtle trap opens up. A prototype that looks polished and complete gets mistaken for certainty. People see something that looks like the real product and start reacting to the font and the colour, instead of telling you whether it actually solves their problem.

I learned the fix more than 30 years ago doing usability work: grayscale. Build the prototype without colour. No one can mistake it for the finished thing, and because it's deliberately simple, you get far more information about the usability and far less about the shade of blue.

There's a bigger version of the same trap. It's tempting to outsource all of your analysis to GenAI, feeding it the interviews and the survey data and asking for the insights. The risk is that you miss the important insights and inherit the tool's biases and hallucinations. So do your own analysis first, then use the tool as a cross-check on what you found, not as a replacement for doing it.

And please, don't use AI agents to simulate real users. Talk to real users, even if only three of them, instead.

Underneath all of it is one honest question worth asking every week: what did we learn this week that changed our plan? If the answer is nothing, the discovery process has become theatre. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of that process, which is great, but speeding up the mechanics just means we need to spend more time thinking and learning.

Where has a polished prototype fooled your team into thinking a question was answered?

## Day 2

### 3. Blog — Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster (older)
**URL:** /blog/why-ai-doesn-t-replace-your-scrum-master/

#### Option A — the confidence gap
GenAI's superpower is speed, its ability to churn out text faster than any human. But there's a catch: it sounds too confident for what it actually "knows".

ScrumMasters, Product Owners and Developers keep asking me whether it's going to automate their job out of existence. Most of those questions come from a misunderstanding of how the current tools actually work. GenAI, properly called a Large Language Model, takes the text in your prompt and predicts the next word, then feeds the result back in and predicts the next, one word at a time. That is not how a human works. We consider what we want to express and then find the best way to say it.

The greatest danger sits right there. Research on the impact of GenAI on critical thinking found that the more confident the tool sounds, the more likely we are to believe it, even though there's no correlation between that confidence and whether the information is any good. It will find a signal in noise even when there's no signal. It starts its reply with "that's a great idea" whether or not it is.

None of that means don't use it. It means use it with guardrails. Before reaching for GenAI in your team, I ask a few questions: does this enhance collaboration? Is it addressing the team's actual bottleneck, or just shaving five minutes off a ten-minute task? Can we afford the errors it will make, and do we know the subject well enough to catch them?

GenAI is a valuable tool. It just isn't the only tool in a ScrumMaster's tool chest, and the real work of understanding a team and their situation can't be automated.

Where have you found GenAI helping or harming your team?

#### Option B — the tools that stole Scrum's language
I keep seeing tools that promise to automate the parts of Scrum that are entirely about human connection, and it's worth naming why they miss.

One vendor promises to replace the Daily Scrum with text, voice and video messages, then run reports on a schedule and share them with multiple admins. But the Daily Scrum exists to give the team time to understand what their peers are working on, hear about impediments others face, and spark collaboration for the day. None of that is served by an automated tool. This tool has nothing to do with Scrum, except that it stole the language.

The same vendor pitched running Retrospectives on autopilot by gathering individual survey submissions: "replace retrospective meetings with scheduled team surveys." Is replacing human interaction with writing to an AI really the way to build effective teams? Is keeping to a schedule the most important thing about a Retrospective?

I'm not against using GenAI here. Automated data collection can make it more likely that valuable data actually reaches the Retrospective. Meeting notes and action items can save a little time, as long as participants review them right after. But grouping exercises in a Retrospective exist to start a conversation among people about how their problems connect, so handing that to AI grouping, or worse, AI-generated action items, replaces the human insight that was the whole point.

Before you adopt any of these, ask where your team is actually bottlenecked, and whether the tool helps there or just automates away a conversation.

Which "AI for Scrum" tool have you seen that clearly missed the point of the event?

### 4. Blog — The Jenga Effect (older)
**URL:** /blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/

#### Option A — the tower about to topple
I recently met a team where the client was the Product Owner. They kept saying their Product Backlog didn't make sense. They didn't understand the product they were trying to build, and they'd never seen a vision or a strategy. Despite all that, their PO wanted more features, faster, now, please.

Their product looked like a Jenga tower just before it topples. It hit quality and usability, and worse, the team was on the verge of burnout from the whiplash of the client's misunderstandings about how products actually get built.

It helps to be clear about what the role involves. The Product Owner owns the vision, the why behind the product. They own the strategy, the how of getting there. They own prioritization, the what we work on next and the reason for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, and build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together. Clients typically just want to know that it works.

People from the client side understand the business problem well, but not the product build. That's not a character flaw, it's a different trade. Most clients lack the background in product work to play the role effectively, aren't prepared to make it a full-time job, and in government often rotate out every 6 to 12 months, which is the opposite of what the role needs.

So don't make your client the Product Owner. Make them a stakeholder. A good Product Owner ensures the product solves the client's problem, but does it while holding the big picture, not just the next feature.

Have you watched the Jenga tower wobble on a team you've worked with?

#### Option B — being a PO is a trade craft
People underestimate the Product Owner role constantly, and the clearest tell is how many run away from it. Many people, once they discover the actual work involved in being a PO, leave after a few months.

Look at what the role really asks. A Product Owner owns the vision, the why. They own the strategy, the how. They own prioritization, the what next and the justification for it. On top of that they need to understand the regulatory environment, usability, accessibility and security, interview a range of end users, digest what they hear, and design and run experiments. And they have to build enough of a relationship with the team to find a rhythm together: how much detail does this team need, which decisions can they handle on their own.

That's a trade craft. Effective Product Owners have a background in product management, and where they're weak, they take the time to learn, because it's their craft. It isn't something you pick up on the side while rotating out every 6 to 12 months, which is exactly what happens in a lot of organizations, government especially.

This is why handing the role to a client rarely works. They understand the business problem well, but not the product build, and they're not set up to make it a full-time role. Your client makes an excellent stakeholder. The Product Owner makes sure the product solves the client's problem, while holding the big picture, not just the next feature.

If your PO is doing the job off the corner of a desk, that's not a shortcut. It's the Jenga tower waiting to fall.

Is your Product Owner actually resourced to do the craft, or fitting it around another full-time job?

## Day 3

### 5. Blog — Don't Let Sprint Review be a Missed Opportunity (older)
**URL:** /blog/dont-let-sprint-review-be-a-missed-opportunity/

#### Option A — Show and Tell vs Show and Play
Too many Sprint Reviews are a Show and Tell. Someone demos every nook and cranny of a feature while the room nods along, says "good job", and offers nothing substantive. The goal of the event is to increase engagement with stakeholders and end users, not decrease it, and talking at people does the opposite.

I watched one go sideways recently. Every early feature drew vague praise and no real questions. The Director of Support spent the meeting on his phone. Then two features got torn apart late, once for a fraud risk that Marketing had apparently flagged weeks earlier, and the whole thing spiralled until the ScrumMaster called an early stop. By the end the developer doing the demo muttered that next time he's asked, the answer is no.

Two things would have changed that day. First, it starts long before the meeting: when the strategic work happens in Product Backlog Refinement, make sure key stakeholders like Marketing and Support are actually involved, so their concerns surface early instead of exploding in the Review. Second, replace Show and Tell with Show and Play. Have someone walk through the high-level features, then pair each developer with a stakeholder or end user and invite them to actually use the product, focused on the work completed this Sprint.

Show and Play generates a much deeper level of feedback, and there's nothing like watching someone else use your application to see exactly where they get confused. It's a trick borrowed from usability testing, and it beats a monologue every time.

A good Sprint Review gets features accepted and deployed. A great one engages the attendees and creates productive discussion about product direction.

What's the last Sprint Review you were in that people actually enjoyed?

#### Option B — the ambush traces back to Refinement
The worst Sprint Reviews aren't boring, they're ambushes. A feature gets demoed, and only then does someone from Marketing or Support say "we can't ship that." Cue the frustrated "why didn't you tell us this before we wasted the team's effort?" and the equally frustrated "I tried to warn you weeks ago, but you didn't listen."

I watched exactly that happen. Two finished features got torn apart late in a Review over fraud risks that Marketing believed they'd flagged earlier. The team had built the wrong thing, nobody caught it until the demo, and morale took the hit.

Here's the thing: a Sprint Review is the wrong place to discover that. The fix starts long before the meeting. When the strategic work happens in Product Backlog Refinement, make sure the key stakeholders, the Marketing director, the Support lead, are actually involved. When an item carries real risk or challenge, invite those stakeholders into the Refinement session so they can give input and clarity while it's still cheap to change course.

It helps for the ScrumMaster and Product Owner to commit to a couple of hours a month reviewing the strategy together, specifically hunting for the things that could turn into surprises. Those two habits go a long way toward keeping the Review free of ambushes.

A Sprint Review should be where you confirm you built the right thing, not where you find out you didn't.

When did a Sprint Review surface a problem that should have come up in Refinement?
