1	---
2	name: evergreen-posting
3	description: Compile Mark's selected social drafts into the batch JSON the posting pipeline consumes (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky), validating character limits and URL budgets, threading the link when it won't fit, and marking the source calendars so nothing is promoted twice. Blog/glossary/newsletter prose is authored and selected UPSTREAM as Markdown via the vault linkedin-style draft skill; this skill condenses the selected options to three platforms and writes the JSON, it does not re-draft that prose. Quiz posts are still drafted here from seeds. Use when Mark says "build the batch JSON", "compile the selected drafts", "schedule social media", or asks for the evergreen batch.
4	---
5	
6	# Evergreen Social Media Posting
7	
8	Compile a batch JSON file of three-platform posts (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky) for the posting pipeline, and track what's been promoted so the next batch picks unused material. This skill owns the **machine layer**: the JSON schema, character-limit and URL-budget validation, threading, UTM handling, and calendar/seed tracking. It is the counterpart to the vault `linkedin-style` draft skill, which owns the **human layer**.
9	
10	**The seam: draft in Obsidian, compile here.** Blog / glossary / newsletter posts are drafted as LinkedIn-shaped Markdown and *selected by Mark* in Obsidian via `linkedin-style` draft mode (vault `APR/Efforts/Social Media/*-drafts.md`). This skill takes the selected options, condenses each to the three platforms, threads the link where it won't fit, validates, and writes the JSON. It does **not** re-draft that prose - reuse Mark's chosen sentences and only tighten for length. The one exception is **AI Failure Modes quiz posts**, still drafted here from seeds (formulaic and low-judgement). Mark reviews the Markdown, never the JSON.
11	
12	> **Read [`_social-posting-conventions.md`](../_social-posting-conventions.md) first.** It is the single source of truth for character limits, threading, the hashtag list, URL handling, and style. This skill only adds evergreen-specific guidance on top.
13	
14	## Output file
15	
16	**Location:** `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/{name}.json`
17	
18	Use a short descriptive name (`next-few-days.json`, `week-of-2026-06-15.json`). Mark says when to overwrite vs. add — default to overwriting `next-few-days.json` because the posting workflow drains and refills it.
19	
20	**Structure:** A flat array. Each entry is one "set" (one piece of content posted across three platforms). The pipeline picks them up in order.
21	
22	```json
23	[
24	  {
25	    "linkedin": "Body text. No URL inline.\n\n#Hashtag1 #Hashtag2",
26	    "mastodon": "Shorter version. No URL inline.\n\n#Hashtag1",
27	    "bluesky": "Shortest version. No URL inline.",
28	    "url": "https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/some-post/",
29	    "image": ""
30	  },
31	  {
32	    "linkedin": "Body text.\n\n#Hashtag1 #Hashtag2",
33	    "mastodon": "Shorter version.\n\n#Hashtag1",
34	    "bluesky": [
35	      "Full message, no link, up to 290 chars. #Hashtag1 #Hashtag2",
36	      "Full post:"
37	    ],
38	    "url": "https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/some-post/",
39	    "image": ""
40	  },
41	  {
42	    "linkedin": "A quiz post drawn from a seed block.\n\n#Hashtag1 #Hashtag2",
43	    "mastodon": "Shorter version.\n\n#Hashtag1",
44	    "bluesky": "Shortest version.",
45	    "url": "https://agilepainrelief.com/quiz/ai-failure-modes/",
46	    "seed": "Senior devs felt 20% faster using AI on familiar codebases.",
47	    "image": ""
48	  }
49	]
50	```
51	
52	### Field rules
53	
54	- **linkedin**: always a single string.
55	- **mastodon / bluesky**: a single string (one post) **or an array of strings** (a thread: `[0]` is the root, the rest become replies). Use the array form when content + link won't fit in one post — see "Threading" below.
56	- **All bodies**: post body only, ending with hashtags. **No URLs inline.** The posting pipeline reads `url` and places the link in each platform's body (LinkedIn included — there is no first comment; on a threaded platform it goes in the **last** part). Putting a URL in a body *and* setting `url` is a hard pre-flight error.
57	- **url**: canonical post URL, no query string. The pipeline appends per-platform UTM (`?utm_source=linkedin&utm_campaign=archive-reshare` etc.) — do not pre-fill UTM params.
58	- **seed**: quiz entries only. An exact substring of the seed block this post came from, used by the pipeline to mark that block `[POSTED ...]` once Buffer accepts the post. Blog/glossary entries are matched by `url` and need no `seed`. See "Tracking what's been used".
59	- **image**: a cover-image URL, or `""` for no image. **The batch pipeline does not scrape `og:image`** — `resolveCoverImage` in `batchPost.ts` uses this field and nothing else, so `""` means the post goes out with no image attached. (The older single-post path, `npm run post`, does auto-fetch og:image. The batch path never has.) Default to `""` unless Mark asks for images; see below before turning them on.
60	
61	  If you do set it: **every entry in a batch needs a distinct image URL.** Auto-fetch was dropped from the batch path precisely because Buffer's duplicate detection matches shared image assets across posts pointing at the same source page, and evergreen reshares the same pages repeatedly. Reusing one URL across entries re-creates that collision and Buffer skips the post. Also note that attaching an image changes the post's shape: LinkedIn replaces its own link-preview card with the image and the URL falls back to plain body text, and Mastodon/Bluesky become image posts rather than link unfurls. Don't try to predict Astro-hashed image paths — take the URL from the rendered page or ask Mark.
62	
63	### Character limits (hard)
64	
65	The limits table lives in [`_social-posting-conventions.md`](../_social-posting-conventions.md) and the enforcement lives in `npm run validate`. Neither is restated here.
66	
67	The one thing worth carrying while you draft: **the `url` is appended to each platform's last part and counts against it.** On Bluesky that costs roughly 100-130 characters, so a single-part Bluesky body has to land near **150** — or thread it, and only the short final part pays. LinkedIn and Mastodon have room to spare.
68	
69	Always validate after editing, from the Astro repo root:
70	
71	```bash
72	npm run validate -- --file analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/FILE.json
73	```
74	
75	This runs **the pipeline's own pre-flight** (`preflight` in `batchPost.ts`) — the exact check `npm run batch` runs before it will schedule anything, with no token and no network calls. Do not hand-write a character-counting script: there is one implementation of these rules and this is it. If the command passes, the batch will pass.
76	
77	`LI=` / `MS=` / `BS=` report the **worst** part on that platform (so a threaded entry passes only when every part fits), measured after the `url` and its per-platform UTM have been appended. It also catches inline URLs, blank thread parts, and malformed entries.
78	
79	### Threading (link in a reply)
80	
81	When a Bluesky (or Mastodon) post won't fit content + link, **thread it**: the root post carries the full message with no link, and the link rides in a short reply. Wired end-to-end — set that platform's field to an array of strings:
82	
83	```json
84	"bluesky": [
85	  "The full message, hashtags and all. Up to 290 chars on its own.",
86	  "Full post:"
87	]
88	```
89	
90	The pipeline appends `url` (with UTM) to the **last** part only, so the root keeps its whole 290-char budget for the message and only the reply pays the ~100-130 chars the link costs. Each part is validated against the full per-platform limit independently.
91	
92	Rules of thumb:
93	
94	- **Prefer a single post.** Thread only when condensing to fit would gut the message.
95	- **Bluesky 2-3 parts max, Mastodon 1-2 preferred / 3 max** (per [`_social-posting-conventions.md`](../_social-posting-conventions.md)).
96	- **Hashtags go on the root** when the reply is just a link, so the message that gets boosted carries them.
97	- Keep the link part short and functional ("Full post:", "Read it here:"). It is a link carrier, not a second beat.
98	- The reply must be non-empty; blank parts fail pre-flight.
99	
100	## Content selection
101	
102	**Blog / glossary / newsletter items are selected upstream** in the `-drafts` Markdown (via `linkedin-style`); by the time this skill runs, Mark has already picked the items and the option per item. This skill's selection job is limited to (a) confirming those selected items and their order and (b) picking unused **quiz** seeds. The sources below remain the source of truth for queue state and tracking.
103	
104	### Sources
105	
106	- **Quiz hooks** — `social-media/planning/AI Failure Modes Quiz Generated Posts.md`. Each block (separated by `-`) is one promo angle. Skip blocks marked `[POSTED YYYY-MM-DD]`.
107	- **Blog posts and glossary entries** — `social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md`. The "Posting Queue" section is the source of truth. Skip items marked `[x]`. TIER 1 (GenAI / supports webinar) first, then TIER 2 (proven traffic drivers), then TIER 3.
108	- **Past promo language** — `analytics/history.json` (recent), `analytics/history-archive.json`, `analytics/old_history.json`. Grep for the slug to find prior posts. **If a piece has been promoted before, mirror the prior style** — the angle, the hook, the hashtags. Don't reinvent.
109	
110	### Default cadence
111	
112	The scheduler posts **2 slots per weekday** (10:00 and 13:30 ET). That number is defined in `social-media-posting/buffer-post/slotPlan.mjs` and is the authority — don't restate a different figure here. The honest mix at 2 slots is **1 quiz + 1 blog/glossary**, so N days = N×2 sets. 4 days = 8 sets (4 quiz + 4 blog/glossary). Confirm if unclear.
113	
114	Writing more sets than there are slots doesn't fail; the extras simply spill into the following week's slots, which is rarely what Mark means by "4 days of content".
115	
116	Interleave so a single day's posts don't all hit the same theme. Each day's blog/glossary should be a different category from the quiz hook themes.
117	
118	### When the user says "non-AI" or "scrum staple"
119	
120	Reach into TIER 2 (Proven Traffic Drivers) and TIER 3 (Scrum & Leadership). Spotify Model, Daily Scrum, Sprint Backlog, Sprint Goals, Team Size — all reliable. The audience wants both AI skepticism and Scrum staples; rotate.
121	
122	## Writing the posts
123	
124	For blog / glossary / newsletter, **condense the selected Markdown option** into each platform: reuse Mark's chosen sentences and tighten for length, don't re-draft. For quiz posts, draft from the seed. Either way, the per-platform shaping below applies.
125	
126	### LinkedIn
127	
128	- **Long form is fine** (up to ~1500 chars typically). Mark explicitly said LinkedIn for the quiz can be longer than Mastodon.
129	- Lead with the data point or the provocative claim. Never lead with "check out my blog."
130	- Hook → evidence → so-what → CTA → hashtags. CTA last.
131	- Skeptical AI takes outperform hype.
132	
133	### Mastodon
134	
135	- Tighter than LinkedIn but keep the data hook; same CTA structure, shorter.
136	- Single post is almost always fine (the URL counts as a fixed 23 here). Thread only if it still won't fit.
137	
138	### Bluesky
139	
140	- Tightest. The link counts at **full length** (~100-150 chars), so a single-part body has to land around 150-160.
141	- When the message won't survive that squeeze, **thread it** (message in part 1, link in part 2 - see "Threading") rather than gutting it.
142	- The data hook still leads, CTA still closes. **Verify char count** - Bluesky rejects over-limit.
143	
144	### Hashtag set
145	
146	Per [`_social-posting-conventions.md`](../_social-posting-conventions.md): always `#AIinSoftwareDevelopment`; add topic tags from the canonical list (`#Agile` `#Scrum` `#ScrumMaster` `#ProductOwner` `#TechnicalDebt` `#TeamWork` `#Leadership`) when the post matches. LinkedIn 2-4 tags, Mastodon 2-3, Bluesky 2.
147	
148	## LinkedIn caveat on AI-skeptical posts
149	
150	LinkedIn's audience reads AI-skeptical posts as "Mark is anti-AI". He isn't. Every LinkedIn post that critiques AI (data point about failure rates, quality problems, security defects, hallucinations, deskilling, etc.) needs a one-line caveat to position the critique correctly: the goal is *using AI well*, and studying failure modes is the prerequisite for that.
151	
152	**Apply when:** the LinkedIn body argues that AI is breaking, harming, or under-delivering on something. If the post is genuinely neutral or non-AI (e.g., the Spotify Model, Feature Factory without AI angle, Daily Scrum), skip the caveat.
153	
154	**Placement:** between the last analysis paragraph and the CTA (or directly before the hashtags on posts with no separate CTA line). One short sentence, two at most.
155	
156	**Vary the wording** across posts in the same batch — the audience is the same person on multiple days, and a repeated stock phrase reads as a disclaimer they can tune out. Working variants:
157	
158	- "Not anti-AI. We study the failure modes so we can avoid the traps. Without that, we're flying blind."
159	- "Studying where AI breaks isn't anti-AI. It's the precondition for using it well."
160	- "I use these tools too. Knowing the failure modes is how we use them well."
161	- "I'm not against AI. Studying the failure modes helps avoid key mistakes."
162	- "Not anti-AI. The fastest path to using these tools well is knowing where they break."
163	- "I'm not anti-tool. Understanding the failure modes is the prerequisite for using them without making larger mistakes."
164	- "I'm not anti-AI. The point is knowing the trade-offs before they bite."
165	- "Studying failure modes is how we get to using AI well. The alternative is shipping blind."
166	
167	**LinkedIn only by default.** Mastodon and Bluesky audiences read these critiques as obviously pro-skeptical and don't need the disclaimer. Add to Mastodon if char budget allows and the post is unusually strong; skip on Bluesky (no room).
168	
169	**Don't:**
170	- Open with the caveat. The data hook still leads.
171	- Use the same wording twice in one batch.
172	- Add the caveat to non-AI posts (it reads as defensive).
173	- Stretch the caveat beyond two short sentences. It's a frame, not an argument.
174	
175	## AI Failure Modes quiz CTAs — explicit subject required
176	
177	When the post links to `https://agilepainrelief.com/quiz/ai-failure-modes/`, the CTA must:
178	
179	1. **Name the subject explicitly** — the phrase `AI Failure Modes in Development Teams` (or a close variant). Generic CTAs like "test your knowledge of how AI fails" don't tell the reader what they're being invited to.
180	2. **Frame as a knowledge test, not a learning resource.** Challenge the reader's understanding, don't promise to teach them.
181	3. **Vary the wording** across posts in the same batch so a reader scrolling several in a week doesn't see the same line.
182	
183	Working variants — use a different one per post:
184	
185	- "Test your knowledge of AI Failure Modes in Development Teams."
186	- "How well do you know the AI Failure Modes hitting Development Teams? Test yourself."
187	- "Think you can spot the AI Failure Modes in Development Teams? Test yourself."
188	- "Think you know the AI Failure Modes in Development Teams? Test yourself."
189	- "How many AI Failure Modes in Development Teams can you actually identify? Test yourself."
190	- "How many AI Failure Modes can you spot in Development Teams?"
191	
192	Avoid:
193	
194	- "Twelve questions on how GenAI fails. Three minutes." — sounds like a lesson; subject is vague.
195	- "Test your knowledge of how AI fails." — test framing is there but subject is vague.
196	- "Learn about how AI is failing." — passive consumption.
197	
198	LinkedIn can include the descriptor ("Twelve questions, three minutes, real research with citations") **after** the named challenge, never as a replacement for it.
199	
200	## Style and formatting
201	
202	- **No em dashes.** Use a colon, comma, or restructure. Per project CLAUDE.md.
203	- **No non-breaking spaces (U+00A0).** ASCII spaces only.
204	- **Straight quotes and apostrophes** are fine in the JSON values — these are social posts, not website content. Past `history.json` entries mix both; straight is simpler.
205	- **Curly arrow** `→` is fine if you use it, but ASCII `->` reads cleaner in mixed environments.
206	- Never invent stats. Every number in a quiz post should map to one of the hooks in `AI Failure Modes Quiz Generated Posts.md` or to the blog post being promoted.
207	
208	## Tracking what's been used
209	
210	**The pipeline does this. Do not hand-edit the calendar or the seed file.**
211	
212	When `npm run batch` gets a post accepted by Buffer, it stamps the source itself, using the slot's ET date:
213	
214	- **Calendar** (`complete-social-media-calendar.md`) — matched by the entry's `url`. `- [ ] Title https://…/blog/slug/` becomes `- [x] Title (YYYY-MM-DD) https://…/blog/slug/`. A reshare appends another date: `(2026-05-29, 2026-07-27)`. The legacy `, 3x` shorthand already in the file is preserved.
215	- **Quiz seeds** (`AI Failure Modes Quiz Generated Posts.md`) — matched by the entry's **`seed`** field. The block gets `[POSTED YYYY-MM-DD]` prepended, and a re-post appends a date to the existing marker.
216	
217	Marking runs only on a real (non-`--dry-run`) schedule, is idempotent, and refuses to guess: an unmatched or ambiguous `seed`/`url` is reported in the run summary and nothing is edited. Because it happens at the moment Buffer accepts the post, there is no pre-marking to avoid and nothing to un-mark — if Mark later deletes a post from Buffer, un-check that one line by hand.
218	
219	**Your job is to set `seed` correctly on every quiz entry.** Copy an exact, distinctive substring of the seed block (the first sentence is ideal). It must match one block and only one — a near-miss is reported rather than guessed at, which leaves the seed unmarked and liable to be reused next batch.
220	
221	## Workflow
222	
223	1. **Confirm scope.** N days × 2 slots/day, default 1 quiz : 1 blog. Ask if anything else is wanted (different ratio, non-AI emphasis, specific posts to prioritise).
224	2. **Pick the items.** Open `complete-social-media-calendar.md`, list candidate `[ ]` entries from TIER 1 / 2 / 3. Open the quiz seed file, list unused blocks. Aim for variety.
225	3. **Check past promo language.** For each blog/glossary, grep `analytics/*.json` for the slug. If there's prior promo copy, anchor your draft to that style.
226	4. **Draft the three platforms per set.** LinkedIn first (longest), then Mastodon (compress), then Bluesky (compress harder).
227	5. **Set `seed`** on every quiz entry (exact substring of its seed block) and `url` on every entry.
228	6. **Write the file** to `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/{name}.json`.
229	7. **Validate.** `npm run validate -- --file analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/{name}.json`. Fix anything it flags and re-run until clean. This covers character counts and inline URLs; there is nothing to check by hand.
230	
231	Marking the calendar and the seed file is not a step — `npm run batch` does it when Buffer accepts each post.
232	
233	## Common mistakes to avoid
234	
235	- **URLs inline in post text.** They belong in the `url` field only. The pipeline appends URLs per platform; inline URLs end up duplicated or stranded.
236	- **Generic quiz CTAs.** "Test your knowledge of how AI fails" is too vague. Name the subject: AI Failure Modes in Development Teams.
237	- **UTM params on the `url` value.** The pipeline adds them per platform. Pre-filling locks the URL to one platform.
238	- **Em dashes.** Mark doesn't use them. Colon, comma, or restructure.
239	- **Hand-editing the calendar or seed file.** The pipeline marks both. Editing them yourself causes double-marking.
240	- **A vague or missing `seed` on a quiz entry.** Too short and it matches several blocks; slightly reworded and it matches none. Either way the seed goes unmarked and gets reused.
241	- **Hand-rolling a character-count script.** `npm run validate` runs the pipeline's own pre-flight. A second implementation is how the rules drift apart.
242	- **Trying to predict cover-image URLs.** Astro hashes them at build. Use `image: ""` (no image) unless you have a real URL — the batch pipeline does not scrape og:image, so a guessed path is a broken asset, not a fallback.
243	- **Reusing one image URL across a batch.** Buffer dedups on shared image assets and skips the duplicates. Distinct image per entry, or `""`.
244	- **Lifting prior post language verbatim across all platforms.** Mirror the angle and hashtags, but write fresh sentences per platform — recycled copy reads as recycled.
245	- **Saying "twelve questions, three minutes" before naming the subject.** Order matters: subject + challenge first, descriptor second.
246	
247	## Related skills and files
248	
249	- `social-media-adapt` — for adapting a single LinkedIn post into Mastodon + Bluesky threaded JSON (different format from this skill).

---
name: evergreen-posting
description: Compile Mark's selected social drafts into the batch JSON the posting pipeline consumes (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky), validating character limits and URL budgets, threading the link when it won't fit, and marking the source calendars so nothing is promoted twice. Blog/glossary/newsletter prose is authored and selected UPSTREAM as Markdown via the vault linkedin-style draft skill; this skill condenses the selected options to three platforms and writes the JSON, it does not re-draft that prose. Quiz posts are still drafted here from seeds. Use when Mark says "build the batch JSON", "compile the selected drafts", "schedule social media", or asks for the evergreen batch.
---

# Evergreen Social Media Posting

Compile a batch JSON file of three-platform posts (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky) for the posting pipeline, and track what's been promoted so the next batch picks unused material. This skill owns the **machine layer**: the JSON schema, character-limit and URL-budget validation, threading, UTM handling, and calendar/seed tracking. It is the counterpart to the vault `linkedin-style` draft skill, which owns the **human layer**.

**The seam: draft in Obsidian, compile here.** Blog / glossary / newsletter posts are drafted as LinkedIn-shaped Markdown and *selected by Mark* in Obsidian via `linkedin-style` draft mode (vault `APR/Efforts/Social Media/*-drafts.md`). This skill takes the selected options, condenses each to the three platforms, threads the link where it won't fit, validates, and writes the JSON. It does **not** re-draft that prose - reuse Mark's chosen sentences and only tighten for length. The one exception is **AI Failure Modes quiz posts**, still drafted here from seeds (formulaic and low-judgement). Mark reviews the Markdown, never the JSON.

> **Read [`_social-posting-conventions.md`](../_social-posting-conventions.md) first.** It is the single source of truth for character limits, threading, the hashtag list, URL handling, and style. This skill only adds evergreen-specific guidance on top.

## Output file

**Location:** `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/{name}.json`

Use a short descriptive name (`next-few-days.json`, `week-of-2026-06-15.json`). Mark says when to overwrite vs. add — default to overwriting `next-few-days.json` because the posting workflow drains and refills it.

**Structure:** A flat array. Each entry is one "set" (one piece of content posted across three platforms). The pipeline picks them up in order.

```json
[
  {
    "linkedin": "Body text. No URL inline.\n\n#Hashtag1 #Hashtag2",
    "mastodon": "Shorter version. No URL inline.\n\n#Hashtag1",
    "bluesky": "Shortest version. No URL inline.",
    "url": "https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/some-post/",
    "image": ""
  },
  {
    "linkedin": "Body text.\n\n#Hashtag1 #Hashtag2",
    "mastodon": "Shorter version.\n\n#Hashtag1",
    "bluesky": [
      "Full message, no link, up to 290 chars. #Hashtag1 #Hashtag2",
      "Full post:"
    ],
    "url": "https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/some-post/",
    "image": ""
  },
  {
    "linkedin": "A quiz post drawn from a seed block.\n\n#Hashtag1 #Hashtag2",
    "mastodon": "Shorter version.\n\n#Hashtag1",
    "bluesky": "Shortest version.",
    "url": "https://agilepainrelief.com/quiz/ai-failure-modes/",
    "seed": "Senior devs felt 20% faster using AI on familiar codebases.",
    "image": ""
  }
]
```

### Field rules

- **linkedin**: always a single string.
- **mastodon / bluesky**: a single string (one post) **or an array of strings** (a thread: `[0]` is the root, the rest become replies). Use the array form when content + link won't fit in one post — see "Threading" below.
- **All bodies**: post body only, ending with hashtags. **No URLs inline.** The posting pipeline reads `url` and places the link in each platform's body (LinkedIn included — there is no first comment; on a threaded platform it goes in the **last** part). Putting a URL in a body *and* setting `url` is a hard pre-flight error.
- **url**: canonical post URL, no query string. The pipeline appends per-platform UTM (`?utm_source=linkedin&utm_campaign=archive-reshare` etc.) — do not pre-fill UTM params.
- **seed**: quiz entries only. An exact substring of the seed block this post came from, used by the pipeline to mark that block `[POSTED ...]` once Buffer accepts the post. Blog/glossary entries are matched by `url` and need no `seed`. See "Tracking what's been used".
- **image**: a cover-image URL, or `""` for no image. **The batch pipeline does not scrape `og:image`** — `resolveCoverImage` in `batchPost.ts` uses this field and nothing else, so `""` means the post goes out with no image attached. (The older single-post path, `npm run post`, does auto-fetch og:image. The batch path never has.) Default to `""` unless Mark asks for images; see below before turning them on.

  If you do set it: **every entry in a batch needs a distinct image URL.** Auto-fetch was dropped from the batch path precisely because Buffer's duplicate detection matches shared image assets across posts pointing at the same source page, and evergreen reshares the same pages repeatedly. Reusing one URL across entries re-creates that collision and Buffer skips the post. Also note that attaching an image changes the post's shape: LinkedIn replaces its own link-preview card with the image and the URL falls back to plain body text, and Mastodon/Bluesky become image posts rather than link unfurls. Don't try to predict Astro-hashed image paths — take the URL from the rendered page or ask Mark.

### Character limits (hard)

The limits table lives in [`_social-posting-conventions.md`](../_social-posting-conventions.md) and the enforcement lives in `npm run validate`. Neither is restated here.

The one thing worth carrying while you draft: **the `url` is appended to each platform's last part and counts against it.** On Bluesky that costs roughly 100-130 characters, so a single-part Bluesky body has to land near **150** — or thread it, and only the short final part pays. LinkedIn and Mastodon have room to spare.

Always validate after editing, from the Astro repo root:

```bash
npm run validate -- --file analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/FILE.json
```

This runs **the pipeline's own pre-flight** (`preflight` in `batchPost.ts`) — the exact check `npm run batch` runs before it will schedule anything, with no token and no network calls. Do not hand-write a character-counting script: there is one implementation of these rules and this is it. If the command passes, the batch will pass.

`LI=` / `MS=` / `BS=` report the **worst** part on that platform (so a threaded entry passes only when every part fits), measured after the `url` and its per-platform UTM have been appended. It also catches inline URLs, blank thread parts, and malformed entries.

### Threading (link in a reply)

When a Bluesky (or Mastodon) post won't fit content + link, **thread it**: the root post carries the full message with no link, and the link rides in a short reply. Wired end-to-end — set that platform's field to an array of strings:

```json
"bluesky": [
  "The full message, hashtags and all. Up to 290 chars on its own.",
  "Full post:"
]
```

The pipeline appends `url` (with UTM) to the **last** part only, so the root keeps its whole 290-char budget for the message and only the reply pays the ~100-130 chars the link costs. Each part is validated against the full per-platform limit independently.

Rules of thumb:

- **Prefer a single post.** Thread only when condensing to fit would gut the message.
- **Bluesky 2-3 parts max, Mastodon 1-2 preferred / 3 max** (per [`_social-posting-conventions.md`](../_social-posting-conventions.md)).
- **Hashtags go on the root** when the reply is just a link, so the message that gets boosted carries them.
- Keep the link part short and functional ("Full post:", "Read it here:"). It is a link carrier, not a second beat.
- The reply must be non-empty; blank parts fail pre-flight.

## Content selection

**Blog / glossary / newsletter items are selected upstream** in the `-drafts` Markdown (via `linkedin-style`); by the time this skill runs, Mark has already picked the items and the option per item. This skill's selection job is limited to (a) confirming those selected items and their order and (b) picking unused **quiz** seeds. The sources below remain the source of truth for queue state and tracking.

### Sources

- **Quiz hooks** — `social-media/planning/AI Failure Modes Quiz Generated Posts.md`. Each block (separated by `-`) is one promo angle. Skip blocks marked `[POSTED YYYY-MM-DD]`.
- **Blog posts and glossary entries** — `social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md`. The "Posting Queue" section is the source of truth. Skip items marked `[x]`. TIER 1 (GenAI / supports webinar) first, then TIER 2 (proven traffic drivers), then TIER 3.
- **Past promo language** — `analytics/history.json` (recent), `analytics/history-archive.json`, `analytics/old_history.json`. Grep for the slug to find prior posts. **If a piece has been promoted before, mirror the prior style** — the angle, the hook, the hashtags. Don't reinvent.

### Default cadence

The scheduler posts **2 slots per weekday** (10:00 and 13:30 ET). That number is defined in `social-media-posting/buffer-post/slotPlan.mjs` and is the authority — don't restate a different figure here. The honest mix at 2 slots is **1 quiz + 1 blog/glossary**, so N days = N×2 sets. 4 days = 8 sets (4 quiz + 4 blog/glossary). Confirm if unclear.

Writing more sets than there are slots doesn't fail; the extras simply spill into the following week's slots, which is rarely what Mark means by "4 days of content".

Interleave so a single day's posts don't all hit the same theme. Each day's blog/glossary should be a different category from the quiz hook themes.

### When the user says "non-AI" or "scrum staple"

Reach into TIER 2 (Proven Traffic Drivers) and TIER 3 (Scrum & Leadership). Spotify Model, Daily Scrum, Sprint Backlog, Sprint Goals, Team Size — all reliable. The audience wants both AI skepticism and Scrum staples; rotate.

## Writing the posts

For blog / glossary / newsletter, **condense the selected Markdown option** into each platform: reuse Mark's chosen sentences and tighten for length, don't re-draft. For quiz posts, draft from the seed. Either way, the per-platform shaping below applies.

### LinkedIn

- **Long form is fine** (up to ~1500 chars typically). Mark explicitly said LinkedIn for the quiz can be longer than Mastodon.
- Lead with the data point or the provocative claim. Never lead with "check out my blog."
- Hook → evidence → so-what → CTA → hashtags. CTA last.
- Skeptical AI takes outperform hype.

### Mastodon

- Tighter than LinkedIn but keep the data hook; same CTA structure, shorter.
- Single post is almost always fine (the URL counts as a fixed 23 here). Thread only if it still won't fit.

### Bluesky

- Tightest. The link counts at **full length** (~100-150 chars), so a single-part body has to land around 150-160.
- When the message won't survive that squeeze, **thread it** (message in part 1, link in part 2 - see "Threading") rather than gutting it.
- The data hook still leads, CTA still closes. **Verify char count** - Bluesky rejects over-limit.

### Hashtag set

Per [`_social-posting-conventions.md`](../_social-posting-conventions.md): always `#AIinSoftwareDevelopment`; add topic tags from the canonical list (`#Agile` `#Scrum` `#ScrumMaster` `#ProductOwner` `#TechnicalDebt` `#TeamWork` `#Leadership`) when the post matches. LinkedIn 2-4 tags, Mastodon 2-3, Bluesky 2.

## LinkedIn caveat on AI-skeptical posts

LinkedIn's audience reads AI-skeptical posts as "Mark is anti-AI". He isn't. Every LinkedIn post that critiques AI (data point about failure rates, quality problems, security defects, hallucinations, deskilling, etc.) needs a one-line caveat to position the critique correctly: the goal is *using AI well*, and studying failure modes is the prerequisite for that.

**Apply when:** the LinkedIn body argues that AI is breaking, harming, or under-delivering on something. If the post is genuinely neutral or non-AI (e.g., the Spotify Model, Feature Factory without AI angle, Daily Scrum), skip the caveat.

**Placement:** between the last analysis paragraph and the CTA (or directly before the hashtags on posts with no separate CTA line). One short sentence, two at most.

**Vary the wording** across posts in the same batch — the audience is the same person on multiple days, and a repeated stock phrase reads as a disclaimer they can tune out. Working variants:

- "Not anti-AI. We study the failure modes so we can avoid the traps. Without that, we're flying blind."
- "Studying where AI breaks isn't anti-AI. It's the precondition for using it well."
- "I use these tools too. Knowing the failure modes is how we use them well."
- "I'm not against AI. Studying the failure modes helps avoid key mistakes."
- "Not anti-AI. The fastest path to using these tools well is knowing where they break."
- "I'm not anti-tool. Understanding the failure modes is the prerequisite for using them without making larger mistakes."
- "I'm not anti-AI. The point is knowing the trade-offs before they bite."
- "Studying failure modes is how we get to using AI well. The alternative is shipping blind."

**LinkedIn only by default.** Mastodon and Bluesky audiences read these critiques as obviously pro-skeptical and don't need the disclaimer. Add to Mastodon if char budget allows and the post is unusually strong; skip on Bluesky (no room).

**Don't:**
- Open with the caveat. The data hook still leads.
- Use the same wording twice in one batch.
- Add the caveat to non-AI posts (it reads as defensive).
- Stretch the caveat beyond two short sentences. It's a frame, not an argument.

## AI Failure Modes quiz CTAs — explicit subject required

When the post links to `https://agilepainrelief.com/quiz/ai-failure-modes/`, the CTA must:

1. **Name the subject explicitly** — the phrase `AI Failure Modes in Development Teams` (or a close variant). Generic CTAs like "test your knowledge of how AI fails" don't tell the reader what they're being invited to.
2. **Frame as a knowledge test, not a learning resource.** Challenge the reader's understanding, don't promise to teach them.
3. **Vary the wording** across posts in the same batch so a reader scrolling several in a week doesn't see the same line.

Working variants — use a different one per post:

- "Test your knowledge of AI Failure Modes in Development Teams."
- "How well do you know the AI Failure Modes hitting Development Teams? Test yourself."
- "Think you can spot the AI Failure Modes in Development Teams? Test yourself."
- "Think you know the AI Failure Modes in Development Teams? Test yourself."
- "How many AI Failure Modes in Development Teams can you actually identify? Test yourself."
- "How many AI Failure Modes can you spot in Development Teams?"

Avoid:

- "Twelve questions on how GenAI fails. Three minutes." — sounds like a lesson; subject is vague.
- "Test your knowledge of how AI fails." — test framing is there but subject is vague.
- "Learn about how AI is failing." — passive consumption.

LinkedIn can include the descriptor ("Twelve questions, three minutes, real research with citations") **after** the named challenge, never as a replacement for it.

## Style and formatting

- **No em dashes.** Use a colon, comma, or restructure. Per project CLAUDE.md.
- **No non-breaking spaces (U+00A0).** ASCII spaces only.
- **Straight quotes and apostrophes** are fine in the JSON values — these are social posts, not website content. Past `history.json` entries mix both; straight is simpler.
- **Curly arrow** `→` is fine if you use it, but ASCII `->` reads cleaner in mixed environments.
- Never invent stats. Every number in a quiz post should map to one of the hooks in `AI Failure Modes Quiz Generated Posts.md` or to the blog post being promoted.

## Tracking what's been used

**The pipeline does this. Do not hand-edit the calendar or the seed file.**

When `npm run batch` gets a post accepted by Buffer, it stamps the source itself, using the slot's ET date:

- **Calendar** (`complete-social-media-calendar.md`) — matched by the entry's `url`. `- [ ] Title https://…/blog/slug/` becomes `- [x] Title (YYYY-MM-DD) https://…/blog/slug/`. A reshare appends another date: `(2026-05-29, 2026-07-27)`. The legacy `, 3x` shorthand already in the file is preserved.
- **Quiz seeds** (`AI Failure Modes Quiz Generated Posts.md`) — matched by the entry's **`seed`** field. The block gets `[POSTED YYYY-MM-DD]` prepended, and a re-post appends a date to the existing marker.

Marking runs only on a real (non-`--dry-run`) schedule, is idempotent, and refuses to guess: an unmatched or ambiguous `seed`/`url` is reported in the run summary and nothing is edited. Because it happens at the moment Buffer accepts the post, there is no pre-marking to avoid and nothing to un-mark — if Mark later deletes a post from Buffer, un-check that one line by hand.

**Your job is to set `seed` correctly on every quiz entry.** Copy an exact, distinctive substring of the seed block (the first sentence is ideal). It must match one block and only one — a near-miss is reported rather than guessed at, which leaves the seed unmarked and liable to be reused next batch.

## Workflow

1. **Confirm scope.** N days × 2 slots/day, default 1 quiz : 1 blog. Ask if anything else is wanted (different ratio, non-AI emphasis, specific posts to prioritise).
2. **Pick the items.** Open `complete-social-media-calendar.md`, list candidate `[ ]` entries from TIER 1 / 2 / 3. Open the quiz seed file, list unused blocks. Aim for variety.
3. **Check past promo language.** For each blog/glossary, grep `analytics/*.json` for the slug. If there's prior promo copy, anchor your draft to that style.
4. **Draft the three platforms per set.** LinkedIn first (longest), then Mastodon (compress), then Bluesky (compress harder).
5. **Set `seed`** on every quiz entry (exact substring of its seed block) and `url` on every entry.
6. **Write the file** to `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/{name}.json`.
7. **Validate.** `npm run validate -- --file analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/{name}.json`. Fix anything it flags and re-run until clean. This covers character counts and inline URLs; there is nothing to check by hand.

Marking the calendar and the seed file is not a step — `npm run batch` does it when Buffer accepts each post.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **URLs inline in post text.** They belong in the `url` field only. The pipeline appends URLs per platform; inline URLs end up duplicated or stranded.
- **Generic quiz CTAs.** "Test your knowledge of how AI fails" is too vague. Name the subject: AI Failure Modes in Development Teams.
- **UTM params on the `url` value.** The pipeline adds them per platform. Pre-filling locks the URL to one platform.
- **Em dashes.** Mark doesn't use them. Colon, comma, or restructure.
- **Hand-editing the calendar or seed file.** The pipeline marks both. Editing them yourself causes double-marking.
- **A vague or missing `seed` on a quiz entry.** Too short and it matches several blocks; slightly reworded and it matches none. Either way the seed goes unmarked and gets reused.
- **Hand-rolling a character-count script.** `npm run validate` runs the pipeline's own pre-flight. A second implementation is how the rules drift apart.
- **Trying to predict cover-image URLs.** Astro hashes them at build. Use `image: ""` (no image) unless you have a real URL — the batch pipeline does not scrape og:image, so a guessed path is a broken asset, not a fallback.
- **Reusing one image URL across a batch.** Buffer dedups on shared image assets and skips the duplicates. Distinct image per entry, or `""`.
- **Lifting prior post language verbatim across all platforms.** Mirror the angle and hashtags, but write fresh sentences per platform — recycled copy reads as recycled.
- **Saying "twelve questions, three minutes" before naming the subject.** Order matters: subject + challenge first, descriptor second.

## Related skills and files

- `social-media-adapt` — for adapting a single LinkedIn post into Mastodon + Bluesky threaded JSON (different format from this skill).
- `social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md` — content queue.
- `social-media/planning/AI Failure Modes Quiz Generated Posts.md` — quiz hook seeds.
- `analytics/history.json` + `history-archive.json` + `old_history.json` — past promo language.
- `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/` — output directory.

## Judgement calls the checker won't make

### Hashtags

`#AIinSoftwareDevelopment` is the house tag. Topic tags when they genuinely fit: `#Agile` `#Scrum` `#ScrumMaster` `#ProductOwner` `#TechnicalDebt` `#TeamWork` `#Leadership`. `#BuildInPublic` and `#ProductCamp` also see regular use.

Counts are **not** enforced, deliberately. Recent practice runs leaner than any written rule (LinkedIn averages under 1 tag, and roughly half of Bluesky posts carry none), and on Bluesky a tag costs characters the message usually needs more. Use them where they earn their place; put them at the end of the final part.

### Emoji

Use them on every platform, lightly.

- **1-2 per post.** An opening emoji to catch the eye; an optional second to mark a structural turn. More reads as cluttered.
- **Never on a vulnerability beat or a serious moment** (a confession, a burnout point): it undercuts the weight.
- **Bluesky:** they cost characters, so only spend them when they earn the space.

### Sourcing

**Never invent stats.** Every number must trace to a real source: a quiz-hook seed, or the post being linked.

### Tone

Mastodon is community-focused and less corporate than LinkedIn; it rewards technical accuracy and cited sources. Bluesky wants brevity and directness. LinkedIn leads with the data point or the provocative claim, never "check out my blog".

## URLs and links

- **The link goes in the post body on every platform, LinkedIn included.** There is no "link in the first comment"; that pattern is retired.
- **`evergreen-posting`:** never inline a URL. Put it in the `url` field and the pipeline places it per platform. **`social-media-adapt`:** the URL goes inline in the body.
- **Never shorten a URL, and never pre-fill UTM.** The pipeline appends `?utm_source=...&utm_campaign=archive-reshare` per platform; pre-filling locks every platform to one source (and is now a hard error).
- **Cover images:** `social-media-adapt` (`npm run post`) auto-fetches `og:image`. The **batch** path does not scrape — it posts whatever is in `image`, and `""` means none. Default to `""`; if you do use images, every entry in the batch needs a **distinct** URL, because Buffer dedups on shared image assets and silently skips the repeat.

    "linkedin": "🛡️ Psychological safety gets misunderstood a lot, and almost always as something it isn't.

The first misread: people treat it as trust. It isn't. We can trust each other and still not be safe. Amy Edmondson's definition is "the belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes." Trust is about the other person. Safety is knowing that if you take a chance or make a mistake, you'll be supported and not punished.

The second: people treat it as the avoidance of conflict, or agreement for the sake of agreement. Also wrong. It's an environment where we can be honest about what we've seen and not be punished for it. If anything, higher safety produces more open disagreement, not less.

The third does real harm: treating safety as a licence to point out everyone else's mistakes. It isn't that either. It's about being able to acknowledge your own mistakes, and what you learned, without repercussions. The moment it becomes a tool for calling other people out, it stops being safety.

Get those three straight and a lot of "we tried psychological safety and it didn't work" stories start to make sense. Usually the team was running one of the counterfeits.

Which do you run into most: safety-as-trust, safety-as-no-conflict, or safety-as-calling-people-out?

    "linkedin": "🧪 I'm seeing more and more products clearly built with the help of GenAI. They're full of features that don't fit together, and some don't solve a real problem.

Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive.

At Product Camp Ottawa I asked a room how many had shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code. A third to a half put their hands up. Then I asked how many of those features were built from a hypothesis tested with real users before production code was written. Only three people, roughly 15% of those who shipped with GenAI.

Here's the mechanism. Before GenAI, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance. With GenAI that doesn't change; we still have more features than we can test. No one would put more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck, yet that's what we do when we generate more code. Classic Theory of Constraints.

Every feature is a hypothesis: if we build this, it will solve a specific problem for a group of users. GenAI speeds up the mechanics of Discovery, running experiments, building prototypes, analyzing data. Speeding up the mechanics is great, but it means we need to spend more time thinking and learning, not less.

The biggest risk is theatre: running the discovery process without learning anything. Ask one question this week, what did we learn that changed our plan? If nothing, it's theatre.

Not anti-AI: the point is knowing the trade-offs before they bite.

-    "linkedin": "🏋️ Here's how I explain Technical Debt to non-technical people. Imagine your developers are in a large gym. Time how long it takes them to run across and back, and repeat until the number is stable. Now scatter a few chairs across the middle at random and ask them to run again. They're slower. Add more chairs. Eventually there are so many they can't walk around them, and they have to crawl to get across the room.

The chairs are the technical debt. The extra time is the interest your team pays on it, every day, on every trip across the room. Nobody chose to make the gym unusable; the chairs just accumulated a few at a time until moving became painful.

There's a new source of chairs worth naming. AI-generated code has become a major new source of technical debt. It's fast and it often runs, which is exactly what makes the chairs easy to add without noticing, until the day the team is crawling.

The point isn't to keep the gym perfectly empty. It's to keep it clear enough that people can still run.

How many chairs has your team quietly added this year, and when will you clear a few?

+    "linkedin": "🛡️ Psychological safety gets misunderstood a lot, and almost always as something it isn't.

The first misread: people treat it as trust. It isn't. We can trust each other and still not be safe. Amy Edmondson's definition is "the belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes." Trust is about the other person. Safety is knowing that if you take a chance or make a mistake, you'll be supported and not punished.

The second: people treat it as the avoidance of conflict, or agreement for the sake of agreement. Also wrong. It's an environment where we can be honest about what we've seen and not be punished for it. If anything, higher safety produces more open disagreement, not less.

The third does real harm: treating safety as a licence to point out everyone else's mistakes. It isn't that either. It's about being able to acknowledge your own mistakes, and what you learned, without repercussions. The moment it becomes a tool for calling other people out, it stops being safety.

Get those three straight and a lot of "we tried psychological safety and it didn't work" stories start to make sense. Usually the team was running one of the counterfeits.

Which do you run into most: safety-as-trust, safety-as-no-conflict, or safety-as-calling-people-out?

-    "linkedin": "🗂️ Product Backlog Refinement has a quiet failure mode: everyone nods that they understand the item, and yet each person is holding a different picture in their head. It looks like agreement. It isn't. The gap only surfaces mid-Sprint, when the work turns out to mean three different things to three different people.

A couple of anti-patterns feed that. Jumping to the solution, where the team designs the "how" before anyone has agreed on the "why" and the "what." And forgetting the user and the why altogether, treating refinement as a queue of tickets to process rather than problems to solve for real people. The people and their needs should be front and centre.

When you're stuck and don't have agreement about a feature, write an example. In adult life, when two people get stuck in a conversation, we reach for an example to break the logjam, then somehow forget to do it as a team. It can be a pencil sketch of the interface, or a quick happy path showing how someone would actually use the feature. My rule is just enough detail to get everyone on the same page, and I delay the detailed acceptance criteria until after Sprint Planning.

The goal isn't a tidy backlog. It's a team that leaves the conversation holding the same picture.

Which item on your board does everyone "understand" in a slightly different way?

-    "linkedin": "🧩 We all want to believe that going from 2 people to 4 doubles what a team gets done. We know intuitively it doesn't, and Amdahl's Law explains why: some work happens in parallel, but some has to happen one step at a time, and that serial part sets a ceiling no amount of extra people can lift. Even when 80% of the work parallelises, it takes 3 people to double one person's output, and 16 to quadruple it.

Speed doesn't come from throwing more people at the job and making bigger teams. It comes from building a high-performing team that's the right size for communication and quality. With teams of 9 or larger, I recommend splitting into two, because separate teams of 4 and 5 reliably get more done than the original large one.

+    "linkedin": "📏 Most arguments about bonuses skip the real problem, which isn't the money, it's the target.

Goodhart's Law puts it cleanly: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. In software we see it constantly. Tie a developer's bonus to personal velocity and velocity stops telling you anything about throughput. Tie a tester's to defects found and "quality" quietly detaches from the number. The moment people are paid to move a metric, they move the metric, not the thing you actually cared about.

What surprised me digging into the research was how narrow it is. With a couple of exceptions, researchers assumed the people designing the incentive had chosen a good target. But from the Agile world we know most targets are either outright dangerous, like velocity as a measure of throughput, or far enough from the truth that focusing on them causes harm, like defects as a proxy for quality.

The deeper fix is to stop confusing output with outcome. More features delivered is output. Features with good quality that actually solved the customer's problem is outcome. A bonus might get you more of the target, but if the target was poorly chosen, more of it doesn't give you more of what you wanted.

Before you attach a reward to a number, ask the harder question: if people optimise this number and nothing else, do we still get what we want?

What's a metric your organization rewards that stopped measuring the thing it was meant to?
